title: Grade 10 daily reading
overview: A year of nightly independent reading across fourteen British and American writers from 1847 to 1924: sustained episodes from five novels and a long story (Brontë, Eliot, Chopin, Wharton, Crane, Cather, Gilman), two documentary memoirs (Washington, Addams), and complete poems by Edward Thomas, Robert Browning, Elizabeth Barrett Browning, Amy Lowell and Edna St. Vincent Millay. Each week alternates a run of narrative or memoir with a week of five poets, so long works return in instalments while poetry keeps close rereading in practice. Discussion moves from what a narrator or speaker observes toward judgments about evidence, institutions, memory, and endings that refuse a single meaning. Period language and difficult subjects, including slavery, child cruelty, war, and suicide, are presented as written, with brief context. The 25–30 minute plans include deliberate rereading and discussion; they are teaching estimates, not measured reading levels or completion quotas.

progression.focus: Separating what a voice observes from what it concludes
progression.rationale: Jane Eyre’s Gateshead and Lowood chapters and Washington’s childhood and Hampton years make unequal power concrete in scenes a reader can reconstruct. The first poetry weeks practice tracking a speaker’s shifts in image, pronoun and tone through short complete poems.

progression.focus: Testing institutions against their stated purposes
progression.rationale: Lowood’s epidemic and Jane’s departure, Washington’s founding of Tuskegee and his Atlanta address, and Addams’s first Hull-House years ask readers to compare professed aims with practice and to weigh a public argument’s audience. Poems add speakers whose confidence needs interrogation.

Silas Marner’s exclusion, robbery and the Rainbow inn’s debate, together with Addams’s accounts of labor and child-labor reform, require readers to evaluate testimony, rumor and generalization. The Awakening opens with a narrator who observes Edna from outside before moving inside her perception.

Later Silas Marner chapters follow responsibility deferred and accepted; The Awakening follows Edna’s widening refusals, Arobin’s kiss and her final swim, an ending readers must interpret from images rather than statement. Ethan Frome begins with a narrator assembling a story from gaps. Poems ask readers to hold two readings of a line at once.

My Ántonia’s framed recollection, including the wolves story heard at third hand, and Ethan Frome’s retold winter, through the sled run and the Epilogue that answers the Prologue’s questions, make the act of narration visible, so readers distinguish an account’s emotional force from its evidence. The Red Badge of Courage begins by testing heroic expectation against rumor and fear.

progression.focus: Independent interpretation of unreliable and uncertain voices
progression.rationale: Crane’s self-justifying soldier, Cather’s chapters on Mr. Shimerda’s death and burial and her later town chapters, and the complete Yellow Wall Paper, read over three nights, demand that readers separate a narrator’s claims from what the text lets them infer. The final poetry weeks ask for independent, evidence-based disagreement about complete poems.

days.title: Jane Eyre excerpt: A refuge turned into a weapon
days.challenge: Track how the adult narrator gives language to a child’s unequal treatment.
days.focus: Books function both as imaginative shelter and as instruments of household power.
days.context: Ten-year-old Jane lives with her aunt Mrs. Reed and her cousins after her parents’ deaths. She narrates this childhood retrospectively.
days.contentNote: Contains child abuse, physical injury, demeaning class language, and comparisons to slavery and imperial cruelty.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, complete chapter; from “There was no possibility of taking a walk that day. We had been wandering, indeed, in” through “ed-room, and lock her in there.” Four hands were immediately laid upon me, and I was borne upstairs.”.

questions.prompt: How does the window-seat protect Jane without fully separating her from the world outside?
facilitatorNotes: Notice the curtain’s privacy and the glass’s incomplete separation. Her shelter remains vulnerable to discovery; the natural desolation also enters her imaginative reading.
evidence: I was shrined in double retirement.
protecting, but not separating me from the drear November day.

questions.prompt: What changes when the book passes from Jane’s knee into John’s hands?
facilitatorNotes: Jane uses the book to imagine distant places; John asserts property rights, then throws it. Ask how ownership becomes an excuse to control another person’s body and access to reading.
evidence: With Bewick on my knee, I was then happy: happy at least in my way.
the volume was flung, it hit me

questions.prompt: Why do Jane’s comparisons to Roman emperors matter more than a simple insult would?
facilitatorNotes: Her reading supplies a framework for naming tyranny that the household denies. Her historical analogy can be persuasive while still showing a child’s heightened anger; discuss both effects.
evidence: You are like a murderer—you are like a slave-driver—you are like the Roman emperors!
Also I had drawn parallels in silence

days.title: Jane Eyre excerpt: The room and the rules
days.challenge: Separate the servants’ moral judgments from the visual and spatial evidence of confinement.
days.focus: The red-room turns wealth, obligation, and memory into a system of punishment.
days.context: After John injures her and she resists, Jane is locked in the room where her uncle died. This passage follows the punishment into the room.
days.contentNote: Contains threats of restraint and death, child mistreatment, religious intimidation, and a slavery comparison.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, opening through the return to retrospective thought; from “I resisted all the way: a new thing for me, and a circumstance which greatly strength” through “ vigour; I had to stem a rapid rush of retrospective thought before I quailed to the dismal present.”.

questions.prompt: How do Bessie and Abbot turn Jane’s dependence into a reason she should accept unequal treatment?
facilitatorNotes: They connect material support with submission, rather than testing whether John’s violence is wrong. Compare “less than a servant” with their claim that advice is for her good.
evidence: you are less than a servant
They will have a great deal of money, and you will have none

questions.prompt: Which details make the red-room simultaneously grand and hostile?
facilitatorNotes: The stately furniture and “pale throne” suggest power, while lack of fire and ordinary use makes grandeur unwelcoming. Invite different choices of detail if the reader explains the contrast.
evidence: one of the largest and stateliest chambers in the mansion
This room was chill, because it seldom had a fire

questions.prompt: What does Jane’s mirror image add to the confinement scene?
facilitatorNotes: She sees herself as a strange, fearful creature inside an altered version of the room. The image externalizes her alienation rather than establishing that a spirit is present.
evidence: the strange little figure there gazing at me
had the effect of a real spirit

days.title: Jane Eyre excerpt: Reason, fear, and disbelief
days.challenge: Distinguish the child’s terrified interpretation from the adult narrator’s later explanation.
days.focus: Retrospective narration makes fear intelligible without endorsing the household’s accusation of deceit.
days.context: Jane remains locked in the red-room. She reviews the unequal rules of the house before an unexplained light intensifies her fear.
days.contentNote: Contains child abuse, a child’s thoughts of starving herself to death, ghost fears, and descriptions of panic and collapse.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, injustice reflections through unconsciousness; from “All John Reed’s violent tyrannies, all his sisters’ proud indifference, all his mothe” through “ay; and soon after she was gone, I suppose I had a species of fit: unconsciousness closed the scene.”.

questions.prompt: How does the list of the Reed children’s conduct build Jane’s charge of injustice?
facilitatorNotes: The list supplies comparative evidence: serious cruelty is tolerated while Jane’s resistance is condemned. Discuss whether the accumulation sounds like a reasoned case, an angry memory, or both.
evidence: John no one thwarted, much less punished
I dared commit no fault: I strove to fulfil every duty

questions.prompt: What is the effect of placing the lantern explanation beside the child’s supernatural fear?
facilitatorNotes: The adult explanation supplies a likely ordinary cause while preserving the child’s bodily terror. A rational explanation does not make the punishment harmless.
evidence: a gleam from a lantern carried by some one across the lawn
prepared as my mind was for horror

questions.prompt: Why is Mrs. Reed’s word “artifice” especially damaging here?
facilitatorNotes: It treats distress as calculated manipulation, preventing sympathy and producing more confinement. Ask which earlier details allow readers to evaluate that judgment independently.
evidence: I abhor artifice, particularly in children
you will now stay here an hour longer

days.title: Jane Eyre excerpt: Comfort that arrives too late
days.challenge: Trace the altered emotional meanings of familiar objects, stories, and songs.
days.focus: The aftermath of fear changes perception even when outward treatment temporarily improves.
days.context: Jane wakes after collapsing in the red-room. Mr. Lloyd, an apothecary who treats the household’s servants, has come to examine her.
days.contentNote: Contains the aftermath of child abuse, references to death and supernatural fears, and a historical derogatory term in a quoted song.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, recovery through Bessie’s song; from “The next thing I remember is, waking up with a feeling as if I had had a frightful ni” through “ivine the morbid suffering to which I was a prey? In the course of the morning Mr. Lloyd came again.”.

questions.prompt: Why does a stranger’s presence make Jane feel safer than her familiar household does?
facilitatorNotes: His lack of connection to the Reeds permits the possibility of a fair hearing. The distinction between apothecary and family physician also reveals unequal treatment within the house.
evidence: an individual not belonging to Gateshead, and not related to Mrs. Reed
I felt so sheltered and befriended

questions.prompt: How do the painted plate and Gulliver’s Travels demonstrate a change that Jane cannot simply choose to reverse?
facilitatorNotes: Both once gave pleasure, yet their colors or images now seem drained or frightening. Readers can describe how memory and distress alter interpretation without diagnosing Jane medically.
evidence: the tints of the flowers, seemed strangely faded
all was eerie and dreary

questions.prompt: Why does the orphan ballad fail as straightforward consolation?
facilitatorNotes: Its offered protection also echoes Jane’s isolation, exhaustion, and desire for care. Bessie’s “don’t cry” overlooks the way the song sharpens those feelings.
evidence: Over the path of the poor orphan child.
She might as well have said to the fire, “don’t burn!”

days.title: Jane Eyre excerpt: The difficulty of being believed
days.challenge: Notice how class assumptions obstruct even a comparatively sympathetic conversation.
days.focus: Jane begins to speak for herself while also reproducing prejudices she has absorbed.
days.context: Mr. Lloyd returns to ask why Jane is unhappy. Bessie first supplies explanations for her; later the apothecary questions Jane alone.
days.contentNote: Contains child mistreatment, class prejudice, deaths of parents, and adults’ disparaging judgments of a child’s appearance.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, Mr. Lloyd’s questions through the servants’ supper conversation; from ““What, already up!” said he, as he entered the nursery. “Well, nurse, how is she?”” through ““So could I—with a roast onion. Come, we’ll go down.” They went.”.

questions.prompt: How do Jane’s corrections of “carriage” and “fall” change the account Mr. Lloyd receives?
facilitatorNotes: She distinguishes misery from disappointment and assault from an accident. Examine how the short corrections reclaim facts that Bessie’s account obscures.
evidence: I cry because I am miserable.
I was knocked down

questions.prompt: Why does Jane reject the possibility of kind but poor relatives?
facilitatorNotes: She equates poverty with degradation and loss of education or status. The narrator’s admission exposes a limitation in Jane’s thinking rather than making her wholly free of household values.
evidence: poverty for me was synonymous with degradation
I was not heroic enough to purchase liberty at the price of caste.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of ending with the servants discussing Georgiana’s beauty and then supper?
facilitatorNotes: Their sympathy is conditional on appearance, and the quick move to food makes Jane’s loss seem disposable to them. Other readings may emphasize ordinary callousness rather than deliberate malice.
evidence: if she were a nice, pretty child, one might compassionate her forlornness
I could fancy a Welsh rabbit for supper.

days.title: Up from Slavery: childhood, family records, and the schoolhouse
days.challenge: Distinguish a remembered childhood scene from the adult narrator’s qualifications about uncertain family history.
days.focus: How material details and gaps in the record establish an autobiographical voice.
days.context: Washington published this account in 1901 as an established educator. He begins with childhood under slavery, while repeatedly identifying what he cannot recover.
days.contentNote: This memoir describes enslavement, deprivation, and racial discrimination, and uses the racial terminology of its time. Washington’s views on slavery, Africa, labor, and racial progress were influential and contested in his own day; discussion first reconstructs his reasoning and then weighs it.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, opening through the schoolhouse comparison; begins “I WAS born a slave on a plantation in Franklin County, Virginia. I am not quite sure of the exa”; ends “ get into a schoolhouse and study in this way would be about the same as getting into paradise.”.

questions.prompt: Why does a life story begin with uncertainty about a birthday rather than a confident date? Connect that uncertainty to the account of family records.
facilitatorNotes: The missing date is evidence of denied records and family continuity, rather than simple forgetfulness. His cautious wording establishes limits to his knowledge; it does not make all later memories unreliable.
evidence: I do not know the month or the day.

questions.prompt: How does the seemingly unnecessary cat-hole expose the condition of the cabin? What changes when the narrator adds the summer fireplace?
facilitatorNotes: The cat-hole is bitterly comic because many gaps already admit animals and cold. Winter exposure and summer heat show that the kitchen serves the plantation at the family’s expense.
evidence: at least a half-dozen other places in the cabin

questions.prompt: Why does Washington reject the label “thieving” for his mother’s chicken while saying he would condemn a similar act now?
facilitatorNotes: He distinguishes an abstract property rule from an enslaved mother’s conditions and purpose. Discuss whether his account challenges the ownership system itself or makes a specific exception; both readings need the surrounding explanation.
evidence: She was simply a victim of the system of slavery.

days.title: Up from Slavery: news, meals, and the flax shirt
days.challenge: Trace how private sensory memories support an account of collective information and unequal living conditions.
days.focus: Informal news networks and the narrative force of ordinary objects.
days.context: The childhood account continues with the Civil War. The young Washington hears adult conversations and learns about freedom before he can read.
days.contentNote: This memoir describes enslavement, deprivation, and racial discrimination, and uses the racial terminology of its time. Washington’s views on slavery, Africa, labor, and racial progress were influential and contested in his own day; discussion first reconstructs his reasoning and then weighs it.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, mother’s prayer through John breaking in the shirt; begins “So far as I can now recall, the first knowledge that I got of the fact that we were slaves, and”; ends “was "broken in." Until I had grown to be quite a youth this single garment was all that I wore.”.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct the route by which battle news reaches the enslaved community. How does it complicate the narrator’s phrase “ignorant ... so far as books or newspapers were concerned”?
facilitatorNotes: The mail carrier listens to white conversations at the post office and relays news before reaching the big house. Exclusion from literacy does not prevent political attention, interpretation, or organized communication.
evidence: sent to the post-office for the mail

questions.prompt: What does the ginger-cake ambition reveal that the general account of wartime food shortages would not?
facilitatorNotes: The child imagines freedom through a concrete privilege witnessed but unavailable to him. His desire exposes everyday inequality; readers need not confuse the child’s immediate wish with the adult’s whole definition of freedom.
evidence: the height of my ambition would be reached

questions.prompt: Why does the flax-shirt episode end with John rather than with the shirt’s roughness?
facilitatorNotes: The painful comparisons establish bodily coercion, then John’s willingness to endure it foregrounds care and sacrifice within an enslaved family. The ending gives the brother agency without making the suffering acceptable.
evidence: he generously agreed to put it on in my stead

days.title: Up from Slavery: loyalty, argument, and emancipation
days.challenge: Separate reported examples, sweeping historical claims, and the narrator’s religious explanation of events.
days.focus: The tension between reconciliation rhetoric and the material meaning of freedom.
days.context: Washington moves from childhood memories into adult arguments about slavery’s effects before returning to the day freedom was announced on the plantation.
days.contentNote: This memoir describes enslavement, deprivation, and racial discrimination, and uses the racial terminology of its time. Washington’s views on slavery, Africa, labor, and racial progress were influential and contested in his own day; discussion first reconstructs his reasoning and then weighs it.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, wartime sympathy through the chapter’s conclusion; begins “One may get the idea, from what I have said, that there was bitter feeling toward the white peo”; ends “ to the "big house" to have a whispered conversation with their former owners as to the future.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Washington interrupt his stories of loyalty with “I have never seen one who did not want to be free”? What misreading is he trying to prevent?
facilitatorNotes: Loyalty stories could be used to claim contentment with slavery. The explicit correction separates bonds or acts of care from consent to bondage; the distinction is essential to his argument.
evidence: I have never seen one who did not want to be free

questions.prompt: Washington says he offers his comparison “not to justify slavery” but “to call attention to a fact.” Reconstruct the paragraph’s argument: what does he condemn, what does he claim, and what purpose does he give for saying it?
facilitatorNotes: He condemns slavery as established “for selfish and financial reasons,” refuses bitterness, and claims that the descendants of the enslaved are stronger than people elsewhere, citing missionaries returning to Africa. His purpose is providential: to show how good came out of wrong and to urge hope and reconciliation, addressed to Black and white readers alike. Once the argument is clear, readers may find it persuasive for his audience or question its evidence and its picture of Africa.
evidence: This I say, not to justify slavery

questions.prompt: How do the freedom songs change meaning before the announcement, and why does rejoicing later become anxiety?
facilitatorNotes: The singers openly apply freedom to life on earth after previously masking it as heaven. Joy is followed by urgent problems of home, livelihood, education, and citizenship; this does not cancel the desire for freedom.
evidence: freedom of the body in this world

days.title: Up from Slavery: choosing names and building a school
days.challenge: Follow a shift from symbolic acts of freedom to the practical organization of education.
days.focus: Self-naming, migration, and community investment in literacy.
days.context: After emancipation, Washington’s family moves from Virginia to Malden, West Virginia. The passage follows the new community’s efforts to secure schooling.
days.contentNote: This memoir describes enslavement, deprivation, and racial discrimination, and uses the racial terminology of its time. Washington’s views on slavery, Africa, labor, and racial progress were influential and contested in his own day; discussion first reconstructs his reasoning and then weighs it.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, opening through crowded day and night schools; begins “AFTER the coming of freedom there were two points upon which practically all the people on our ”; ends “ool, Sunday-school, were always crowded, and often many had to be turned away for want of room.”.

questions.prompt: What does the change from “Hatcher’s John” to a chosen name accomplish even when the new middle initial stands for nothing?
facilitatorNotes: The possessive old name identifies an owner, while the chosen name claims public personhood and affiliation. The initial has symbolic social force even without a full middle name.
evidence: the initial "S" standing for no name

questions.prompt: How do the barrel number 18, the spelling-book, and the newspaper reader present three different stages or uses of literacy?
facilitatorNotes: The number is learned within work, the book enables deliberate self-instruction, and the reader supplies communal access to news. Literacy develops through particular encounters and serves more than personal advancement.
evidence: The number allotted to my stepfather was "18."

questions.prompt: What does “board ’round” show about who created and supported the school? How does the older learners’ aim broaden the account?
facilitatorNotes: Families pool payments and food rather than wait for a free public school. Older people seeking to read the Bible show that learning is a collective aspiration extending beyond children or employment.
evidence: each family agreed to pay a certain amount per month

days.title: Up from Slavery: the clock, the cap, and a name
days.challenge: Compare the narrator’s self-criticism with the lessons he draws from other people’s choices.
days.focus: Autobiographical candor and competing measures of advantage.
days.context: Although a school now exists, Washington’s stepfather needs his earnings. He negotiates attendance while confronting visible differences between himself and his classmates.
days.contentNote: This memoir describes enslavement, deprivation, and racial discrimination, and uses the racial terminology of its time. Washington’s views on slavery, Africa, labor, and racial progress were influential and contested in his own day; discussion first reconstructs his reasoning and then weighs it.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, exclusion from day-school through the discussion of ancestry; begins “The opening of the school in the Kanawha Valley, however, brought to me one of the keenest disa”; ends “nd connection serves as a stimulus to help him to overcome obstacles when striving for success.”.

questions.prompt: Why admit moving the furnace clock? Does the statement about the power of facts fully resolve the ethical problem?
facilitatorNotes: The confession presents candor and urgent desire to learn, but the clock regulates other workers as well. Readers can acknowledge the motive while questioning the repeated deception and its effects.
evidence: all the hundred or more workmen depended upon

questions.prompt: How does the homemade cap become a lesson about appearances? What cannot be proved by the later fates of classmates with store hats?
facilitatorNotes: His mother refuses debt to imitate wealth, giving the cap dignity. A few later failures among classmates do not prove purchased hats cause failure; the adult narrator shapes an instructive contrast.
evidence: seeming to be that which she was not

questions.prompt: How do the chosen surname and the later discussion of family history pull in different directions?
facilitatorNotes: Naming himself suggests agency, yet inherited records and expectations can materially support ambition. Washington celebrates self-creation while explaining that destroyed ancestry places unequal burdens on Black youth.
evidence: the Negro youth starts out with the presumption against him.

days.title: Adlestrop
days.challenge: Track a memory that moves from a printed station name to an imagined county-wide soundscape.
days.focus: How an uneventful stop becomes an expansive moment of attention.
days.context: The speaker recalls an unscheduled railway stop. Read once for the physical events, then twice aloud to hear how repeated conjunctions extend the final perception.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem ADLESTROP; begins “YES. I remember Adlestrop--”; ends “Of Oxfordshire and Gloucestershire.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker remember a name when nobody boards or leaves the train?
facilitatorNotes: The empty platform offers almost no human event; the name becomes an anchor for a remembered sensory interval rather than a travel achievement.
evidence: No one left and no one came

questions.prompt: How do the human sounds near the beginning prepare for the blackbird near the end?
facilitatorNotes: Hiss and throat-clearing are brief, ordinary disturbances. The bird song broadens attention beyond them; compare how many lines each sound receives.
evidence: The steam hissed. Someone cleared his throat.

questions.prompt: Does the final stanza literally report hearing every bird in two counties? Defend your reading of its widening distance.
facilitatorNotes: The expanding sound can represent imagination or a subjective impression rather than a survey. The increasing distance and softened description invite that distinction; a literal-minded answer should address the scale.
evidence: Farther and farther, all the birds

days.title: My Star
days.challenge: Distinguish what the speaker observes from the value the speaker assigns to a private experience.
days.focus: The difference between shared measurement and intimate recognition.
days.context: A speaker tries to explain a favored star to friends. Spar is a mineral crystal; its angled surfaces can refract light. Read the short lines aloud, then compare the closing longer lines.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem MY STAR; begins “All that I know”; ends “Mine has opened its soul to me; therefore I love it.”.

questions.prompt: What do the alternating red and blue darts make the friends want, and why might their request fail?
facilitatorNotes: They want access to the same display, but the star ceases its special activity when their attention arrives. The scene makes personal perception difficult to reproduce for an audience.
evidence: They would fain see, too,

questions.prompt: How do the bird and furled flower comparisons change the star from an astronomical object?
facilitatorNotes: Both comparisons suggest something living that can withhold or close itself. The speaker gives the star agency and privacy; other supported interpretations of the closure are welcome.
evidence: Then it stops like a bird; like a flower, hangs furled:

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker dismiss the possibility that the friends’ star is a world?
facilitatorNotes: Size or astronomical importance does not decide this preference. A perceived intimate opening matters more; discuss whether that makes the speaker insightful, possessive, or both.
evidence: Mine has opened its soul to me; therefore I love it.

days.title: Sonnet XLIII
days.challenge: Follow an accumulating argument across repeated syntax, abstractions and a conditional final claim.
days.focus: How the sonnet brings spiritual scale and ordinary need into one account of love.
days.context: This is Elizabeth Barrett Browning’s original English Sonnet XLIII, not a translation despite the collection title. Read for sentence structure, then mark each distinct sense of the repeated declaration.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem XLIII; begins “How do I love thee?  Let me count the ways.”; ends “I shall but love thee better after death.”.

questions.prompt: How does the move from depth, breadth and height to everyday need change the scale of the declaration?
facilitatorNotes: The poem places immeasurable spiritual reach beside daily sustenance. The smaller scale extends rather than cancels the opening claim; ask which image makes love more credible to the reader.
evidence: Most quiet need, by sun and candlelight.

questions.prompt: What distinction does the comparison with people turning from praise establish?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker associates love with freely chosen right action rather than reward or public approval. The comparison makes an ethical claim, not just an intensity claim.
evidence: I love thee purely, as they turn from Praise.

questions.prompt: How does “if God choose” qualify the apparent certainty of the ending?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker desires love beyond death but leaves its possibility to divine choice. A reading of confidence should still recognize the conditional grammar.
evidence: and, if God choose,

days.title: In a Garden
days.challenge: Trace how a sensory setting becomes an address to an absent person without an announced explanation.
days.focus: Water sounds, bodily imagery and the turn from observed garden to imagined intimacy.
days.context: Read the garden first as a physical place and then as a setting shaped by desire. The later night scene is wished for, not simply another reported moment.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem In a Garden; Macmillan 1914 printed pages 244–245; begins “Gushing from the mouths of stone men”; ends “Night, and the water, and you in your whiteness, bathing!”.

questions.prompt: How does water seem alive while stone remains materially present?
facilitatorNotes: Mouths, lips, feet and murmuring animate fountains and plants, yet granite and marble keep the scene built and solid. Discuss how this mixture prepares the later human presence.
evidence: In granite-lipped basins,

questions.prompt: What change in tense and intention occurs when the speaker first mentions “you”?
facilitatorNotes: The poem turns from present description toward a wished-for night and companion. This changes how the earlier sensory abundance is understood.
evidence: And I wished for night and you.

questions.prompt: How does the final isolated line alter the pace and emphasis of the poem?
facilitatorNotes: It condenses the desired scene into night, water and the beloved, after many descriptive details. The exclamation can sound like fulfilment in imagination or intensified longing; support either reading with the preceding wish.
evidence: Night, and the water, and you in your whiteness, bathing!

days.title: City Trees
days.challenge: Read conditional verbs closely and distinguish unheard sound from absent sound.
days.focus: How city noise limits perception without erasing a natural presence.
days.context: The speaker watches trees on a noisy street. Read aloud twice: first emphasize the hypothetical claims, then emphasize the final declaration of knowledge.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem CITY TREES; begins “THE trees along this city street,”; ends “  I know what sound is there.”.

questions.prompt: What does “Save for the traffic and the trains” imply about the difference between city and country trees?
facilitatorNotes: The difference lies in what can be heard around the trees, not necessarily in the trees’ capacity to make sound. The traffic masks something comparable to country music.
evidence: Save for the traffic and the trains,

questions.prompt: Why is “dumb” more complicated than saying the leaves make no sound?
facilitatorNotes: The leaves seem voiceless against louder surroundings, yet the speaker imagines or recognizes their sound. The later certainty complicates a literal reading of silence.
evidence: Against the shrieking city air,

questions.prompt: What evidence supports the last line’s confidence, and what remains an inference?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker watches the wind, which gives a basis for knowing leaves would sound, but direct hearing remains obstructed. Discuss whether the ending stresses imagination, memory, or attentive knowledge.
evidence: I know what sound is there.

days.title: Jane Eyre excerpt: Small objects of affection
days.challenge: Follow shifts from open defiance to private dependence across a compressed passage of time.
days.focus: The doll, Bessie’s occasional tenderness, and the robin reveal Jane’s need to give and receive care.
days.context: Mr. Lloyd has suggested that Jane might attend school, but weeks pass without a definite departure. She remains isolated within Gateshead.
days.contentNote: Contains child abuse, threats and demeaning language, and unequal treatment based on class and appearance.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, waiting for change through hesitation at the breakfast-room door; from “From my discourse with Mr. Lloyd, and from the above reported conference between Bess” through “ in agitated hesitation; the vehement ringing of the breakfast-room bell decided me; I _must_ enter.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Jane’s question about Uncle Reed disturb Mrs. Reed more than her earlier protest?
facilitatorNotes: The question invokes an obligation connected to the dead husband, challenging Mrs. Reed’s own view of her conduct. Her visible fear complicates her usual composure.
evidence: What would Uncle Reed say to you, if he were alive?
her usually cold composed grey eye became troubled with a look like fear

questions.prompt: How does Jane’s care for the shabby doll complicate the household’s description of her as unloving or wicked?
facilitatorNotes: She imagines keeping the doll safe and warm and feels happiness through its supposed happiness. The tenderness offers evidence unavailable to adults who see only her resistance.
evidence: human beings must love something
believing it to be happy likewise

questions.prompt: What contrast is created between Jane feeding the robin and Bessie accusing her of mischief?
facilitatorNotes: Jane completes a small act of care before answering; Bessie reads the visible excitement as wrongdoing. Ask how the narrator gives readers evidence that the adult fails to seek.
evidence: I wanted the bird to be secure of its bread
as if you had been about some mischief

days.title: Jane Eyre excerpt: A lesson in humility
days.challenge: Read the gap between declared religious principles and the material details speakers reveal.
days.focus: Satire exposes how moral instruction can protect privilege and discredit a child in advance.
days.context: Mrs. Reed has summoned Mr. Brocklehurst, the manager of Lowood school, to consider admitting Jane. Jane hopes school will provide a different life.
days.contentNote: Contains religious threats of damnation and death, class humiliation, and an accusation of deceit directed at a child.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, Brocklehurst’s entrance through his departure; from ““Who could want me?” I asked inwardly, as with both hands I turned the stiff door-han” through “rst put into my hand a thin pamphlet sewn in a cover, and having rung for his carriage, he departed.”.

questions.prompt: How does the “black pillar” description prepare readers for Brocklehurst’s questioning?
facilitatorNotes: Its rigid, architectural imagery makes him seem imposing and impersonal before he speaks. The child’s low viewpoint also explains his apparent size; invite attention to both symbolism and perspective.
evidence: a black pillar!
the grim face at the top was like a carved mask

questions.prompt: What contradiction appears in the story of the boy who chooses a Psalm over a gingerbread-nut?
facilitatorNotes: The reported rejection of food is rewarded with two nuts, creating an incentive beneath the display of piety. Discuss whether Brocklehurst notices the irony.
evidence: he then gets two nuts in recompense for his infant piety.

questions.prompt: Why is Augusta’s description of the Lowood pupils an effective test of the adults’ repeated word “consistency”?
facilitatorNotes: The daughter and mother display silk while pupils are trained in plainness and humility. Their praise reveals different standards for rich visitors and dependent children.
evidence: they looked at my dress and mama’s, as if they had never seen a silk gown before.
Consistency, madam, is the first of Christian duties

days.title: Jane Eyre excerpt: Victory and its aftertaste
days.challenge: Hold Jane’s justified protest and her later unease together without reducing either to a simple moral.
days.focus: Images of battle, fire, and poison distinguish self-defense from the satisfactions and costs of vengeance.
days.context: After Brocklehurst leaves, Jane confronts Mrs. Reed about the charge that she is deceitful. The passage then follows her mood after the confrontation.
days.contentNote: Contains descriptions of child abuse and intense anger. An illustration’s duplicated alt-text caption is excluded; the narrative is continuous.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, Jane’s confrontation through reconciliation with Bessie; from “Mrs. Reed and I were left alone: some minutes passed in silence; she was sewing, I wa” through “anting stories, and sang me some of her sweetest songs. Even for me life had its gleams of sunshine.”.

questions.prompt: How does Jane use the accusation of deceit against Mrs. Reed herself?
facilitatorNotes: She argues that saying she loves her aunt would be false and contrasts Mrs. Reed’s good public reputation with private cruelty. Truth-telling becomes a way to contest the adult’s authority.
evidence: if I were, I should say I loved _you;_
People think you a good woman, but you are bad, hard-hearted.

questions.prompt: What do the burnt-heath and wine images add after the narrator calls herself “winner of the field”?
facilitatorNotes: They interrupt a simple triumph: immediate heat and pleasure leave desolation and a corrosive aftertaste. Readers may distinguish regret about rage from any withdrawal of the claim of injustice.
evidence: black and blasted after the flames are dead
its after-flavour, metallic and corroding

questions.prompt: Why does the exchange with Bessie end differently from the confrontation with Mrs. Reed?
facilitatorNotes: Jane asks directly for less scolding, challenges Bessie’s claim of affection, and receives an embrace. There remains unequal power, but the scene allows reciprocal warmth rather than only victory or submission.
evidence: You don’t show it.
we mutually embraced

days.title: Jane Eyre excerpt: The long journey to Lowood
days.challenge: Compare the child’s sense of distance and uncertainty with the narrator’s more measured account.
days.focus: Leaving a harmful home creates both possibility and a new vulnerability.
days.context: Jane is finally leaving Gateshead for Lowood school. Bessie accompanies her to the coach, but Jane must travel the fifty miles alone.
days.contentNote: Contains an unaccompanied child’s fear of kidnapping and accounts of inadequate food and institutional care.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, departure from Gateshead through the first night at Lowood; from “Five o’clock had hardly struck on the morning of the 19th of January, when Bessie bro” through “n minutes the single light was extinguished, and amidst silence and complete darkness I fell asleep.”.

questions.prompt: How do Bessie’s actions complicate Jane’s earlier judgments of her?
facilitatorNotes: The biscuits, lantern, embraces, and appeal to the guard show practical concern. Readers should retain the earlier inconsistency rather than treating this departure as proof that Bessie was always kind.
evidence: wrapped up some biscuits in a paper and put them into my bag
Be sure and take good care of her

questions.prompt: How does the account turn fifty miles into a journey that feels much longer?
facilitatorNotes: The narration reports a day of preternatural length, imagined hundreds of miles, changing landscape, and darkness. The contrast shows distance as experienced by an anxious child.
evidence: the day seemed to me of a preternatural length
we appeared to travel over hundreds of miles of road

questions.prompt: What first impressions of Lowood suggest care, and what details suggest impersonality?
facilitatorNotes: The tall lady considers fatigue and touches Jane gently; the long room, uniform dress, commands, and shared mug suggest a collective system. Different balances are defensible if both kinds of detail are acknowledged.
evidence: then she touched my cheek gently with her forefinger
the mug being common to all

days.title: Jane Eyre excerpt: Bread, discipline, and responsibility
days.challenge: Read institutional routines against bodily needs and the narrator’s ironic phrasing.
days.focus: Miss Temple’s concrete response to hunger tests the school’s claims to moral order.
days.context: After arriving at Lowood the previous evening, Jane joins its morning routine. She has eaten very little during her journey.
days.contentNote: Contains institutional neglect, hunger, and punitive discipline directed at children.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, the first morning through Miss Temple’s decision; from “The night passed rapidly: I was too tired even to dream; I only once awoke to hear th” through “esponsibility,” she added, in an explanatory tone to them, and immediately afterwards left the room.”.

questions.prompt: What does the repeated ringing of bells reveal about the way time and bodies are organized at Lowood?
facilitatorNotes: Bells regulate dressing, prayer, lessons, and meals, while the cold and too few basins make obedience physically difficult. The routine looks precise but does not ensure care.
evidence: there was but one basin to six girls
The indefatigable bell now sounded for the fourth time

questions.prompt: How does “Thanks being returned for what we had not got” change the meaning of the breakfast ritual?
facilitatorNotes: The irony exposes a gap between the formal act of gratitude and actual nourishment. Ask whether the criticism targets prayer itself or its use without attending to children’s conditions.
evidence: Breakfast was over, and none had breakfasted.
Thanks being returned for what we had not got

questions.prompt: Why is “on my responsibility” the decisive phrase in Miss Temple’s order?
facilitatorNotes: She recognizes hunger as a fact and accepts accountability for correcting it, despite the teachers’ surprise. Her authority operates through material help rather than merely demanding silence.
evidence: You had this morning a breakfast which you could not eat
It is to be done on my responsibility

days.title: Up from Slavery: the mine and the measure of success
days.challenge: Evaluate a universal claim against the narrator’s own concrete account of unequal obstacles.
days.focus: The difference between recognizing resilience and minimizing structural exclusion.
days.context: The chapter closes with Washington returning to work and night lessons. His description of the mine leads into a retrospective argument about success.
days.contentNote: This memoir describes enslavement, deprivation, racial discrimination, and historical racial terminology. Washington’s judgments about slavery, Africa, and racial progress are claims to examine, not conclusions supplied by the course.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, return to night-school through the chapter’s conclusion; begins “The time that I was permitted to attend school during the day was short, and my attendance was ”; ends “ot to call attention to myself as an individual, but to the race to which I am proud to belong.”.

questions.prompt: How do darkness and the repeated loss of direction turn the mine into more than a generic example of hard work?
facilitatorNotes: The rooms, extinguished light, and dependence on finding someone else make danger immediate and spatial. They also emphasize the child’s vulnerability rather than an easy path to character-building.
evidence: sometimes my light would go out

questions.prompt: What changes when success is measured by obstacles overcome rather than by position reached? Apply both measures to the boy described here.
facilitatorNotes: The revised measure recognizes effort and endurance hidden by unequal starting points. The child’s educational persistence can count as achievement even without rank or wealth; readers may still question who gets to assess the obstacles.
evidence: the obstacles which he has overcome

questions.prompt: Can the passage prove that merit is always eventually rewarded? Use the account of mining children to test that confidence.
facilitatorNotes: The universal assurance expresses faith and encouragement, not proof. Children losing education and ambition furnish a counterpressure within his own account; avoid treating lack of later success as proof of lack of merit.
evidence: They soon lose ambition to do anything else

days.title: Up from Slavery: the journey to Hampton
days.challenge: Track practical help alongside the story’s religious metaphors of individual determination.
days.focus: The construction of an educational pilgrimage and its supporting network.
days.context: Washington hears about Hampton while working in a mine. He later serves in Mrs. Ruffner’s household before setting out for the school in 1872.
days.contentNote: This memoir describes enslavement, deprivation, and racial discrimination, and uses the racial terminology of its time. Washington’s views on slavery, Africa, labor, and racial progress were influential and contested in his own day; discussion first reconstructs his reasoning and then weighs it.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, opening through the head teacher’s hesitation; begins “ONE day, while at work in the coal-mine, I happened to overhear two miners talking about a grea”; ends “my heart, that I could do as well as they, if I could only get a chance to show what was in me.”.

questions.prompt: How does the dry-goods-box library anticipate the larger school building without making the two opportunities equivalent?
facilitatorNotes: Both turn education into a visible place, and the improvised shelves show initiative with limited resources. Hampton supplies institutional opportunities that a box of available books cannot replace.
evidence: secured a dry-goods box

questions.prompt: Why include gifts as small as a nickel or a handkerchief in a journey usually associated with personal perseverance?
facilitatorNotes: The gifts reveal community hope and material support from people with little money. They prevent a complete account of the journey from attributing every step to an isolated individual.
evidence: others a quarter, or a handkerchief

questions.prompt: What is the effect of recalling the sidewalk during the later Richmond reception, and then ending with the teacher’s uncertainty?
facilitatorNotes: The reception contrasts public honor with former homelessness, while the final admission scene returns readers to vulnerability before success is secure. The retrospective narrator knows the outcome but reconstructs the risk.
evidence: my mind was more upon the sidewalk

days.title: Up from Slavery: the broom examination and Hampton’s costs
days.challenge: Trace how an emblematic scene and concrete financial figures support a philosophy of education.
days.focus: Work, sponsorship, and the limits of the self-made success story.
days.context: The head teacher has hesitated to admit the travel-worn applicant. Her instruction to sweep a room begins the test Washington remembers most vividly.
days.contentNote: This memoir describes enslavement, deprivation, and racial discrimination, and uses the racial terminology of its time. Washington’s views on slavery, Africa, labor, and racial progress were influential and contested in his own day; discussion first reconstructs his reasoning and then weighs it.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, sweeping examination through chapter’s conclusion; begins “After some hours had passed, the head teacher said to me: "The adjoining recitation-room needs ”; ends “when the whole South will appreciate this service in a way that it has not yet been able to do.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Washington call the sweeping of the room his “college examination” and compare it to entering Harvard or Yale? What does the comparison claim for the kind of education Hampton offered?
facilitatorNotes: The comparison raises thoroughness, initiative and self-discipline, the habits Hampton prized, to the dignity of an academic admission, and it carries his pride in passing. Some readers hear a deliberate challenge to the idea that only book learning counts; others notice that the test also reflects the institution’s values about labor. Both readings rest on the scene.
evidence: The sweeping of that room was my college examination

questions.prompt: Make an account of how board, tuition, books, and clothing are supplied. Why is “he paid his own way” an incomplete summary?
facilitatorNotes: Janitor work eventually covers board, but Morgan pays tuition, books are borrowed, and donated clothing helps him remain. The explicit costs and supports coexist with sustained personal labor.
evidence: defray the cost of my tuition

questions.prompt: How does the tent episode both support and complicate the portrait of Armstrong as a nearly perfect leader?
facilitatorNotes: Volunteers show devotion and make space for more students, yet their suffering is concealed from him. The admiration is sincere but cannot prove that he understood every cost of the plan.
evidence: how much I am sure General Armstrong never knew

days.title: Up from Slavery: unpaid debts and a return home
days.challenge: Distinguish disappointment, discouragement, and retrospective self-presentation across changing circumstances.
days.focus: What a success narrative includes when effort does not immediately bring reward.
days.context: After his first Hampton year, Washington needs vacation work and money to return. This excerpt follows two summers and stops after a personal loss.
days.contentNote: This memoir describes enslavement, deprivation, and racial discrimination, and uses the racial terminology of its time. Washington’s views on slavery, Africa, labor, and racial progress were influential and contested in his own day; discussion first reconstructs his reasoning and then weighs it. This passage includes a parent’s death.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, opening through Washington’s account of his mother’s death; begins “AT the end of my first year at Hampton I was confronted with another difficulty. Most of the st”; ends “hat she might be permitted to live to see her children educated and started out into the world.”.

questions.prompt: How do the proposed five-cent coat payment and the employer’s claim to the ten-dollar bill shape the account of money?
facilitatorNotes: Both raise hope of solving a concrete shortage and abruptly frustrate it. The episodes show how others’ decisions affect the student’s resources; the second also invites discussion of the proprietor’s unsupported claim of entitlement.
evidence: five cents, cash down

questions.prompt: Washington says he never became discouraged. How can a reader reconcile that claim with his “drooping spirits” and homesickness without erasing either?
facilitatorNotes: He may use discouragement to mean abandoning a goal rather than feeling distress. Alternatively, the broad retrospective claim smooths a more complex emotional record. Accept interpretations grounded in both kinds of wording.
evidence: cheered my drooping spirits considerably

questions.prompt: Washington concludes that the miners “were worse off at the end of a strike.” What chain of observations leads him there, and how does the conclusion connect to the value he places on saving?
facilitatorNotes: He sees savings spent during strikes, men returning in debt at the same wages or moving at cost, and remembers miners who once had money in the bank. The judgment follows from the importance he gives to thrift and economic independence. Readers can then consider his vantage point as a returning student and what the strikers might have said for themselves.
evidence: my observations convinced me that the miners were worse off

days.title: Up from Slavery: beginning Tuskegee
days.challenge: Separate an institution’s official appropriation from what it can actually purchase.
days.focus: Founding a school through observation, local support, and constrained resources.
days.context: Years have passed: Washington has graduated and taught at Hampton. In 1881 he is recommended to lead a new school in Tuskegee, Alabama. “Normal school” means a school for training teachers.
days.contentNote: This memoir describes enslavement, deprivation, and racial discrimination, and uses the racial terminology of its time. Washington’s views on slavery, Africa, labor, and racial progress were influential and contested in his own day; discussion first reconstructs his reasoning and then weighs it. The opening references Hampton’s education of Indigenous students without presenting their perspectives.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, opening through the first month’s investigation; begins “DURING the time that I had charge of the Indians and the night-school at Hampton, I pursued som”; ends “t a stranger was expected, I had the advantage of seeing the real, everyday life of the people.”.

questions.prompt: Why is the two-thousand-dollar appropriation insufficient even though the legislature has supported a school?
facilitatorNotes: It pays instructors only, leaving land, buildings, and equipment unfunded. The distinction between a grant’s amount and its permitted uses explains the improvised facilities.
evidence: only for the payment of the salaries of the instructors

questions.prompt: How does the umbrella scene answer the expectation Washington had before arriving?
facilitatorNotes: He expects a ready building and equipment, but a student must shelter him during lessons. The scene makes material scarcity visible while also showing students’ help; devotion does not repair the roof.
evidence: hold an umbrella over me while I heard the recitations

questions.prompt: Why does Washington travel by mule cart and sleep in cabins before opening his school? How does this way of gathering knowledge shape what he decides the school must do?
facilitatorNotes: Unannounced visits let him see “the real, everyday life of the people” rather than a performance for a guest. What he finds in homes, farms and schools leads him to an education tied to daily life, work and land. Students may also note what any single traveler’s route can and cannot show.
evidence: there had been no notice given in advance

days.title: The Owl
days.challenge: Follow qualifications in the first stanza and an ethical change caused by one persistent sound.
days.focus: How shelter becomes uncomfortable awareness of others’ exposure.
days.context: A traveler has reached an inn. The poem does not ask the reader to ignore that comfort; it explores how a bird’s cry changes its meaning.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem THE OWL; begins “DOWNHILL I came, hungry, and yet not starved;”; ends “Soldiers and poor, unable to rejoice.”.

questions.prompt: Why qualify hunger with “not starved” and cold with remaining heat?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker distinguishes temporary discomfort from more extreme suffering. Those early limits prepare the comparison with people who cannot reach safety.
evidence: hungry, and yet not starved;

questions.prompt: What penetrates the supposedly complete protection of the inn, and why does it matter?
facilitatorNotes: The owl’s cry crosses the boundary that food, fire and walls establish. Its persistence links protected interior experience with the night outside.
evidence: All of the night was quite barred out except

questions.prompt: What two meanings does “salted” bring to food and repose?
facilitatorNotes: It can suggest literal seasoning but also tears, bitterness or moral disturbance. Food and rest remain available, yet knowledge of exposed soldiers and poor people prevents simple satisfaction.
evidence: Salted and sobered, too, by the bird's voice

days.title: Home Thoughts, From Abroad
days.challenge: Reconstruct an absent landscape from the speaker’s present wish and imagined seasonal sequence.
days.focus: Nostalgia as an act of selection, sound and comparison.
days.context: The speaker looks toward an England that is elsewhere. Bole means a tree trunk and dower a gift or portion. Keep the distant home and the speaker’s current surroundings distinct.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem HOME THOUGHTS, FROM ABROAD; begins “Oh, to be in England”; ends “--Far brighter than this gaudy melon-flower!”.

questions.prompt: How does the opening establish that the scene is desired rather than directly witnessed?
facilitatorNotes: The wish to be in England places the speaker abroad. Later sensory detail can be memory or imagination rather than immediate observation.
evidence: Oh, to be in England

questions.prompt: What does the twice-sung thrush song suggest about the speaker’s own attempt to recapture a moment?
facilitatorNotes: The thrush supposedly repeats an apparently spontaneous achievement. The poem likewise reconstructs a remembered rapture through crafted language; discuss the tension between carelessness and repetition.
evidence: The first fine careless rapture!

questions.prompt: What does the final comparison reveal about the speaker’s scale of value?
facilitatorNotes: Small English buttercups outshine the present exotic flower because emotional belonging shapes judgment. The poem’s preference need not establish an objective hierarchy of plants or places.
evidence: Far brighter than this gaudy melon-flower!

days.title: Sonnet XIV
days.challenge: Trace a conditional argument that rejects apparently flattering reasons for attachment.
days.focus: The instability of beauty, agreement and pity as grounds for love.
days.context: Sonnet XIV addresses a beloved directly. On a second reading, mark each proposed reason for love and the danger the speaker attaches to it.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem XIV; begins “If thou must love me, let it be for nought”; ends “Thou may’st love on, through love’s eternity.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker distrust love based on a smile or a pleasing manner?
facilitatorNotes: Both the qualities and the beloved’s response to them can change. The speaker fears affection built on a contingent impression will be undone with it.
evidence: Be changed, or change for thee,

questions.prompt: How might comfort paradoxically destroy a love based on pity?
facilitatorNotes: Successful consolation may stop the tears that originally motivated attachment. The speaker imagines recovery removing the reason for being loved.
evidence: A creature might forget to weep,

questions.prompt: Does “love for love’s sake” solve the problem or leave a difficult demand? Explain from the sonnet’s reasoning.
facilitatorNotes: It seeks a foundation independent of changing traits, but readers may question how such love can be separated from the person’s qualities. Accept either conclusion if it engages the rejected grounds and promised duration.
evidence: But love me for love’s sake, that evermore

days.title: The Taxi
days.challenge: Read motion as emotional distortion and track repeated images of impact or injury.
days.focus: How an ordinary taxi journey turns separation into a hostile environment.
days.context: The title supplies the vehicle, while the poem itself emphasizes what the departing passenger perceives. Reread slowly to distinguish literal street motion from figurative violence.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem The Taxi; Macmillan 1914 printed pages 96; begins “When I go away from you”; ends “To wound myself upon the sharp edges of the night?”.

questions.prompt: What does the slackened drum comparison imply beyond simple sadness?
facilitatorNotes: A loosened drum loses resonance and energy. The world still exists but feels acoustically and emotionally deadened when the speaker leaves the beloved.
evidence: Like a slackened drum.

questions.prompt: How do streets and lamps seem to act upon the passenger?
facilitatorNotes: Streets wedge the beloved farther away and lamps prick the speaker’s eyes. The setting becomes an agent of separation and pain rather than neutral scenery.
evidence: And the lamps of the city prick my eyes

questions.prompt: How does the final question change responsibility for the pain described earlier?
facilitatorNotes: After blaming sharp stars, wind and streets, the speaker asks why they choose to leave. It brings agency back to the traveler, though the reason for leaving stays unstated.
evidence: Why should I leave you,

days.title: Travel
days.challenge: Hold two apparently conflicting claims together without reducing the speaker to simple unhappiness.
days.focus: Travel desire that persists alongside present friendship and affection.
days.context: The railway is physically distant but insistently present to the speaker’s senses. Track the repeated negative phrasing before discussing what kind of journey is desired.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem TRAVEL; begins “THE railroad track is miles away,”; ends “  No matter where it's going.”.

questions.prompt: How does the day stanza turn physical distance into psychological closeness?
facilitatorNotes: The railway is miles away and voices are loud, yet every whistle enters the speaker’s awareness. Desire intensifies selective attention.
evidence: THE railroad track is miles away,

questions.prompt: What changes between the day and night stanzas, and what does not?
facilitatorNotes: Voices give way to stillness, while whistles gain the visual accompaniment of red cinders. The speaker remains intensely aware of each train despite the changed setting.
evidence: And hear its engine steaming.

questions.prompt: Why is the final desire to take any train more surprising after the statement about friends?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker values current friendships and predicts no better ones, so travel is not explained simply by misery or social dissatisfaction. Restlessness can coexist with attachment.
evidence: No matter where it's going.

days.title: Jane Eyre excerpt: Reading the institution
days.challenge: Infer a school’s structure from a child’s questions, a public inscription, and another pupil’s careful answers.
days.focus: Helen’s measured language complicates Jane’s first attempts to classify people as good or bad.
days.context: Miss Temple has supplied extra food after an inedible breakfast. Outdoors, Jane meets an older pupil reading Rasselas and asks about Lowood.
days.contentNote: Contains institutional neglect, hunger, and public humiliation of a pupil.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, the garden through the end of the first day; from “The bread and cheese was presently brought in and distributed, to the high delight an” through “hen the glass of water and the piece of oat-cake, prayers, and bed. Such was my first day at Lowood.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Jane find the name Rasselas attractive but the actual book disappointing?
facilitatorNotes: Her expectations come from imaginative stories of fairies and genii, while Helen’s reading offers a different kind of interest. The contrast establishes intellectual difference without making Jane incapable of growth.
evidence: a name that struck me as strange, and consequently attractive
I saw nothing about fairies, nothing about genii

questions.prompt: How does Helen’s account of the school complicate the inscription about “good works”?
facilitatorNotes: The public statement praises benefaction, while the conversation identifies payment, subscriptions, control, and accountability. Ask how financial support and moral authority are being connected rather than assuming charity cancels responsibility.
evidence: Let your light so shine before men
she has to answer to Mr. Brocklehurst for all she does

questions.prompt: Why does Jane end the punishment scene wondering what sort of girl Helen is?
facilitatorNotes: Helen’s composure does not fit Jane’s expectation that public disgrace must produce visible shame. Jane guesses that Helen attends to inward memories, revealing both curiosity and the limits of her understanding.
evidence: she neither wept nor blushed
her sight seems turned in, gone down into her heart

days.title: Jane Eyre excerpt: The evidence of a punishment
days.challenge: Test a teacher’s judgment against facts the narrator supplies and then against the punished pupil’s own explanation.
days.focus: Helen’s endurance and Jane’s anger offer competing responses to institutional power.
days.context: Jane now takes lessons at Lowood and observes Helen Burns in Miss Scatcherd’s history class. That evening she seeks Helen out.
days.contentNote: Contains corporal punishment, inadequate food and heating, and a discussion of enduring mistreatment.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, frozen water through Helen’s account of her faults; from “The next day commenced as before, getting up and dressing by rushlight; but this morn” through “nts. This is all very provoking to Miss Scatcherd, who is naturally neat, punctual, and particular.””.

questions.prompt: What does the frozen water allow readers to know that Miss Scatcherd’s rebuke ignores?
facilitatorNotes: The pupils could not wash normally, so dirty nails are not adequate evidence of deliberate neglect. The detail makes the teacher’s certainty open to challenge.
evidence: the water in the pitchers was frozen
You dirty, disagreeable girl! you have never cleaned your nails this morning!

questions.prompt: How do Helen’s accurate history answers and the trace of a tear challenge the label “Hardened girl”?
facilitatorNotes: She shows intellectual attention and private feeling that the teacher’s label erases. Her outward stillness should not be read as absence of thought or pain.
evidence: her memory seemed to have retained the substance of the whole lesson
the trace of a tear glistened on her thin cheek

questions.prompt: What different consequences do Jane and Helen imagine when they discuss breaking the rod?
facilitatorNotes: Jane imagines resisting the source of pain; Helen considers expulsion, relatives, and religious duty. Discuss the reasoning without presenting a child’s endurance of abuse as an obligation for readers.
evidence: I should break it under her nose.
evil consequences will extend to all connected with you

days.title: Jane Eyre excerpt: What can overcome hate?
days.challenge: Follow a philosophical disagreement embedded in a friendship rather than a formal essay.
days.focus: Helen distinguishes forgiveness from approval, while Jane insists that resistance can limit further harm.
days.context: Helen has described her own inattention and her wish to complete her education. Jane continues to question her forgiving attitude toward people who punish her.
days.contentNote: Contains historical religious and colonial prejudice, discussion of violence and mistreatment, and religious reflections on death.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, contrasting teachers through the interrupted meditation; from ““And cross and cruel,” I added; but Helen Burns would not admit my addition: she kept” through “Helen sighed as her reverie fled, and getting up, obeyed the monitor without reply as without delay.”.

questions.prompt: How does Helen’s explanation of attention complicate Jane’s statement that it is easy to be careful?
facilitatorNotes: Interest, memory, and a teacher’s language affect Helen’s concentration. Her account of the imagined brook gives an inward experience Jane cannot assume everyone shares.
evidence: listening to the visionary brook
the information she communicates is often just what I wished to gain

questions.prompt: What practical argument does Jane give for resistance, and how does Helen challenge it?
facilitatorNotes: Jane argues that unchecked cruelty will worsen; Helen denies that violence reliably heals injury. Readers may find force in both without treating either speaker’s position as the entire novel’s verdict.
evidence: they would never alter, but would grow worse and worse
It is not violence that best overcomes hate

questions.prompt: What is the effect of the monitor’s command immediately after Helen’s vision of spiritual freedom?
facilitatorNotes: The return to a disordered drawer abruptly places a wide spiritual meditation inside petty institutional demands. Helen’s prompt obedience may look consistent, poignant, or limiting; ask for reasons.
evidence: I can so clearly distinguish between the criminal and his crime
go and put your drawer in order

days.title: Jane Eyre excerpt: Rules for other people
days.challenge: Connect physical deprivation, budgetary details, and dramatic irony in an extended institutional critique.
days.focus: The visitors’ clothing exposes the unequal application of Brocklehurst’s doctrine of self-denial.
days.context: Jane has spent several weeks at Lowood. Brocklehurst arrives to inspect the school, including Miss Temple’s decision to replace spoiled food.
days.contentNote: Contains deprivation, bullying over food, public shaming, religiously justified neglect, and coercive control of girls’ appearance.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, winter hardships through the Brocklehurst family’s arrival; from “My first quarter at Lowood seemed an age; and not the golden age either; it comprised” through “ but I had no time to listen to what they said; other matters called off and enchanted my attention.”.

questions.prompt: How does the account of older girls taking food show that neglect creates further harm among pupils?
facilitatorNotes: Scarcity becomes a pressure that reproduces coercion within the group. Jane’s account does not simply identify one bad pupil; it shows how insufficient provision shapes relations.
evidence: they would coax or menace the little ones out of their portion
forced from me by the exigency of hunger

questions.prompt: How does Brocklehurst redefine Miss Temple’s bread and cheese, and what does that redefinition let him avoid?
facilitatorNotes: He treats necessary replacement food as indulgence and hunger as spiritual opportunity. This lets him avoid judging the failure to supply an edible meal.
evidence: Who introduced this innovation? and by what authority?
you little think how you starve their immortal souls!

questions.prompt: Why is the timing of the family’s entrance more forceful than a direct statement that Brocklehurst is hypocritical?
facilitatorNotes: Their silk, furs, and elaborate curls answer his speech visually at the moment he condemns costly apparel and hair. Readers can compare the two standards for themselves.
evidence: these, I repeat, must be cut off
she wore a false front of French curls

days.title: Jane Eyre excerpt: A pedestal of infamy
days.challenge: Evaluate an accusation’s source and observe how spectacle amplifies a claim without verifying it.
days.focus: Helen’s small gesture creates a form of resistance that does not resemble Jane’s imagined retaliation.
days.context: Jane fears Brocklehurst will repeat Mrs. Reed’s charge of deceit. While trying to hide behind her slate, she accidentally drops it.
days.contentNote: Contains public humiliation of a child, threats of punishment, derogatory religious comparisons, and disability-related language used in an accusation.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, the broken slate through Helen’s passing smile; from “Hitherto, while gathering up the discourse of Mr. Brocklehurst and Miss Temple, I had” through “Miss Scatcherd’s can only see those minute defects, and are blind to the full brightness of the orb.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Miss Temple’s reassuring whisper hurt Jane instead of comforting her immediately?
facilitatorNotes: Jane values Miss Temple’s respect and fears the coming accusation will destroy it. Kindness raises the stakes because it is precisely the relationship Jane wishes to preserve.
evidence: I saw it was an accident; you shall not be punished.
The kind whisper went to my heart like a dagger.

questions.prompt: What evidence does Brocklehurst actually provide for the charge that Jane is a liar?
facilitatorNotes: He supplies Mrs. Reed’s account and her charitable reputation, not a tested incident or Jane’s defense. The staged elevation and audience reactions create an impression of certainty without adding evidence.
evidence: This I learned from her benefactress
her excellent patroness was obliged to separate her

questions.prompt: How does Helen’s smile challenge both the command to isolate Jane and the “untidy” label she herself wears?
facilitatorNotes: The smile conveys solidarity despite orders against speaking and reveals courage that official labels miss. The final planet image makes narrow fault-finding the object of criticism.
evidence: smiled at me as she again went by
blind to the full brightness of the orb

days.title: Up from Slavery: what should a school teach?
days.challenge: Compare educational diagnosis with the narrator’s assumptions about whose knowledge counts.
days.focus: The difference between applied learning and a restriction of ambition.
days.context: Tuskegee opens with thirty students, many already teachers. Washington explains the practical curriculum he wants and introduces Olivia Davidson, his fellow educator.
days.contentNote: This memoir describes enslavement, deprivation, and racial discrimination, and uses the racial terminology of its time. Washington’s views on slavery, Africa, labor, and racial progress were influential and contested in his own day; discussion first reconstructs his reasoning and then weighs it.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, opening through Davidson’s declaration of racial identity; begins “I CONFESS that what I saw during my month of travel and investigation left me with a very heavy”; ends “nd for no considerations would she consent to deceive any one in regard to her racial identity.”.

questions.prompt: What do the white opponents fear losing if Black people become educated? How does that fear differ from Washington’s criticism of book learning?
facilitatorNotes: Opponents fear losing farm and domestic labor; Washington criticizes knowledge detached from practical use. The motives differ, but readers should ask whether a practical curriculum could nevertheless satisfy restrictive expectations.
evidence: difficult to secure them for domestic service

questions.prompt: How do “banking and discount” and the multiplication table expose the distinction between a subject’s prestige and mastery?
facilitatorNotes: The examples question memorized labels and advanced-looking credentials without foundations. Not owning a bank account alone does not prove inability to understand banking, so the narrator’s examples deserve differentiated evaluation.
evidence: thoroughly to master the multiplication table

questions.prompt: Why close this portrait of Davidson with her refusal to conceal her racial identity?
facilitatorNotes: Her education and nursing already establish competence and commitment. The refusal adds integrity under pressure to trade identity for comfort, complicating any assumption that advancement simply means assimilating to white expectations.
evidence: under no circumstances and for no considerations

days.title: Up from Slavery: four attempts at a brick kiln
days.challenge: Distinguish the sequence of a practical experiment from the broader social claims drawn from it.
days.focus: Productive labor as learning, economic exchange, and persuasion.
days.context: With Tuskegee established, Washington explains why students construct buildings and manufacture bricks. The account includes both costly failures and later success.
days.contentNote: This memoir describes enslavement, deprivation, and racial discrimination, and uses the racial terminology of its time. Washington’s views on slavery, Africa, labor, and racial progress were influential and contested in his own day; discussion first reconstructs his reasoning and then weighs it.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, opening through the contrast with Greek analysis; begins “FROM the very beginning, at Tuskegee, I was determined to have the students do not only the agr”; ends “ first product, and with the demand will come the ability to appreciate it and to profit by it.”.

questions.prompt: Why does “I helped put it up” matter to Washington’s argument beyond the building’s price?
facilitatorNotes: The student claims responsibility and collective ownership, discouraging damage. Washington presents construction as a change in relationship to the school, not merely inexpensive labor.
evidence: That is our building. I helped put it up.

questions.prompt: What does the fourth kiln’s success establish, and what technical information is missing if someone wanted to reproduce the result?
facilitatorNotes: The sequence shows persistence, funding, and acquired skill, but does not specify the corrected kiln design, firing conditions, or clay properties. It is a memoir of learning rather than a usable manufacturing procedure.
evidence: This time, I am glad to say, we were successful.

questions.prompt: Washington argues that “the visible, the tangible” softens prejudice more than “pages of discussion.” How does the brickyard story support this, and why does the argument suit a school built on industrial training?
facilitatorNotes: Good bricks met a local need, white customers came, business interests became “intermingled,” and mutual dependence produced better relations, which he says brickmakers carried across the South. The principle justifies Tuskegee’s method of demonstrating skill rather than arguing in the abstract. Discussion can then ask what such demonstrations can change and what they cannot, such as laws.
evidence: the visible, the tangible

days.title: Up from Slavery: presenting a school to donors
days.challenge: Analyze how an autobiographer’s fundraising role shapes his portrait of wealthy supporters.
days.focus: Facts, dignity, gratitude, and the interests of a persuasive speaker.
days.context: Tuskegee needs another building. Washington describes Armstrong’s help and the strategies he develops while seeking support in Northern cities.
days.contentNote: This memoir describes enslavement, deprivation, and racial discrimination, and uses the racial terminology of its time. Washington’s views on slavery, Africa, labor, and racial progress were influential and contested in his own day; discussion first reconstructs his reasoning and then weighs it.
