excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, opening through unexpected gifts after disappointing journeys; begins “WHEN we opened our boarding department, we provided rooms in the attic of Porter Hall, our firs”; ends “ouraged, that generous help has come from some one who I had had little idea would give at all.”.

questions.prompt: Why is Armstrong’s offer more significant than simply arranging a speaking tour?
facilitatorNotes: Hampton pays expenses for a tour benefiting another school and lends its reputation and contacts. Washington uses the arrangement to depict education as a shared cause rather than competition for a fixed pool of money.
evidence: not in the interests of Hampton, but in the interests of Tuskegee

questions.prompt: Does Washington’s distinction between presenting facts and “begging” mean that the presentation is neutral?
facilitatorNotes: No. Selected facts about graduates and needed buildings aim to persuade, even without a blunt demand. The distinction protects dignity and gives donors a role, but his purpose still influences selection and emphasis.
evidence: the mere making known of the facts regarding Tuskegee

questions.prompt: What does Washington conclude from the two Boston visits, and how does that conclusion change the way he describes asking for money?
facilitatorNotes: He reads the contrast as a trend in which the cordial giver is becoming common, and he recasts the fundraiser as an agent doing the donors’ own work rather than a beggar. The reframing gives dignity to the asker and a share in the cause to the giver; it also addresses future donors among his readers. Students may weigh whether two visits can carry the trend, after stating his reasoning.
evidence: not as beggars, but as agents for doing their work

days.title: Up from Slavery: the Atlanta address
days.challenge: Track changes of audience and examine the terms concealed within memorable analogies.
days.focus: Economic interdependence, public rights, and the rhetoric of accommodation.
days.context: In 1895 Washington addresses the Cotton States and International Exposition in Atlanta, speaking to Southern white and Black listeners and Northern visitors. The speech, later called the Atlanta Compromise, made him nationally prominent and was both praised and sharply criticized.
days.contentNote: This memoir describes enslavement, deprivation, and racial discrimination, and uses the racial terminology of its time. Washington’s views on slavery, Africa, labor, and racial progress were influential and contested in his own day; discussion first reconstructs his reasoning and then weighs it.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIV, introduction and full reproduced Atlanta Exposition address; begins “THE Atlanta Exposition, at which I had been asked to make an address as a representative of the”; ends “d with our material prosperity, will bring into our beloved South a new heaven and a new earth.”.

questions.prompt: How does “Cast down your bucket where you are” change its practical meaning when Washington turns from Black listeners to white listeners?
facilitatorNotes: For Black listeners it urges local work, enterprise, and relationships; for white listeners it urges investment in and employment of their Black neighbors. The shared refrain presents unequal audiences as mutually dependent.
evidence: Cast down your bucket where you are

questions.prompt: What can the fingers-and-hand analogy make seem compatible, and what does it leave undefined?
facilitatorNotes: It combines social separation with cooperation in common progress. The boundaries of “purely social” remain unspecified; readers should test whether the metaphor obscures conflicts over institutions, power, and access.
evidence: as separate as the fingers, yet one as the hand

questions.prompt: How does the sentence about privileges of law complicate the claim that Washington simply rejects rights? Why can a reader still object to his priorities?
facilitatorNotes: He explicitly calls legal privileges important and right, yet ranks preparation and economic opportunity above agitation for social equality. That ordering can be criticized for delaying equal treatment even while the text affirms some rights.
evidence: It is important and right that all privileges of the law be ours

days.title: Up from Slavery: applause, criticism, and voting rights
days.challenge: Distinguish favorable testimony selected by an author from independent evaluation of his public policy.
days.focus: How a memoir represents critics and converts personal recognition into a political argument.
days.context: After reproducing the Atlanta address, Washington recounts praise, objections, invitations, and his own position on voting. The letters belong to the memoir’s original documentary record.
days.contentNote: This memoir describes enslavement, deprivation, and racial discrimination, and uses the racial terminology of its time. Washington’s views on slavery, Africa, labor, and racial progress were influential and contested in his own day; discussion first reconstructs his reasoning and then weighs it.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIV, reception of the address through chapter’s conclusion; begins “The first thing that I remember, after I had finished speaking, was that Governor Bullock rushe”; ends “er tests are required, they should be made to apply with equal and exact justice to both races.”.

questions.prompt: Compare the space and direct quotation given to praise with the treatment of Black critics. How does the difference shape the reader’s access to the dispute?
facilitatorNotes: Supporters receive named endorsements and full letters; critics are mainly paraphrased and said to have come around. Their exact arguments and evidence remain unavailable, so the memoir does not provide a balanced debate.
evidence: what they termed the "rights" of the race

questions.prompt: Why does Washington print Gilman’s letter in full, and why does he stress that he will judge “not only” the coloured schools’ exhibits “but also” the white schools’? How does the episode work in his account of the response to the Atlanta speech?
facilitatorNotes: The letter is documentary proof from a university president; the appointment shows recognition of his competence across the color line while the speech was being debated, supporting his conviction that “time will show” whether he is right. Readers may also ask how much one appointment can establish.
evidence: pass not only upon the exhibits of the coloured schools

questions.prompt: How do the final paragraphs combine a defense of voting with acceptance of restrictions? What condition does Washington insist upon?
facilitatorNotes: He says people learn self-government by voting and generally supports free suffrage, yet accepts temporary education or property tests. He demands equal application across races; readers may question whether even equally worded tests create unequal exclusions.
evidence: equal and exact justice to both races

days.title: The Manor Farm
days.challenge: Follow personification as an ordinary winter observation becomes an imagined historical season.
days.focus: The attraction and possible limits of timeless rural harmony.
days.context: Rills are small streams; catkins are hanging flower clusters. Compare the first description of thaw with the speaker’s later claim that the place seems outside seasonal change.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem THE MANOR FARM; begins “THE rock-like mud unfroze a little and rills”; ends “This England, Old already, was called Merry.”.

questions.prompt: What changes the speaker’s judgment of the thin February sunlight?
facilitatorNotes: The grouped farm, church and ancient yew give the light a setting of stillness and continuity. The change is in perception, not in the month itself.
evidence: Till I came down to the old Manor Farm,

questions.prompt: How does the solitary fly contribute to the scene’s apparent silence?
facilitatorNotes: A tiny ordinary disturbance emphasizes how little else moves or sounds. The poem keeps material life present within its near-suspended atmosphere.
evidence: Against a fly, a solitary fly.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker correct “Winter” to a season of unchangeable bliss?
facilitatorNotes: The personified winter seems to contain every season at once. That imaginative correction makes a local moment feel timeless; readers may find the resulting old England consoling or idealized.
evidence: Rather a season of bliss unchangeable

days.title: Memorabilia
days.challenge: Infer the unstated connection between a personal encounter and an apparently separate moorland memory.
days.focus: Selective remembrance and the unequal value people attach to the same experience.
days.context: Shelley is the poet named by the speaker. The listener has met him, but the poem provides no details of that encounter; its second half offers a different memory instead.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem MEMORABILIA; begins “Ah, did you once see Shelley plain,”; ends “  Well, I forget the rest.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the listener’s laughter matter after the speaker’s excited questions?
facilitatorNotes: It exposes a mismatch of value: the speaker treats the meeting as extraordinary while the witness does not share that awe. The poem leaves the listener’s exact feelings open.
evidence: My starting moves your laughter!

questions.prompt: How does the hand's-breadth of moor resemble the remembered encounter with Shelley?
facilitatorNotes: A tiny portion becomes luminous while surrounding miles or years fade. What matters to memory is not proportional to physical extent or duration.
evidence: Yet a hand's-breadth of it shines alone

questions.prompt: What does the eagle-feather provide that a detailed travel account would not?
facilitatorNotes: The single portable trace concentrates the encounter’s significance. The final forgetting may sound casual, but it reinforces the power of one chosen remnant.
evidence: Well, I forget the rest.

days.title: Sonnet XXI
days.challenge: Follow an argument that welcomes repetition but refuses to make speech sufficient.
days.focus: Reassurance through recurring words and the love that must also exist beyond them.
days.context: Sonnet XXI addresses a beloved who apparently finds repeated declarations tiresome. Iterance means repetition; the poem makes repetition audible rather than merely defending it.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem XXI; begins “Say over again, and yet once over again,”; ends “To love me also in silence with thy soul.”.

questions.prompt: How does the cuckoo comparison answer the complaint that repeated words are monotonous?
facilitatorNotes: The returning call belongs to the renewal of spring. Recurrence can signal living assurance rather than emptiness, though a reader may still hear the speaker’s need for reassurance.
evidence: Comes the fresh Spring in all her green completed.

questions.prompt: Why compare repeated declarations to numerous stars and flowers?
facilitatorNotes: Abundance in nature appears welcome, so the rhetorical questions challenge the idea that love’s affirmation can be excessive. Ask whether the comparison fully answers the beloved’s concern.
evidence: Who can fear

questions.prompt: How does the last line qualify the repeated command to speak?
facilitatorNotes: Words remain desirable but must correspond to inward, silent love. The ending prevents the poem from treating verbal repetition as a complete substitute for feeling.
evidence: To love me also in silence with thy soul.

days.title: A London Thoroughfare. 2 A.M.
days.challenge: Distinguish brightness from reassurance and follow the river metaphor into a paradox.
days.focus: A city full of light that leaves its observer estranged.
days.context: The speaker observes a London street at two in the morning. Separate details available to any watcher from judgments shaped by the speaker’s sense of not belonging.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem A London Thoroughfare.  2 A.M.; Macmillan 1914 printed pages 43–44; begins “They have watered the street,”; ends “And this is an alien city.”.

questions.prompt: How does the river comparison change between its first appearance and “leading nowhere”?
facilitatorNotes: At first it makes wet pavement and passing vehicles visually continuous; later it denies that movement has a meaningful destination. The metaphor shifts from appearance toward the speaker’s judgment.
evidence: A river leading nowhere.

questions.prompt: Why can the moon not light a city that already glitters?
facilitatorNotes: Artificial light overwhelms the weaker moon. Physical brightness does not bring emotional comfort, so the poem separates visibility from welcome.
evidence: She cannot light the city;

questions.prompt: What makes the thin, lustreless moon more valuable to this speaker than the bright street?
facilitatorNotes: Familiarity outweighs brilliance. The moon offers something recognizable within an alien setting; the ending does not establish that the city is intrinsically worthless.
evidence: I know the moon,

days.title: Journey
days.challenge: Track the personification of obligation and distinguish physical movement from imaginative possession.
days.focus: A traveler who cannot stop yet claims the beauty beside the road.
days.context: Care becomes an insistent companion in this poem. Read the interrupted movement around “Yet onward” aloud, then compare the opening wish to lie down with the ending’s account of feet and heart.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem JOURNEY; begins “AH, could I lay me down in this long grass”; ends “My feet to follow, and my heart to hold.”.

questions.prompt: How does the unrelenting hand give Care power over the traveler?
facilitatorNotes: It turns an abstract burden into a companion who physically pulls the speaker away from pleasant places. The speaker’s backward looks suggest divided attention rather than indifference to beauty.
evidence: Yet at my hand an unrelenting hand

questions.prompt: What is the effect of making vines wait, trees dance and roads beckon?
facilitatorNotes: The landscape seems to invite the speaker into a relationship. The repeated statement that only the heart responds distinguishes inward participation from the body’s continuing journey.
evidence: Only my heart, only my heart responds.

questions.prompt: Does the final claim that the world belongs to the speaker cancel the earlier weariness?
facilitatorNotes: It offers imaginative possession while the feet still have to follow the road. The ending can be consoling without erasing fatigue; compare physical pain with the sustained reach of the eye.
evidence: My feet to follow, and my heart to hold.

days.title: Jane Eyre excerpt: A hearing instead of a verdict
days.challenge: Distinguish emotional reassurance from an evidence-based process for correcting a public accusation.
days.focus: Helen and Miss Temple offer different but complementary ways to resist a damaging reputation.
days.context: Brocklehurst has called Jane a liar before the school. Helen brings food after the punishment, and Miss Temple invites both girls to her room.
days.contentNote: Contains a distressed child’s wish to die, extreme descriptions of injury, historical racialized comparison, and memories of abuse.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, after the punishment through Miss Temple’s promise to write; from “Ere the half-hour ended, five o’clock struck; school was dismissed, and all were gone” through “head, her clustered and shining curls, and beaming dark eyes), she proceeded to address Helen Burns.”.

questions.prompt: What does Helen challenge when she replaces Jane’s “everybody” with eighty people and then millions?
facilitatorNotes: She challenges the apparent universality of shame, though Jane reasonably feels that the people she actually knows matter most. Discuss why perspective can help without erasing immediate pain.
evidence: there are only eighty people who have heard you called so
But what have I to do with millions?

questions.prompt: How does Miss Temple’s request differ from Brocklehurst’s public accusation?
facilitatorNotes: She identifies the source of the claim, invites a defense, asks for accuracy, and seeks corroboration. These are procedures for assessing truth rather than simply accepting status as authority.
evidence: add nothing and exaggerate nothing
I know something of Mr. Lloyd; I shall write to him

questions.prompt: Why does Jane notice that a restrained account sounds more credible?
facilitatorNotes: She has begun shaping experience for a listener, influenced by Helen’s counsel. Ask whether the passage exposes an unfair burden on an injured speaker, shows a useful rhetorical skill, or both.
evidence: Thus restrained and simplified, it sounded more credible
I felt as I went on that Miss Temple fully believed me.

days.title: Jane Eyre excerpt: What nourishment makes possible
days.challenge: Trace connections between bodily provision, intellectual freedom, and public recognition.
days.focus: The tea scene reveals capacities that punitive labels and deprivation conceal.
days.context: Miss Temple has heard Jane’s defense and will consult Mr. Lloyd. She now attends to Helen’s health and shares tea with both pupils.
days.contentNote: Contains hunger, illness, stigmatizing public punishment, and descriptions of an institution’s neglect.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, Helen’s health through Jane’s renewed studies; from ““How are you to-night, Helen? Have you coughed much to-day?”” through “I would not now have exchanged Lowood with all its privations for Gateshead and its daily luxuries.”.

questions.prompt: How does the seed-cake episode repeat and develop Miss Temple’s earlier response to the burnt breakfast?
facilitatorNotes: She recognizes a material shortfall and supplies food rather than redescribing hunger as a virtue. The personal gift also creates a setting where the girls can become guests instead of disciplined bodies.
evidence: Fortunately, I have it in my power to supply deficiencies for this once.
cut slices with a generous hand

questions.prompt: What does Helen’s conversation reveal that the next morning’s “Slattern” label cannot capture?
facilitatorNotes: Her eloquence, knowledge, and responsiveness flourish under kindness. Contrast the detailed account of her intellectual life with the single public label about tidiness.
evidence: a beauty neither of fine colour nor long eyelash
the word “Slattern,”

questions.prompt: How do Jane’s bedtime imaginings change after she is publicly cleared?
facilitatorNotes: Imagined meals yield to drawings and possible reading in French. The change links recognition and educational access to a future she can make rather than merely a need she can imagine satisfying.
evidence: I feasted instead on the spectacle of ideal drawings
all the work of my own hands

days.title: Jane Eyre excerpt: Spring outside the sickroom
days.challenge: Read a beautiful landscape against the narrative’s delayed disclosure of suffering.
days.focus: The contrast between new freedom and epidemic exposes unequal experiences of the same place.
days.context: Spring arrives at Lowood, but an outbreak of illness changes the school’s routines. Helen is separately ill with what the period called consumption.
days.contentNote: Contains epidemic illness and deaths of children. The narration’s historical explanations of disease are part of the novel, not current medical guidance; a historical derogatory group term is retained.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, spring at Lowood through the nurse’s refusal; from “But the privations, or rather the hardships, of Lowood lessened. Spring drew on: she ” through “lroom: I was just in time; it was nine o’clock, and Miss Miller was calling the pupils to go to bed.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator describe the landscape’s beauty before revealing the reason for Jane’s freedom?
facilitatorNotes: The delayed explanation unsettles an apparently joyful seasonal change. Readers learn that pleasure and liberty coexist with, and partly result from, other pupils’ illness.
evidence: for this unwonted liberty and pleasure there was a cause
transformed the seminary into an hospital

questions.prompt: What does the improved food during the crisis suggest about the school’s earlier claims of necessary economy?
facilitatorNotes: The absence of inspection and a more liberal housekeeper change portions. The text suggests that previous deprivation was tied to management choices, not simply an unavoidable shortage.
evidence: household matters were not scrutinised into
our breakfast-basins were better filled

questions.prompt: How does Jane’s understanding of “she’ll not be here long” show a change in her relation to death?
facilitatorNotes: She would formerly have understood a journey home, but now recognizes impending death. The beautiful evening helps sharpen her attachment to the present world and her uncertainty about what follows.
evidence: would have only conveyed the notion that she was about to be removed to Northumberland
but I knew instantly now!

days.title: Jane Eyre excerpt: Keeping company at the last
days.challenge: Hold faith, uncertainty, care, and grief in tension during a scene narrated across different times.
days.focus: Jane’s concrete presence answers Helen’s need even when their beliefs do not become identical.
days.context: Learning that Helen may soon die, Jane leaves the dormitory at night to find her in Miss Temple’s room.
days.contentNote: Contains a child’s death, grief, religious discussion of the afterlife, and Helen’s belief that others will not miss her. Discuss those judgments as her perspective, not as a measure of her worth.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, the nighttime visit through the grave inscription; from “It might be two hours later, probably near eleven, when I—not having been able to fal” through “ound; but now a grey marble tablet marks the spot, inscribed with her name, and the word “Resurgam.””.

questions.prompt: How does Helen continue to care for Jane even while she is gravely ill?
facilitatorNotes: Her attention turns to Jane’s bare feet, warmth, and need for reassurance. These practical actions embody their friendship alongside the larger religious statements.
evidence: your little feet are bare; lie down and cover yourself with my quilt
Are you warm, darling?

questions.prompt: Why does Jane ask some questions aloud but keep “Does it exist?” to herself?
facilitatorNotes: Her uncertainty persists beside Helen’s assurance, while physical closeness becomes more urgent than resolving doctrine. Different readings of tact, fear, or the limits of language can be supported.
evidence: I believe; I have faith: I am going to God.
Where is that region? Does it exist?

questions.prompt: What do the delayed report of death and the final grave inscription add to the scene?
facilitatorNotes: The child learns what happened afterward, while the adult narrator extends the scene into years of memory. “Resurgam,” meaning “I shall rise again,” preserves a statement of hope without requiring Jane’s childhood questions to disappear.
evidence: I was asleep, and Helen was—dead.
for fifteen years after her death it was only covered by a grassy mound

days.title: Jane Eyre excerpt: Inventing a way out
days.challenge: Analyze changes in narrative pace and the difference between imagined freedom and an achievable plan.
days.focus: Jane transforms longing into an action available to a young woman with limited money and connections.
days.context: After the epidemic, Lowood is reformed. Jane remains for six years as a pupil and two as a teacher; Miss Temple’s marriage then changes her sense of belonging.
days.contentNote: Contains retrospective references to children’s deaths and an ethnic stereotype in the description of a teacher.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, the eight-year transition through posting the advertisement; from “Hitherto I have recorded in detail the events of my insignificant existence: to the f” through “e post-office, and came back through heavy rain, with streaming garments, but with a relieved heart.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator pass over eight years after describing a few childhood days in such detail?
facilitatorNotes: She openly makes selection a principle of autobiography: uniform years can be compressed while formative conflicts receive space. Ask what this reveals about memory as composition rather than a complete record.
evidence: I now pass a space of eight years almost in silence
invoke Memory where I know her responses will possess some degree of interest

questions.prompt: What distinction does Jane make between losing the power to be tranquil and losing the reason for tranquility?
facilitatorNotes: She does not simply become incapable after Miss Temple leaves; she discovers that her settled life depended on a particular relationship and no longer answers her desires. This makes departure an emerging choice as well as a loss.
evidence: it was not the power to be tranquil which had failed me
the reason for tranquillity was no more

questions.prompt: How does “a new servitude” become a more effective phrase than “Liberty” in Jane’s planning?
facilitatorNotes: It names a limited but practical change: paid work in another household. The advertisement and postal arrangements convert the inward wish into a concrete action without pretending she has escaped dependence entirely.
evidence: grant me at least a new servitude!
I had it in a clear practical form

days.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: choosing a house and learning to listen
days.challenge: Distinguish a reformer’s initial theories from the corrections offered by neighbors and experience.
days.focus: Reciprocity and the limits of speaking for a community.
days.context: In 1889 Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr establish Hull-House in Chicago. This 1910 memoir recalls both their hopes and the objections raised to their plan.
days.contentNote: Addams writes as a settlement-house founder about immigrants and poverty. Historical ethnic labels, class assumptions, and some patronizing judgments are preserved for critical reading, not endorsed.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, opening through the first guest’s lesson for public speaking; begins “THE next January found Miss Starr and myself in Chicago, searching for a neighborhood in which ”; ends “iousness that I had an auditor who knew the conditions more intimately than I could hope to do.”.

questions.prompt: Why can companionship be both a “cave” and a means of remaining in touch with the world?
facilitatorNotes: A group can become absorbed in itself, yet colleagues also challenge assumptions and support practical work. Addams acknowledges the criticism instead of presenting communal residence as automatically beneficial.
evidence: lose themselves in the cave of their own companionship

questions.prompt: What does the reporter’s refusal to accept the translated song reveal about the label “anarchist”?
facilitatorNotes: The label controls his interpretation before he understands the words. When a harmless translation fails to dislodge suspicion, the incident exposes prejudice masquerading as investigation.
evidence: had probably "fooled" me

questions.prompt: How does the first guest change Addams’s later speaking practice? Why is bringing a neighbor more than a courtesy?
facilitatorNotes: Visitors mistake an educated neighbor for an outsider and generalize about people in front of her. Addams thereafter brings a local listener who can check her own sweeping claims, introducing accountability into representation.
evidence: curb any hasty generalization

days.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: streets, stories, and classes
days.challenge: Connect spatial description with institutions while noticing whose assumptions govern the description.
days.focus: Education as social experience within unequal material conditions.
days.context: After moving in, the residents learn about the neighborhood’s housing, work, reading groups, and children. The passage shifts repeatedly between public conditions and small encounters.
days.contentNote: Addams writes as a settlement-house founder about immigrants and poverty. Historical ethnic labels, class assumptions, and some patronizing judgments are preserved for critical reading, not endorsed.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, description of Halsted Street through school-to-work clubs; begins “Halsted Street has grown so familiar during twenty years of residence that it is difficult to r”; ends “roduction in manual training is given, nor have they been caught by any other abiding interest.”.

questions.prompt: How does calling poor housing temporary help it remain unchanged for two generations?
facilitatorNotes: Officials and owners tolerate conditions they would reject as permanent, while families actually grow up amid them. The contradiction exposes how a convenient label can delay responsibility.
evidence: until at least two generations of children have been born and reared in them

questions.prompt: Why place the reading group’s dinner and dishwashing beside its study of Romola?
facilitatorNotes: Shared domestic activity makes participants guests and contributors, joining serious reading with social exchange. The photographs and food are part of a setting for learning, not merely distractions from it.
evidence: help us wash the dishes afterwards

questions.prompt: What conflict does the sewing class reveal between a teacher’s standard of neatness and the girls’ standard for a useful day?
facilitatorNotes: The teacher values skill and careful practice, while girls urgently need a garment to take home. Poverty changes the cost of a lesson; dismissing their priorities as laziness would ignore the evidence.
evidence: count the day lost when they could not carry home a garment

days.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: old neighbors and shared needs
days.challenge: Read anecdotes of connection alongside examples that resist an easy story of successful reform.
days.focus: How shared experience can challenge categories of deserving neighbors.
days.context: Addams insists that Hull-House should serve adults as well as children. The passage ends by moving from individual encounters to the organization’s formal purpose.
days.contentNote: Addams writes as a settlement-house founder about immigrants and poverty. Historical ethnic labels, class assumptions, and some patronizing judgments are preserved for critical reading, not endorsed. Includes brief accounts of domestic violence, infant neglect and death, and illness.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, adult participation through the charter statement; begins “In spite of these flourishing clubs for children early established at Hull-House, and the fact ”; ends “rprises, and to investigate and improve the conditions in the industrial districts of Chicago."”.

questions.prompt: How does discovering the ninety-year-old woman’s Gaelic change her social position?
facilitatorNotes: Someone first treated chiefly as a troublesome tenant becomes a bearer of valued knowledge, and the neighborhood feels pride. The change suggests that education can uncover existing capacities as well as teach new ones.
evidence: the neighborhood was filled with pride

questions.prompt: Why does the old settler’s memory of a “Yankee notion” answer his complaint about foreign pictures?
facilitatorNotes: A familiar object once comforted him away from home; recognizing the parallel makes immigrants’ attachment to familiar images intelligible. The analogy invites sympathy without requiring identical histories.
evidence: they feel as we did when we saw a Yankee notion from Down East

questions.prompt: What does the woman’s surprise at American roses reveal about access that the distance to a florist or park would conceal?
facilitatorNotes: Physical proximity does not ensure knowledge, time, confidence, or companionship for visiting. Her restricted experience warns against assuming that a nearby amenity is meaningfully available to everyone.
evidence: no one had taken her

days.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: education without an outlet
days.challenge: Follow an argument that changes the apparent beneficiary of social service.
days.focus: The costs of separating educated young people from useful action.
days.context: Addams reprints part of a lecture delivered in 1892, framing it with later recollections. Her “subjective necessity” concerns what draws privileged young people toward settlement work.
days.contentNote: Addams writes as a settlement-house founder about immigrants and poverty. Historical ethnic labels, class assumptions, and some patronizing judgments are preserved for critical reading, not endorsed.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, introductory recollection and first portion of the Plymouth lecture; begins “THE Ethical Culture Societies held a summer school at Plymouth, Massachusetts, in 1892, to whic”; ends “the need of putting theory into action, and respond quickly to the Settlement form of activity.”.

questions.prompt: Why retain an early lecture rather than rewrite the motives entirely from the older narrator’s perspective?
facilitatorNotes: Addams wants the freshness of early aspirations and records the movement’s own acceptance of the statement. The framing also lets her qualify the title and distinguish the original hopes from later knowledge.
evidence: impossible to formulate with the same freshness

questions.prompt: How does the hotel window organize the imagined traveler’s relationship to working people?
facilitatorNotes: The glass lets the traveler observe labor while remaining socially separated from it; the waiter creates a moment of possible fellowship. The scene illustrates alienation among the comfortable as well as material inequality.
evidence: the plate-glass window of your hotel

questions.prompt: What contradiction does Addams locate in the upbringing of educated daughters? How does the unused-limbs analogy sharpen it?
facilitatorNotes: Families cultivate altruism and teach about suffering, then forbid sustained action when daughters return from college. Limbs trained or withheld unevenly make the resulting incapacity seem produced by education rather than natural weakness.
evidence: allowed to use their legs but not their arms

days.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: a chorus and an experiment
days.challenge: Distinguish the author’s religious interpretation from the operational principles of her institution.
days.focus: Reciprocity, mixed motives, and evidence in reform.
days.context: The lecture turns from frustrated young people to religious motives, then describes the settlement as a flexible experiment rather than a finished solution.
days.contentNote: Addams writes as a settlement-house founder about immigrants and poverty. Historical ethnic labels, class assumptions, and some patronizing judgments are preserved for critical reading, not endorsed. This is Addams’s interpretation of Christianity and early Christian history; readers can evaluate the argument without sharing its beliefs.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, Christian humanitarianism through the lecture’s conclusion; begins “Other motives which I believe make toward the Settlement are the result of a certain renaissanc”; ends “refore identical with that necessity, which urges us on toward social and individual salvation.”.

questions.prompt: In the chorus analogy, what does the settlement receive from its neighbors rather than simply give them?
facilitatorNotes: It receives collective strength, volume, and shared purpose in exchange for cultivated individual voices. The image challenges a one-way gift model even though it still distinguishes levels of training.
evidence: the volume and strength of the chorus

questions.prompt: Why does Addams allow a desire for applause into her account of noble motives?
facilitatorNotes: She admits that self-sacrifice can coexist with ambition and a wish for wider approval. This complicates a purely selfless founding story and supports her claim that analyzing motives is imperfect.
evidence: bass notes from toughened palms

questions.prompt: How can sympathy be an instrument for collecting facts without allowing sympathy to decide the facts in advance?
facilitatorNotes: Living beside neighbors may reveal otherwise inaccessible experiences, while patience and openness to correction discipline the inquiry. The passage establishes a productive tension; it does not supply a guarantee against confirmation bias.
evidence: scientific patience in the accumulation of facts

days.title: The Path
days.challenge: Distinguish a path’s actual uses from the destination imagined for it.
days.focus: Childhood attention, traces of movement and an abruptly limited promise.
days.context: A narrow raised path runs beside a road above a steep wood. Draw its spatial relation to the road before interpreting its apparent legendary destination.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem THE PATH; begins “RUNNING along a bank, a parapet”; ends “And stay; till, sudden, it ends where the wood ends.”.

questions.prompt: How do children and adults use the same landscape differently?
facilitatorNotes: Children take the elevated path to look into the steep wood; adults remain with the road’s view and secondhand reports. The contrast concerns chosen attention as well as height.
evidence: and what the children tell.

questions.prompt: What do the liquid comparisons suggest about generations of children who are rarely actually seen?
facilitatorNotes: Trickling silver and a current of feet make repeated movement visible in the worn surface. The path bears accumulated presence despite the present absence of children.
evidence: With the current of their feet, year after year.

questions.prompt: How does the last clause revise the imagined legendary destination?
facilitatorNotes: The path’s promise stops at the literal edge of the wood. Discuss whether this ending punctures fantasy, returns us to attentive observation, or preserves the attraction of imagining.
evidence: till, sudden, it ends where the wood ends.

days.title: Confessions
days.challenge: Reconstruct remembered space from a sickroom’s objects and assess the speaker’s ironic concessions.
days.focus: A dying speaker’s defense of remembered pleasure against an expected confession.
days.context: A religious visitor appears to ask a dying person about sorrow and repentance. Physic bottles contain medicine; the speaker uses their arrangement to recover a past meeting.
days.contentNote: A deathbed speaker recalls a concealed romantic meeting; the poem invites analysis of the speaker’s perspective.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem CONFESSIONS; begins “What is he buzzing in my ears?”; ends “  But then, how it was sweet!”.

questions.prompt: How does the question about a vale of tears set up an answer the speaker refuses to give?
facilitatorNotes: The visitor seems to expect a sorrowful view of life, but the speaker recalls sweetness instead. The poem makes the visitor’s framing audible without letting it determine the conclusion.
evidence: Ah, reverend sir, not I!

questions.prompt: How do the curtain and ether bottle transform the sickroom?
facilitatorNotes: The curtain supplies a June sky and a bottle becomes the remembered house. The speaker’s imaginative map replaces medical objects with the setting of desire.
evidence: Is the house o'er-topping all.

questions.prompt: How sincere is the ending’s description of the meeting as sad, bad and mad?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker borrows a condemning vocabulary but answers it with remembered sweetness. A reading can hear apology, playful defiance, or both; explain the final contrast.
evidence: But then, how it was sweet!

days.title: Sonnet XXVIII
days.challenge: Reconstruct a relationship’s development from a sequence of letters without assuming the final letter’s content.
days.focus: Material traces of intimacy and the boundary between expression and privacy.
days.context: Sonnet XXVIII describes the speaker handling saved letters. The poem quotes or paraphrases several messages, then refuses to disclose the last one.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem XXVIII; begins “My letters! all dead paper, mute and white!”; ends “If, what this said, I dared repeat at last!”.

questions.prompt: How does the opening make paper seem both lifeless and alive?
facilitatorNotes: The letters cannot speak by themselves, yet the speaker’s trembling touch and remembered messages make them quiver with significance. The contrast joins physical fragility with emotional force.
evidence: all dead paper, mute and white!

questions.prompt: What progression appears between a proposed visit, a declaration of love and “I am thine”?
facilitatorNotes: The sequence moves from friendship and an arranged meeting toward explicit commitment. Changes in the speaker’s bodily response make those steps emotionally consequential rather than merely chronological.
evidence: Said, Dear I love thee; and I sank and quailed

questions.prompt: Why is the withheld final message an important ending rather than missing information to be supplied?
facilitatorNotes: The refusal protects intimacy and makes the reader feel the limits of access. The text does not permit us to reconstruct its exact words, though we can discuss the intensity implied by withholding.
evidence: If, what this said, I dared repeat at last!

days.title: The Pike
days.challenge: Reconstruct one brief movement from shifting colors and changes in visibility.
days.focus: A fish perceived through reflected light rather than an explanatory description.
days.context: Read once to locate fish, reeds and opposite bank. Then mark which expressions describe the animal directly and which describe the light through which it appears.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem The Pike; Macmillan 1914 printed pages 234–235; begins “In the brown water,”; ends “Received it.”.

questions.prompt: How does the opening make the pike difficult to distinguish from its surroundings?
facilitatorNotes: Shade, brown water and stem shadows conceal its still body. The movement of its tail makes it newly perceptible.
evidence: He lay unnoticed.

questions.prompt: Why describe brightness as running under the water instead of simply saying the fish swims?
facilitatorNotes: The observer perceives moving color and light. The wording makes the visual effect occupy the grammatical place that a named fish might normally take.
evidence: And a green-and-copper brightness

questions.prompt: How can the fish be both darkness and a gleam, and what happens to it at the end?
facilitatorNotes: Shade and reflected light coexist on the moving form. Willow reflections receive it, dissolving a sharply identified creature back into its visual surroundings rather than asserting that it has left the pool.
evidence: A darkness and a gleam,

days.title: Song of a Second April
days.challenge: Follow the placement of one exception within a sustained account of seasonal recurrence.
days.focus: A returning spring whose continuities sharpen a personal absence.
days.context: Hepaticas are early spring flowers, and mullein is a plant with tall stalks. The title’s second April invites comparison with a previous spring; distinguish what repeats from what cannot return.
days.contentNote: The poem centers on the absence of a deeply loved person.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem SONG OF A SECOND APRIL; begins “APRIL this year, not otherwise”; ends “You that alone I cared to keep.”.

questions.prompt: How do dazzling mud and dingy snow complicate an idealized spring scene?
facilitatorNotes: Brightness and dullness coexist in ordinary transitional weather. The mixed description gives the repeated season a concrete texture rather than making it unbroken prettiness.
evidence: Of dazzling mud and dingy snow;

questions.prompt: What does the contrast between merry workers and earnest children contribute?
facilitatorNotes: The adults and children both participate fully in continuing life, but their expected moods are playfully reversed. Their activity intensifies the contrast with the absent person.
evidence: And children earnest at their play.

questions.prompt: Why delay the statement that “only you are gone” until almost the end?
facilitatorNotes: The accumulated evidence of recurrence makes the exception sharper. “Only” minimizes the number of changes while the last line makes that one loss emotionally decisive.
evidence: You that alone I cared to keep.

days.title: Silas Marner excerpt: How a village invents a stranger
days.challenge: Distinguish the narrator’s account from the villagers’ confident but unsupported explanations.
days.focus: Collective storytelling turns unfamiliar work, appearance, and illness into suspicion.
days.context: The novel opens in rural England before rapid transport and communication. Silas is a linen weaver who came to Raveloe from another town.
days.contentNote: Includes stigmatizing descriptions of illness and disability, class prejudice, and supernatural explanations for medical symptoms.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, opening portrait of weavers and Raveloe; from “In the days when the spinning-wheels hummed busily in the farmhouses--and even great ” through “ner had laid by a fine sight of money somewhere, and that he could buy up "bigger men" than himself.”.

questions.prompt: Why does knowing someone’s father and mother count as an explanation of that person in the opening paragraph?
facilitatorNotes: Kinship supplies the village’s standard of trust; a mobile worker lacks the social network that makes familiar conduct seem intelligible. The question exposes a limit of local knowledge.
evidence: how was a man to be explained unless you at least knew somebody who knew his father and mother?

questions.prompt: How does the description of fearful imaginations qualify the villagers’ claims about the weaver’s eyes?
facilitatorNotes: Fear is well supplied with memories while desire and hope lack images. The passage locates the threatening interpretation in observers rather than proving that Silas has harmful powers.
evidence: a perpetual pasture to fear

questions.prompt: What changes during Silas’s fifteen years in Raveloe: the evidence, the frequency of stories, or their credibility?
facilitatorNotes: The villagers repeat their stories less but believe them more. Habit creates apparent certainty without new evidence; his useful weaving helps protect him without making him understood.
evidence: they did not say them quite so often, but they believed them much more strongly when they did say them.

days.title: Silas Marner excerpt: A verdict built from betrayal
days.challenge: Follow the difference between certainty, material evidence, and a procedure treated as infallible.
days.focus: The betrayal of friendship becomes a crisis of faith when the community refuses another explanation.
days.context: The narrator now looks back to Silas’s life before Raveloe. At Lantern Yard he belonged to a close religious congregation and was engaged to Sarah.
days.contentNote: Contains theft, a false accusation, religious exclusion, death, and a spiritual crisis.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, Lantern Yard recollections through departure; from “But while opinion concerning him had remained nearly stationary, and his daily habits” through “fterwards it was known to the brethren in Lantern Yard that Silas Marner had departed from the town.”.

questions.prompt: How do William Dane’s confidence and Silas’s self-doubt influence their standing before the theft occurs?
facilitatorNotes: Assurance looks like spiritual authority, while honest uncertainty makes Silas vulnerable. Ask whether the community has mistaken a manner of speaking for evidence of character.
evidence: calling and election sure

questions.prompt: Why do the knife, the money bag, and the drawing of lots fail to give Silas a fair hearing?
facilitatorNotes: The objects can be planted, and Silas recalls lending the knife. The lots are treated as divine judgment rather than a test capable of considering his explanation. Distinguish what readers suspect from what the congregation establishes.
evidence: God will clear me.
you have woven a plot to lay the sin at my door.

questions.prompt: What does the narrator ask of readers by describing sorrows arising from false ideas?
facilitatorNotes: Readers need not accept the congregation’s beliefs to recognize the depth of Silas’s loss. The narrator separates compassionate understanding from agreement with an explanation of events.
evidence: sorrows that spring from false ideas for which no man is culpable

days.title: Silas Marner excerpt: The cure that deepens exile
days.challenge: Trace how the same action acquires different meanings for Silas and his neighbors.
days.focus: Work and healing briefly connect past and present, but a community’s expectations obstruct reciprocity.
days.context: Silas has left Lantern Yard after a false accusation and moved to Raveloe. His old religious language and friendships no longer provide security.
days.contentNote: Contains illness, historically described herbal treatment, and superstitious suspicion of a healer.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, displacement through Sally Oates’s recovery; from “Even people whose lives have been made various by learning, sometimes find it hard to” through “hood, heightened the repulsion between him and his neighbours, and made his isolation more complete.”.

questions.prompt: What does the comparison with a child knowing one face and one lap explain about Silas’s lost faith?
facilitatorNotes: His beliefs were embodied in particular people and practices. Moving does not simply let him substitute another church for the community whose betrayal destroyed those associations.
evidence: as the little child knows nothing of parental love, but only knows one face and one lap

questions.prompt: How is weaving both a support and a sign of deprivation?
facilitatorNotes: Its repetitive purpose gets him through time, but the bridge image implies emptiness on either side. Work sustains life while narrowing the relations that give it meaning.
evidence: bridge over the loveless chasms of his life.

questions.prompt: Why does helping Sally Oates fail to establish the neighborly relationship it briefly promises?
facilitatorNotes: Silas acts from remembered care and limited knowledge; neighbors demand charms and interpret refusal as hostility. His refusal to deceive them is misunderstood as withholding power.
evidence: a sense of unity between his past and present life

days.title: Silas Marner excerpt: Coins, a pot, and a shrinking life
days.challenge: Read objects as evidence of emotional need without making them equivalent to human relationships.
days.focus: The narrator finds attachment and vulnerability beneath the outward appearance of a miser.
days.context: After a failed attempt to help his neighbors, Silas withdraws into weaving and saving the money his work earns.
days.contentNote: Contains loneliness and references to imprisonment and deprivation.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, accumulation through the fifteenth Christmas; from “Gradually the guineas, the crowns, and the half-crowns, grew to a heap, and Marner dr” through “er Marner's life, and his history became blent in a singular manner with the life of his neighbours.”.

questions.prompt: Why would exchanging Silas’s coins for other coins of the same value feel like a loss to him?
facilitatorNotes: Their individual surfaces have become familiar companions. The economic equivalence of coins cannot explain his attachment, which gives money the role once held by people.
evidence: unknown faces

questions.prompt: How does the broken brown pot complicate a description of Silas as merely greedy?
facilitatorNotes: He values its service and familiarity despite its negligible resale value. Keeping the fragments shows a capacity for affectionate memory that still seeks an object.
evidence: for a memorial.

questions.prompt: What tension joins the imagined unborn children to the image of a shrinking stream?
facilitatorNotes: The gold appears to promise a future increase, yet the narrator describes a diminishing inner life. Expansion of possessions and expansion of life are moving in opposite directions.
evidence: as if they had been unborn children
a little shivering thread

days.title: Silas Marner excerpt: Borrowing courage from tomorrow
days.challenge: Separate the pressures on Godfrey from the decisions by which he prolongs them.
days.focus: A secret marriage makes postponement attractive, while imagined rescue displaces responsibility.
days.context: Godfrey Cass is the eldest son of Raveloe’s wealthy squire. His brother Dunstan knows about Godfrey’s secret marriage and pressures him for money; Wildfire is Godfrey’s horse.
days.contentNote: Contains blackmail, hostile class and gender judgments, alcohol abuse, threats of violence, and a passing reference to suicide.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, Godfrey’s reflections and the arrangement to sell Wildfire; from “Godfrey stood, still with his back to the fire, uneasily moving his fingers among the” through “room, followed humbly by the unresenting Snuff--perhaps because she saw no other career open to her.”.

questions.prompt: Why can Godfrey face physical danger more readily than confession?
facilitatorNotes: Confession offers certain immediate shame, whereas concealment leaves room to imagine escape. The contrast identifies a moral limitation without claiming that he lacks every form of courage.
evidence: rather trust to casualties than to his own resolve

questions.prompt: What does the horse bargain reveal about the brothers’ different uses of uncertainty?
facilitatorNotes: Godfrey hopes the sale will repair a financial breach; Dunstan uses his knowledge of the marriage to dictate terms. Discuss how both shift costs into a future they have not secured.
evidence: Wildfire

questions.prompt: How does the last description of the dog alter the emotional effect of Godfrey’s suffering?
facilitatorNotes: His need for sympathy coexists with impatience toward a dependent creature. The ironic account of the dog’s limited alternatives quietly tests the generosity of his wish to be rescued.
evidence: perhaps because she saw no other career open to her.

days.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: food, coal, and a boarding club
days.challenge: Compare several experiments whose outcomes require different explanations.
days.focus: Local preferences, financial viability, and resident initiative.
days.context: Addams describes early programs at Hull-House. A public kitchen changes purpose, a coal cooperative closes, and working women establish their own boarding club.
days.contentNote: Addams writes as a settlement-house founder about immigrants and poverty. Historical ethnic labels, class assumptions, and some patronizing judgments are preserved for critical reading, not endorsed.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, opening through the Jane Club’s first three years; begins “IF the early American Settlements stood for a more exigent standard in philanthropic activities”; ends “ed all of the six apartments which the original building contained, and numbered fifty members.”.

questions.prompt: What did the kitchen’s planners know, and what had they failed to learn, before deciding what food to provide?
facilitatorNotes: They studied nutrition, cost, and long work hours but underestimated inherited tastes and local preferences. Useful technical knowledge did not by itself establish what neighbors wanted to eat.
evidence: We did not reckon, however, with the wide diversity

questions.prompt: Why do large gross receipts fail to show that the coal association can survive?
facilitatorNotes: Receipts measure money coming in, not the margin after costs and free coal distributions. Its compassionate policy can be intelligible while undermining solvency; the passage does not supply a full balance sheet.
evidence: could not remain solvent

questions.prompt: What difference between the coal association and the Jane Club does Addams tentatively connect to success?
facilitatorNotes: The boarding club answers a need articulated by the women themselves and remains under their management after initial help. Her “perhaps” appropriately leaves other possible causes open.
evidence: the members managed the club themselves

days.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: money with a history
days.challenge: Follow ethical reasoning that reaches a practical decision without claiming a universal formula.
days.focus: The relationship between charitable gifts and the labor practices that produce them.
days.context: Hull-House needs a building for the Jane Club. A large offer forces the residents to consider the donor’s treatment of working girls, then to examine related cases.
days.contentNote: Addams writes as a settlement-house founder about immigrants and poverty. Historical ethnic labels, class assumptions, and some patronizing judgments are preserved for critical reading, not endorsed. Includes discussion of slavery and exploitative labor.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, the Jane Club building dilemma through cooperative ideals; begins “It was in connection with our efforts to secure a building for the Jane Club, that we first fou”; ends “ve coal association," might well have convinced me of the persistency of the coöperative ideal.”.

questions.prompt: Why does a gift meant to house working girls become unacceptable when the donor is named?
facilitatorNotes: The donor is known for underpaying girls, so accepting his wealth would join relief to the practices generating the need. The intended benefit does not erase the money’s social history.
evidence: notorious for underpaying the girls

questions.prompt: What limits the public value of refusing the gift in this particular case?
facilitatorNotes: A Hull-House representative solicited it, making public exposure problematic. They can maintain a boundary without using the refusal as the public moral statement it might otherwise become.
evidence: our refusal of this money could not be made public

questions.prompt: What irony joins the New York settlement worker’s letter with the businessman’s daughter’s visit?
facilitatorNotes: The worker worries about the businessman’s ethics, while the businessman worries that the settlement lacks religious teaching. Each judges the other by a different account of moral legitimacy.
evidence: if his conscience was only clear

days.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: from neighborhood harm to factory law
days.challenge: Trace the movement from personal encounters to investigation, advocacy, legislation, and public response.
days.focus: Why compassion needs evidence and why passing a law does not settle its effects.
days.context: Addams recalls how residents learned about child labor and worked with Florence Kelley, unions, and other organizations for Illinois factory legislation.
days.contentNote: Addams writes as a settlement-house founder about immigrants and poverty. Historical ethnic labels, class assumptions, and some patronizing judgments are preserved for critical reading, not endorsed. Includes brief historical accounts of fatal workplace injury, a child’s suicide, and drugging and implied sexual exploitation of a young woman.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, opening through glass manufacturers’ opposition; begins “OUR very first Christmas at Hull-House, when we as yet knew nothing of child labor, a number of”; ends “hildren that they were convinced the manufacturing of glass could not be carried on without it.”.

questions.prompt: Why do the girls’ refusal of Christmas candy and the missing machine guard disrupt the residents’ expectations in different ways?
facilitatorNotes: The candy exposes exhausting labor behind a gift intended as pleasure. The uninstalled guard exposes employers’ failure to act even after death, overturning the assumption that shared horror would produce change.
evidence: they did nothing whatever

questions.prompt: What changes when Addams insists on adding carefully collected information to general impressions?
facilitatorNotes: Experience establishes an urgent problem but does not by itself map its extent or support enforceable remedies. Investigation connects neighborhood accounts to a legislative committee and a wider coalition.
evidence: add carefully collected information to our general impression

questions.prompt: Why does Addams describe a law’s operation as a limited referendum after the eight-hour provision is overturned?
facilitatorNotes: Experience under the law lets people judge consequences and debate later proposals more concretely. This is an analogy about learning and public support, not a claim that the statute was literally adopted by referendum.
evidence: discussed with experience and conviction

days.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: enforcement, unions, and consumers
days.challenge: Follow a social problem across workplace, city, state, and national scales.
days.focus: The gap between formal protection and the institutions that sustain it.
days.context: The first factory law exists, but Addams describes resistance to enforcement and the need for continuing organization among workers and consumers.
days.contentNote: Addams writes as a settlement-house founder about immigrants and poverty. Historical ethnic labels, class assumptions, and some patronizing judgments are preserved for critical reading, not endorsed.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, the pioneer ideal through conciliation and arbitration; begins “Fifteen years ago the State of Illinois, as well as Chicago, exhibited many characteristics of ”; ends “r justice and righteousness in industrial relations was made infinitely more difficult thereby.”.

questions.prompt: How does associating factory regulation with “anarchy” work as an argument, according to Addams?
facilitatorNotes: Opponents connect the law to Governor Altgeld’s unrelated pardon, using a feared label instead of analyzing the provisions. Readers can distinguish this association from an argument about costs or enforceability.
evidence: couple it with that detested word

questions.prompt: Why do union cards matter to women sewing at home, even when some workers know little of the organization’s theory?
facilitatorNotes: Cards connect access to better-paying work with collective organization. Material leverage can make a protective standard effective before every member develops the same political explanation.
evidence: you had a card

questions.prompt: What does the women’s club president’s rejected application reveal that a simple account of cooperation would omit?
facilitatorNotes: Working women fear a class outsider may not represent their interests, despite admiration for her. Her later leadership shows change over time without making their earlier distrust unintelligible.
evidence: seemed to belong to the other side

days.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: the labor museum
days.challenge: Examine how an exhibit changes the authority assigned to people already present in a community.
days.focus: Workmanship, historical comparison, and the risks of a reformer’s generalizations.
days.context: Addams explains how the Hull-House Labor Museum links immigrants’ older craft skills to industrial work and to their children’s lives.
days.contentNote: Addams writes as a settlement-house founder about immigrants and poverty. Historical ethnic labels, class assumptions, and some patronizing judgments are preserved for critical reading, not endorsed.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, opening through the account of household arts; begins “FROM our very first months at Hull-House we found it much easier to deal with the first generat”; ends “ch are such direct expressions of the solicitude and affection at the basis of all family life.”.

questions.prompt: What does the spinning woman offer that Addams’s abstract search for a bridge between generations had not?
facilitatorNotes: A concrete practice connects a parent’s skill, a child’s factory work, and a longer history of production. The proposed bridge becomes demonstrable rather than a plea that children simply respect their elders.
evidence: the inherited resources of their daily occupation

questions.prompt: How does the visit of Russian sewing women reverse the first unsuccessful attempt to entertain them?
facilitatorNotes: The women move from disappointed recipients of improvised hospitality to knowledgeable demonstrators. Existing skills become visible, turning guests into teachers and revising the hosts’ assumptions about them.
evidence: they themselves did the entertaining

questions.prompt: How should readers test the claim of peaceful, orderly industrial evolution against the tailor’s account of hardship?
facilitatorNotes: A sequence of tools can show technical relationships without proving that change is peaceful for workers. The tailor’s analogy and the description of cruelty complicate the museum’s smooth progress narrative.
evidence: Human progress is slow and perhaps never more cruel

days.title: The Combe
days.challenge: Track how one final event changes the meaning of an initially physical description.
days.focus: An ancient landscape darkened by human cruelty.
days.context: A combe is a hollow or valley. The poem describes a secluded place and then reveals an act that changes the speaker’s view of it.
days.contentNote: Describes a badger dug out and killed by hounds. Discussion concerns the speaker’s response to cruelty.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem THE COMBE; begins “THE Combe was ever dark, ancient and dark.”; ends “That most ancient Briton of English beasts.”.

questions.prompt: How does the opening make entry into the combe difficult for both people and light?
facilitatorNotes: Blocked mouth, sliding chalk and half precipices create enclosure and instability. The accumulation makes darkness a physical condition before it becomes an ethical one.
evidence: Its mouth is stopped with bramble, thorn, and briar;

questions.prompt: Why does the poem interrupt its list of excluded birds to admit the missel-thrush?
facilitatorNotes: The exception makes the setting particular rather than absolutely lifeless. Its attachment to juniper links a specific creature to the threatened vegetation.
evidence: Except the missel-thrush that loves juniper,

questions.prompt: What changes when the badger is called an ancient Briton rather than merely a beast?
facilitatorNotes: The phrase gives the animal a claim to historical belonging. Its killing seems an injury to the place’s continuity, explaining why the same combe now looks darker.
evidence: That most ancient Briton of English beasts.

days.title: A Face
days.challenge: Separate the imagined portrait from the living subject and examine what the speaker chooses to exclude.
days.focus: Idealization, artistic framing and the desire to hold a fleeting face.
days.context: The speaker imagines painting a face rather than describing an existing portrait. References to Tuscan art and Correggio contrast a gold-backed profile with clustered heavenly faces.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem A FACE; begins “If one could have that little head of hers”; ends “Which fears to lose the wonder, should it wink.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker exclude laughter from the desired portrait?
facilitatorNotes: Laughter disrupts the controlled profile the speaker calls perfect. This can reveal the limits of aesthetic idealization: a lively action is sacrificed to a composed image.
evidence: For that spoils all:

questions.prompt: How does the imagined hyacinth give the lips an action compatible with stillness?
facilitatorNotes: Leaning toward fragrant buds suggests movement and desire while preserving the soft open profile. The speaker constructs a pose rather than simply records the woman.
evidence: Burden of honey-colored buds to kiss

questions.prompt: What does the eye’s fear of blinking suggest about the supposed permanence of an ideal image?
facilitatorNotes: The final wonder remains transient despite elaborate framing. The spectator’s attention cannot fully arrest its emergence and fading.
evidence: Which fears to lose the wonder, should it wink.

days.title: Sonnet XXIX
days.challenge: Sustain a metaphor long enough to notice when its apparent beauty becomes an obstacle.
days.focus: The tension between thinking about a beloved and encountering that person directly.
days.context: Sonnet XXIX makes thoughts into climbing plants and the beloved into a tree. Track what each element does before deciding which form of closeness the speaker prefers.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem XXIX; begins “I think of thee!—my thoughts do twine and bud”; ends “I do not think of thee—I am too near thee.”.

questions.prompt: Why do the flourishing vines become a problem rather than an uncomplicated sign of love?
facilitatorNotes: Their leaves hide the very tree they grow around. Elaborate thoughts can conceal the beloved rather than bring the speaker closer.
evidence: Except the straggling green which hides the wood.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker ask the imagined tree to do, and how forceful is the request?
facilitatorNotes: It should shake away the encircling thoughts and renew its presence. Words of bursting and shattering make direct encounter an energetic clearing, not a gentle addition to fantasy.
evidence: Drop heavily down,—burst, shattered everywhere!

questions.prompt: How can not thinking of the beloved signify greater intimacy at the end?
facilitatorNotes: Immediate seeing, hearing and breathing with the person replace mediated imagining. The ending is a paradox about presence, not a claim of indifference.
evidence: I do not think of thee—I am too near thee.

days.title: The Giver of Stars
days.challenge: Connect apparently opposed elemental images with the changing purpose of the speaker’s requests.
days.focus: Intimacy imagined as both rest and preparation for outward creative action.
days.context: The poem is an address to a beloved. Follow its repeated requests, then compare the private rest in the first stanza with the public task imagined in the second.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem The Giver of Stars; Macmillan 1914 printed pages 97; begins “Hold your soul open for my welcoming.”; ends “And pour into it the beauty which you have begotten.”.

questions.prompt: What kind of relationship does the image of resting on another person’s peace propose?
facilitatorNotes: The beloved offers sustaining quiet rather than merely an object to admire. The request makes the speaker dependent on a receptive presence.
evidence: Outstretched upon your peace, as on a bed of ivory.

questions.prompt: How does fire complicate the earlier cool water image?
facilitatorNotes: The beloved can soothe exhaustion and restore energy. These are successive needs rather than necessarily inconsistent portraits.
evidence: The life and joy of tongues of flame,

questions.prompt: Who is responsible for the beauty offered to the world at the end?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker performs the outward act, but credits the beloved with generating its beauty. Discuss creative agency as shared, while noting that the future achievement remains hoped for.
evidence: And pour into it the beauty which you have begotten.

days.title: Wild Swans
days.challenge: Interpret a sudden shift from self-examination to direct address without treating a metaphor as a literal action.
days.focus: Weariness with inward questioning and an appeal to the freedom of moving birds.
days.context: The poem begins as the speaker watches swans pass overhead. Compare the repeated motions attributed to the heart with the swans’ continuing flight.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem WILD SWANS; begins “I looked in my heart while the wild swans went over.”; ends “The town again, trailing your legs and crying!”.

questions.prompt: What does “a question less or a question more” imply about the usefulness of looking inward?
facilitatorNotes: Changes in the number of questions fail to produce a new experience equal to flight. The phrase makes introspection seem repetitive and inconclusive.
evidence: Only a question less or a question more;

questions.prompt: How does the house metaphor make the heart feel confining?
facilitatorNotes: An airless house with a lockable door becomes an enclosure the speaker can imagine leaving. The action dramatizes a wish to escape a limiting inner life rather than a literal separation from the body.
evidence: House without air, I leave you and lock your door.

questions.prompt: Does calling the swans back achieve the freedom the speaker desires?
facilitatorNotes: The imperative expresses longing but does not report a response. Their legs and cries keep them embodied and independent; the ending opens outward while leaving the speaker’s transformation uncertain.
evidence: The town again, trailing your legs and crying!

days.title: Silas Marner excerpt: Desire pretending to be evidence
days.challenge: Trace the steps by which a convenient possibility becomes permission to steal.
days.focus: Dunstan’s reasoning grows more confident as it becomes less answerable to facts.
days.context: Dunstan has negotiated to sell Godfrey’s horse but rides it in the hunt before delivery. Silas’s isolated cottage lies on the route home.
days.contentNote: Contains a horse’s violent death, theft, and speculation about a person’s death.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, Wildfire’s fatal accident through Dunstan’s theft; from “Keating rode up now, and the transaction became more complicated. It ended in the pur” through “But when he had gone a yard or two, he might take his time. So he stepped forward into the darkness.”.

questions.prompt: How does Dunstan’s decision to hunt after agreeing a price expose his attitude toward consequences?
facilitatorNotes: He treats the bargain as an achievement while taking a risk that can destroy its condition. The horse’s death transfers the result of his pleasure to others as well as himself.
evidence: to be paid on the delivery of Wildfire, safe and sound, at the Batherley stables

questions.prompt: Why does the mist matter to both the practical action and Dunstan’s moral reasoning?
facilitatorNotes: It limits what he can see and reassures him that others cannot see him. Physical uncertainty therefore becomes an opportunity rather than a reason to pause.
evidence: mist is no screen when people get close to each other
the mist, helped by the evening darkness, was more of a screen than he desired

questions.prompt: What happens to the possibility that Silas has died once that idea has served Dunstan’s desire?
facilitatorNotes: A speculative death helps justify taking the money; its uncertainty then drops from his attention. The narrator’s generalization explains motivated reasoning rather than validating the inference.
evidence: A dull mind, once arriving at an inference that flatters a desire

days.title: Silas Marner excerpt: Searching the empty hiding place
days.challenge: Follow the bodily and mental sequence of discovery before judging the resulting accusation.
days.focus: Loss drives Silas toward other people, but desperation initially substitutes suspicion for evidence.
days.context: While Silas briefly leaves home to obtain twine, Dunstan steals his hidden savings. Readers know the thief; Silas returns unaware of the theft.
days.contentNote: Contains theft, severe distress, and a groundless accusation.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, Silas’s return through his walk to the Rainbow; from “When Dunstan Cass turned his back on the cottage, Silas Marner was not more than a hu” through “spirits-and-water where they could themselves hector and condescend in company that called for beer.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the explanation of the unlocked door matter when readers already know the thief?
facilitatorNotes: It reconstructs an ordinary chain of habits and practical decisions. The contrast between his sense of safety and readers’ knowledge makes the loss more painful than a simple lesson about carelessness.
evidence: forty years

questions.prompt: What do the dark-water comparison and the touch of the loom reveal about Silas’s search?
facilitatorNotes: He grasps at explanations that cannot support him, then seeks physical confirmation of reality. His response is rendered as shock and bereavement rather than only anger about money.
evidence: A man falling into dark water seeks a momentary footing even on sliding stones
strongest assurance of reality.

questions.prompt: Why does a human thief become, in one respect, a more bearable explanation than an unseen power?
facilitatorNotes: A person might be traced and the gold recovered. That hope makes an unsupported suspicion of Jem Rodney attractive and pushes Silas toward communal help.
evidence: Jem Rodney

days.title: Silas Marner excerpt: Words, witnesses, and a favorite story
days.challenge: Compare standards of proof in an amusing remembered wedding and a serious dispute about ghosts.
days.focus: The Rainbow conversation shows how custom, performance, and social agreement establish local truth.
days.context: At the village inn, the Rainbow, regulars exchange familiar stories. Mr. Macey remembers a wedding in which the clergyman confused the words; Dowlas is the farrier.
days.contentNote: Contains a child’s death, demeaning language about mental illness, and ghost stories.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, Mr. Macey’s wedding story through the debate about ghosts; from “"Ay, you remember when first Mr Lammeter's father came into these parts, don't you, M” through “n deep disgust at the farrier's crass incompetence to apprehend the conditions of ghostly phenomena.”.

questions.prompt: What is at stake in Macey’s distinction between the meaning and the words of a wedding?
facilitatorNotes: The anecdote tests whether intention, spoken formula, or official record creates a valid bond. The glue comparison makes an abstract disagreement tangible and comic.
evidence: Is't the meanin' or the words as makes folks fast i' wedlock?

questions.prompt: Why compare the repeated story to a favorite tune?
facilitatorNotes: Listeners value the expected turns and their own opportunities to participate. Familiarity is a source of communal pleasure, even when no new information is supplied.
evidence: as if it had been a favourite tune

questions.prompt: Does the proposed ghost wager create a test both sides could accept?
facilitatorNotes: Fear prevents volunteers, while disputes about who can see ghosts make agreement about observation unlikely. The landlord’s compromise preserves sociability without resolving the factual dispute.
evidence: the truth lies between 'em.

days.title: Silas Marner excerpt: A stranger finds witnesses
days.challenge: Notice small changes in group behavior while keeping the villagers’ mistakes in view.
days.focus: Sympathy begins before complete understanding, and Silas withdraws an accusation when contrary evidence arrives.
days.context: Silas reaches the Rainbow after discovering that his savings are gone. The men inside have just been debating ghosts; he suspects the local poacher Jem Rodney.
days.contentNote: Contains theft, fear, and an accusation unsupported by evidence.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, Silas’s entrance through departure with help; from “Yet the next moment there seemed to be some evidence that ghosts had a more condescen” through “rs before him, not as those do who long to rest, but as those who expect to "watch for the morning."”.

questions.prompt: What does the image of pipes moving like insect antennae do to the group’s first reaction?
