facilitatorNotes: It makes their simultaneous alarm comic and physical. The apparently confident storytellers prove vulnerable to the same fears they have been debating.
evidence: like the antennæ of startled insects

questions.prompt: How does the sap-and-bud comparison qualify the apparent suddenness of the villagers’ sympathy?
facilitatorNotes: An outward gesture may reveal a process whose beginnings were hidden. The metaphor invites readers to recognize a new relation without expecting immediate complete understanding.
evidence: there have been many circulations of the sap before we detect the smallest sign of the bud.

questions.prompt: Why is Silas’s apology to Jem a decisive action within a scene still full of confused talk?
facilitatorNotes: He accepts the alibi and acknowledges that his suspicion lacks evidence. His conduct matters especially because he himself has suffered a false accusation that others refused to reconsider.
evidence: There's nothing to witness against you, Jem.

days.title: Silas Marner excerpt: Manufacturing a suspect
days.challenge: Keep an inventory of what was observed, what was suggested, and what later seems remembered.
days.focus: A community can generate agreement by reinforcing a story rather than testing it.
days.context: After the theft, a tinder-box found near Silas’s cottage makes villagers suspect an itinerant pedlar who visited earlier. Readers know Dunstan took the money.
days.contentNote: Contains xenophobic suspicion, class prejudice, and historical derogatory language about disability.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, investigation through the villagers’ discussions; from “When Godfrey Cass returned from Mrs Osgood's party at midnight, he was not much surpr” through “ntending this, when, after mid-day, he was seen setting off on horseback in the direction of Tarley.”.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator’s fertile-memory image undermine the apparent growth of evidence?
facilitatorNotes: Newly accepted facts stimulate recollections that fit the story. Increased detail is not necessarily independent corroboration; the narrator makes the process of invention visible.
evidence: as memory, when duly impregnated with ascertained facts, is sometimes surprisingly fertile

questions.prompt: What changes when a question about an earring becomes a claim about what the pedlar wore?
facilitatorNotes: Suggestion supplies a feature that witnesses later visualize confidently. Trace the route from uncertainty to certainty rather than treating every speaker as a deliberate liar.
evidence: ear-ring

questions.prompt: Why does Silas’s inability to corroborate the story irritate the villagers?
facilitatorNotes: They have invested in an explanation that also displays their helpfulness. His limited recollection obstructs their shared conclusion, although withholding an unsupported claim should make his account more reliable.
evidence: pedlar

days.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: a different door into learning
days.challenge: Compare recognition of skill with the social labels that can conceal it.
days.focus: Education that changes who is regarded as a teacher.
days.context: The museum is now operating. Addams recounts how its activities affect a daughter, working women, and craftspeople whose abilities are often overlooked.
days.contentNote: Addams writes as a settlement-house founder about immigrants and poverty. Historical ethnic labels, class assumptions, and some patronizing judgments are preserved for critical reading, not endorsed.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, Angelina’s mother through the evicted woodcarver; begins “There has been some testimony that the Labor Museum has revealed the charm of woman's primitive”; ends “taly they liked to look at wood carvings but that in America "they only made money out of you."”.

questions.prompt: Why does Angelina’s choice of entrance matter before and after visitors praise her mother?
facilitatorNotes: Separate doors initially hide association with an unfashionable immigrant parent. Using the same door publicly acknowledges a skill newly made prestigious; the spatial change makes a change of respect visible.
evidence: by the same door as did her mother

questions.prompt: Why does the necktie workers’ president refuse to call the museum talk a lecture?
facilitatorNotes: She associates lectures with outsiders improving her mind, but sees this talk as access to the material she handles daily. The distinction reveals meaningful content and ownership of learning, not an absence of intellectual interest.
evidence: getting next to the stuff you work with all the time

questions.prompt: What does the carved doorway episode reveal about the limits of simply encouraging people to use their talents?
facilitatorNotes: The same skill admired in an Italian church is treated as damage in rented housing. Recognition depends on property relations and context, so individual talent alone does not guarantee a welcoming setting.
evidence: on the ground of destroying property

days.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: who can use knowledge?
days.challenge: Analyze explanations of educational failure that implicate methods and access rather than presumed incapacity.
days.focus: Public scholarship, imagination, and the social conditions of learning.
days.context: Near the end of her memoir, Addams considers the educational methods developed at Hull-House and the difficulty of connecting expert knowledge to public questions.
days.contentNote: Addams writes as a settlement-house founder about immigrants and poverty. Historical ethnic labels, class assumptions, and some patronizing judgments are preserved for critical reading, not endorsed.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVIII, opening through the detained boy’s memory of Jean Valjean; begins “IN a paper written years ago I deplored at some length the fact that educational matters are mo”; ends “t it would be queer if I couldn't behave well for three days when he had kept it up for years."”.

questions.prompt: What circular argument does Addams expose when deprivation is used to justify withholding education?
facilitatorNotes: Denied opportunities produce limited development, then those effects are treated as proof that education is useless or improper. The reasoning reproduces its own evidence unless the cause is questioned.
evidence: We stupidly use the effect as an argument for a continuance of the cause.

questions.prompt: Why might an accurate astronomy lecture fail its audience? Does Addams ask lecturers to replace accuracy with entertainment?
facilitatorNotes: Technical novelty and jargon may miss the questions that brought listeners there. She praises direct expression of real and valuable knowledge, so accessibility need not mean abandoning accuracy.
evidence: sympathetic understanding of his audience

questions.prompt: How does the detained boy’s memory of Jean Valjean support a claim about literary education that examination scores would miss?
facilitatorNotes: He uses a fictional example to govern his own conduct under unjust treatment. The anecdote shows a possible practical and imaginative use of literature, though one report cannot establish the effect on every audience member.
evidence: had remembered the way Jean Valjean behaved

days.title: The Awakening: property, observation, and conversation
days.challenge: Notice how description allocates freedom and who becomes an object of another person’s scrutiny.
days.focus: The difference between public conversation and private experience.
days.context: The opening introduces Edna and Léonce Pontellier at a summer resort on Grand Isle, Louisiana, and Robert Lebrun, the landlady’s son.
days.contentNote: The novel examines marital control, desire outside marriage, and women’s restricted choices. Its historical racial labels and assumptions about servants are preserved for critical reading.

excerpt.locator: Chapters I–II; begins “A green and yellow parrot, which hung in a cage outside the door, kept repeating over and over:”; ends “efore dinner, he amused himself with the little Pontellier children, who were very fond of him.”.

questions.prompt: What does the comparison to damaged property add to Léonce’s complaint that Edna is sunburned? Connect it to the handling of her rings.
facilitatorNotes: The comparison makes his appraisal possessive rather than merely concerned. Returning and replacing the rings restores the ordinary marital arrangement while her body is treated as something he values and assesses.
evidence: a valuable piece of personal property

questions.prompt: Why does the shared joke become uninteresting when Edna and Robert tell Léonce? What limit does this place on an observer’s access to their relationship?
facilitatorNotes: Its force belongs to the circumstances and shared experience; a report cannot reproduce that intimacy. Léonce’s boredom does not establish that the original pleasure was trivial to them.
evidence: It did not seem half so amusing when told

questions.prompt: How does the description of Edna’s eyes differ from Robert’s face and eyes? What expectations about their inner lives does that contrast establish?
facilitatorNotes: Edna’s gaze appears turned toward inward contemplation, whereas Robert seems open and untroubled by reflection. These are introductory impressions that readers should test rather than permanent definitions.
evidence: some inward maze of contemplation or thought

days.title: The Awakening: the best husband and the mother-women
days.challenge: Hold a social judgment beside the domestic scene that complicates it.
days.focus: Motherhood as an expectation, an image, and a disputed assessment.
days.context: Léonce returns late from an evening away. The next morning’s social judgments follow a private disagreement that the other women have not witnessed.
days.contentNote: The novel examines marital control, desire outside marriage, and women’s restricted choices. Its historical racial labels and assumptions about servants are preserved for critical reading.

excerpt.locator: Chapters III–IV; begins “It was eleven o'clock that night when Mr. Pontellier returned from Klein's hotel. He was in an ”; ends “able. Mrs. Pontellier gave over being astonished, and concluded that wonders would never cease.”.

questions.prompt: How does the suspected fever turn into a judgment about Edna’s maternal duties? What does Léonce do while expecting her to act?
facilitatorNotes: A disputed observation about Raoul becomes a general accusation of neglect. Léonce invokes business duties while smoking and expecting Edna to check the child; the scene exposes an unequal allocation of care without proving which initial diagnosis was right.
evidence: If it was not a mother's place to look after children

questions.prompt: Why place the women’s praise of the best husband after Edna’s unexplained crying? Does Edna’s agreement settle the discrepancy?
facilitatorNotes: The gifts establish visible generosity, while her distress concerns something she cannot yet articulate. Knowing no better husband is a comparison within her experience, not proof that the marriage meets all her needs.
evidence: the best husband in the world

questions.prompt: What is uneasy about the image of mother-women as ministering angels? Compare that ideal with the Pontellier children’s practical behavior.
facilitatorNotes: The ideal combines exaltation with self-erasure. The children’s capacity to rise after a fall complicates the assumption that constant fluttering protection is necessary; the narration does not simply demonstrate Edna’s failure.
evidence: efface themselves as individuals

days.title: The Awakening: the sea and the remembered meadow
days.challenge: Distinguish the narrator’s access to a character’s history from what that character actually tells her companion.
days.focus: Sensory association, confession, and a divided inner life.
days.context: Edna’s attachment to Robert and friendship with Adèle Ratignolle unsettle habits of reserve. A visit to the beach opens memories of childhood and marriage.
days.contentNote: The novel examines marital control, desire outside marriage, and women’s restricted choices. Its historical racial labels and assumptions about servants are preserved for critical reading.

excerpt.locator: Chapters VI–VII; begins “Edna Pontellier could not have told why, wishing to go to the beach with Robert, she should in ”; ends “mp in her limbs and stiffness of the joints. She leaned draggingly upon his arm as they walked.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the light that begins to show Edna a way also seem to forbid it? How does the sea’s invitation sustain that uncertainty?
facilitatorNotes: Awareness reveals possibilities whose consequences and social limits remain obscure. The sea offers intimate pleasure and solitude, but its abyss prevents a reading of awakening as uncomplicated safety.
evidence: showing the way, forbids it

questions.prompt: Trace the movement from the present sea to the Kentucky meadow. How does the childhood escape from Sunday prayers change the meaning of that landscape?
facilitatorNotes: The apparently unrelated memory gains a bodily link through moving as if swimming. Running from a constraining religious atmosphere makes the meadow both freedom and directionless wandering, an ambiguity she recognizes in her present life.
evidence: as if swimming when she walked

questions.prompt: What does the narrator’s admission that Edna did not reveal everything prevent us from assuming about the conversation?
facilitatorNotes: Readers receive a fuller account of her attractions, marriage, and ambivalence about motherhood than Adèle does. The relief of candor is real but partial; the narrated history cannot be treated as a transcript of complete confession.
evidence: Edna did not reveal so much as all this

days.title: Tears
days.challenge: Compare two remembered scenes while recognizing that the speaker cannot fully recover their meaning.
days.focus: Powerful feeling that survives the loss of articulate knowledge.
days.context: The speaker recalls running hounds and a changing guard. The poem names a military tune but leaves the truths it seemed to communicate unstated.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem TEARS; begins “IT seems I have no tears left. They should have fallen--”; ends “And have forgotten since their beauty passed.”.

questions.prompt: What does the qualification about the ghosts of tears reveal about memory?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker is uncertain whether tears actually fell, yet treats their absent or remembered form as evidence of strong feeling. Memory here includes emotional traces rather than a secure report.
evidence: Their ghosts, if tears have ghosts, did fall

questions.prompt: What links the apparently unlike scenes of hounds and soldiers?
facilitatorNotes: Each joins many bodies in a vivid coordinated spectacle, one in glad movement and one in music and formation. Readers can also note the contrast between animal energy and military order.
evidence: But still all equals in their rage of gladness

questions.prompt: Why is the final admission of forgotten truths central rather than a failure to finish the poem?
facilitatorNotes: The poem preserves the experience of revelation while refusing to invent its recoverable message. Beauty’s passing and memory’s limits are part of the subject.
evidence: And have forgotten since their beauty passed.

days.title: Love Among the Ruins
days.challenge: Track repeated alternations between a vanished city, present pasture and a waiting lover.
days.focus: Private encounter measured against imperial display and historical loss.
days.context: The landscape contains a small ruin of a once-powerful city. The poem repeatedly changes its time frame; mark now and once before interpreting its final preference.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem LOVE AMONG THE RUINS; begins “Where the quiet-coloured end of evening smiles”; ends “    Love is best.”.

questions.prompt: How do the very short answering lines affect the account of the grand city?
facilitatorNotes: They interrupt expansive descriptions with compact echoes or qualifications, sometimes reducing grandeur to a brief aftersound. Compare a place where the short line enlarges a scene with one that punctures it.
evidence: (So they say)

questions.prompt: What changes when the former royal viewing place becomes the place where the girl waits?
facilitatorNotes: The same structure shifts from surveying collective power to awaiting one person. Her gaze reuses the site while changing its scale of importance.
evidence: That a girl with eager eyes and yellow hair

questions.prompt: Has the long account of splendor been unnecessary once the speaker says love is best?
facilitatorNotes: It supplies the formidable rival against which the preference is made. Readers may find the final claim convincing or too sweeping, but should account for the poem’s fascination with what it dismisses.
evidence: Love is best.

days.title: Sonnet I
days.challenge: Track an allusive opening, a vision and a sudden reversal of the speaker’s interpretation.
days.focus: How a life story organized around sorrow is interrupted by an unexpected name.
days.context: Sonnet I opens by recalling an ancient Greek poet’s image of gift-bearing years. The title of this collection does not mean these English sonnets are translations.
days.contentNote: Includes a threatening visionary figure and an initial expectation of death.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem I; begins “I thought once how Theocritus had sung”; ends “The silver answer rang, “Not Death, but Love.””.

questions.prompt: How does the speaker’s own procession of years revise the earlier image of gracious gifts?
facilitatorNotes: The expected sweetness becomes shadow and melancholy in the speaker’s remembered life. The repeated word years ties the two visions together while exposing their difference.
evidence: The sweet, sad years, the melancholy years,

questions.prompt: Why does the unidentified figure initially appear threatening?
facilitatorNotes: It approaches from behind, seizes the speaker’s hair and speaks with mastery. Those details make the guess of Death understandable rather than simply mistaken.
evidence: Behind me, and drew me backward by the hair;

questions.prompt: Does naming the figure Love remove all the earlier violence from the image?
facilitatorNotes: It overturns the speaker’s interpretation but does not erase the force of the encounter. Love may arrive as disruption rather than uncomplicated comfort; support the tonal balance you hear.
evidence: The silver answer rang, “Not Death, but Love.”

days.title: Absence
days.challenge: Separate sensory abundance from emotional satisfaction and examine the cost implied by a metaphor.
days.focus: An empty heart pictured as a cup that love fills with something bodily and vulnerable.
days.context: The speaker contrasts a moonlit room during absence with an imagined or recurrent arrival. The final blood imagery is figurative; attend to its emotional implications.
days.contentNote: Figurative blood imagery expresses emotional vulnerability.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem Absence; Macmillan 1914 printed pages 85; begins “My cup is empty to-night,”; ends “And the bitter-sweet taste of a soul.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the flower scent fail to fill the speaker’s emotional emptiness?
facilitatorNotes: The room can be rich in scent and movement while the heart remains still. The contrast locates lack in the relationship rather than in a featureless environment.
evidence: But the cup of my heart is still,

questions.prompt: What does “When you come” leave uncertain about the time of the second stanza?
facilitatorNotes: It may anticipate an arrival or describe what repeatedly happens. Either reading distinguishes its fullness from the present empty night.
evidence: When you come, it brims

questions.prompt: How does a cup of heart’s blood complicate a simple picture of romantic comfort?
facilitatorNotes: The offered drink suggests intimate giving and vulnerability, while bitter-sweet taste prevents love from being purely pleasant. Accept readings of generosity or costly dependence supported by the imagery.
evidence: And the bitter-sweet taste of a soul.

days.title: Exiled
days.challenge: Compare desired and disliked forms of noise, danger and bodily contact.
days.focus: Homesickness for a demanding coast rather than for simple quiet.
days.context: Piles are structural posts; weirs are barriers used to trap fish; a freshet is a sudden rise of water. These details make the desired Maine coast physically specific.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem EXILED; begins “SEARCHING my heart for its true sorrow,”; ends “  I have a need of water near.”.

questions.prompt: Why is it inaccurate to say the speaker wants the sea merely because it is quiet?
facilitatorNotes: The desired surf is loud, piers groan, gulls cry and a warning bell sounds. The distinction concerns familiar, meaningful sensations rather than sound level alone.
evidence: Wanting the loud sound and the soft sound

questions.prompt: What does wishing to feel fear and dread again reveal about the remembered home?
facilitatorNotes: Even danger belongs to a valued way of life. The speaker prefers an environment with known risks to the alienating city, complicating any reading of the coast as perfectly safe.
evidence: Fear once again the rising freshet,

questions.prompt: How does the wish to hold and handle things change the poem’s account of belonging?
facilitatorNotes: Belonging requires practical bodily contact, not only seeing a view or remembering happiness. The repeated need for water becomes a claim about how the speaker lives.
evidence: I have a need to hold and handle

days.title: Silas Marner excerpt: Confessing just enough
days.challenge: Identify the boundary between what Godfrey admits and what his admission is designed to conceal.
days.focus: Partial truth and paternal intimidation leave Godfrey more dependent on chance.
days.context: Godfrey must explain to his father why rent money is missing and why selling Wildfire cannot replace it. His secret marriage gives Dunstan power over him.
days.contentNote: Contains threats of disinheritance, animal death, profanity, and sexist statements about marriage.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, complete chapter; from “Godfrey rose and took his own breakfast earlier than usual, but lingered in the wains” through “ated in that religion, is the orderly sequence by which the seed brings forth a crop after its kind.”.

questions.prompt: How do the breakfast details complicate the Squire’s complaints about his sons’ idleness and his own poverty?
facilitatorNotes: His late meal, leisure, and lavish feeding of the dog expose the selective nature of his rebuke. Rank makes conduct authoritative that is not especially disciplined.
evidence: a poor man's holiday dinner

questions.prompt: Why does the father’s accurate guess about bribery fail to produce an honest conversation?
facilitatorNotes: His threatening manner and Godfrey’s fear intensify evasion. Accuracy in one inference does not create a relationship in which the son is prepared to confess.
evidence: you've been bribing him not to tell

questions.prompt: What does the narrator accomplish by extending the discussion of Chance to polished men of the present?
facilitatorNotes: The generalization prevents readers from dismissing Godfrey as merely a provincial figure of the past. Examples connect hoped-for escape with ordinary failures to accept foreseeable consequences.
evidence: Favourable Chance, I fancy, is the god of all men who follow their own devices instead of obeying a law they believe in.

days.title: Silas Marner excerpt: Kindness across an unfamiliar language
days.challenge: Separate the success of a caring act from the success of the explanation offered with it.
days.focus: Dolly’s food and goodwill reach Silas more clearly than her religious vocabulary.
days.context: After the robbery, Dolly Winthrop visits the lonely weaver with her young son Aaron and a gift of cakes. Silas’s former congregation has left him unable to trust religious consolation.
days.contentNote: Contains religious exhortation, loneliness, and historical generalizations about gender.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, Dolly Winthrop’s visit with Aaron; from “Another of Silas's comforters, besides Mr Macey, came to him with a mind highly charg” through “ that its little groove of sand was blocked up, and it wandered confusedly against dark obstruction.”.

questions.prompt: How can the letters on the cakes communicate something even though neither adult understands their meaning?
facilitatorNotes: Their doctrinal meaning remains obscure, but Dolly’s intention to offer comfort is clear. Silas can receive goodwill without sharing her interpretation of the symbol.
evidence: no possibility of misunderstanding the desire to give comfort

questions.prompt: Why do chapel, church bells, and the Christmas carol fail to connect the adults’ experiences as Dolly expects?
facilitatorNotes: She assumes familiar local practices are universal; Silas’s worship took another form. Her care is sincere, but its language does not activate the memories she imagines.
evidence: There had been no bells in Lantern Yard.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator let Silas feel relieved when Dolly leaves rather than ending with a simple scene of healing?
facilitatorNotes: The response preserves the difficulty and uneven pace of recovery. Gratitude, a small act of reciprocity toward Aaron, and continued isolation can coexist.
evidence: relieved that he might weave again and moan at his ease.

days.title: Silas Marner excerpt: The open door in the snow
days.challenge: Follow the shifts of viewpoint and separate the narrator’s causal account from Silas’s first interpretation.
days.focus: The child’s arrival joins a fatal journey to the beginning of practical care.
days.context: On New Year’s Eve, Godfrey attends a party at his family’s house while Molly, his unacknowledged wife, approaches with their daughter. Silas is alone, still mourning his stolen savings.
days.contentNote: Contains opium dependence, a mother’s death from exposure, child endangerment, and stigmatizing judgments about poverty and addiction.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, complete chapter; from “While Godfrey Cass was taking draughts of forgetfulness from the sweet presence of Na” through “ there was a human body, with the head sunk low in the furze, and half-covered with the shaken snow.”.

questions.prompt: How does the opening contrast between Godfrey and Molly establish an unequal distribution of comfort and risk?
facilitatorNotes: The party allows him to forget a bond she physically carries through the snow. The narrator judges Molly’s conduct but also asks how deprivation restricts the possibilities of clear and generous thought.
evidence: taking draughts of forgetfulness
carrying her child in her arms.

questions.prompt: What does the child perceive in the light that Silas, waiting for his money, cannot perceive?
facilitatorNotes: She responds to a moving gleam and then warmth, while he searches for a lost object and misses an actual arrival. The alternating viewpoints let readers understand an event he experiences as mysterious.
evidence: That bright living thing must be caught

questions.prompt: How do porridge and wet boots change the scene after the golden curls recall the lost coins?
facilitatorNotes: Concrete needs move Silas from astonishment and memory into action. The boots also become evidence that leads him outside to the child’s mother; symbolic resemblance does not replace practical attention.
evidence: his fingers encountered soft warm curls
the wet boots had at last suggested to Silas that the child had been walking on the snow

days.title: Silas Marner excerpt: A father who will not name himself
days.challenge: Read spoken statements beside the thoughts the narrator reveals but other characters cannot hear.
days.focus: Godfrey’s apparent helpfulness conceals a wish to escape the responsibility Silas begins to accept.
days.context: Silas carries the child to the Red House to fetch a doctor for the woman he found in the snow. Godfrey recognizes his own daughter but has kept his marriage secret.
days.contentNote: Contains a mother’s death, rejection of a child, deceptive behavior, class contempt, and descriptions of a dead body.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIII, complete chapter; from “It was after the early supper-time at the Red House, and the entertainment was in tha” through “ny other reason wanted?--well, then, that the father would be much happier without owning the child.”.

questions.prompt: How does the image of a dark by-street behind an ornamented facade shape Godfrey’s recognition of the child?
facilitatorNotes: His public respectability has hidden a connected but disowned life. The child’s entrance brings the two spaces together before he is willing to acknowledge their relation.
evidence: like a dark by-street

questions.prompt: Why does Dolly’s praise of Godfrey’s tender heart produce dramatic irony?
facilitatorNotes: She sees a young gentleman helping in the snow; readers hear his fear that Molly may survive. His concern is not wholly absent, but it competes with a desire for deliverance from obligation.
evidence: you've a tender heart
the woman might _not_ be dead

questions.prompt: What does the last paragraph expose by moving from the child’s possible happiness to the father’s certain preference?
facilitatorNotes: The imagined argument about her welfare ends by admitting his convenience. Financial support is made to substitute for acknowledgment, while the narrator’s questioning reveals the evasion.
evidence: he would do everything but own it.
the father would be much happier without owning the child.

days.title: Silas Marner excerpt: Learning to become a father
days.challenge: Read the negotiation between possessive feeling, practical instruction, and social responsibility.
days.focus: Dolly’s tact helps turn Silas’s impulse to keep the child into a sustained practice of care.
days.context: Molly has died, and Silas has decided to raise her daughter. Godfrey has supplied money without admitting that he is the father; Dolly helps with clothes and advice.
days.contentNote: Contains parental death, poverty, historical gender assumptions, and a proposed restraint for a small child.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIV, Molly’s burial through the choice of Eppie’s name; from “There was a pauper's burial that week in Raveloe, and up Kench Yard at Batherley it w” through “er his little cart as his father's made for him, and the black-and-white pup as he's got a-rearing."”.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator contrast the small public notice of Molly’s death with its force in other lives?
facilitatorNotes: The contrast challenges the idea that social invisibility measures a person’s significance. It also frames the consequences of an event whose participant received little communal attention.
evidence: charged with the force of destiny

questions.prompt: How does Dolly respond to Silas’s fear that the child will prefer another caregiver?
facilitatorNotes: She teaches him to dress the child, reassures him about the child’s affection, and gives him a task rather than displacing him. Her tact makes assistance compatible with his wish to care personally.
evidence: I can learn, I can learn.
you can put the things on

questions.prompt: What changes when the child receives a name connected to Silas’s mother and sister?
facilitatorNotes: Naming links the new relationship to a past he has largely suppressed. The discussion also shows that Silas has religious knowledge Dolly lacks, even while he accepts her guidance about local practice.
evidence: My mother's name was Hephzibah
We called her Eppie

days.title: The Awakening: learning to swim alone
days.challenge: Compare bodily achievement, perception of danger, and other people’s explanations.
days.focus: The mixed exhilaration and risk of newly discovered power.
days.context: After Mademoiselle Reisz’s piano playing has deeply moved Edna, the summer guests go down to the sea. Edna has been trying to learn to swim throughout the season.
days.contentNote: The novel examines marital control, desire outside marriage, and women’s restricted choices. Its historical racial labels and assumptions about servants are preserved for critical reading.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X; begins “At all events Robert proposed it, and there was not a dissenting voice. There was not one but w”; ends “eep. Again she watched his figure pass in and out of the strips of moonlight as he walked away.”.

questions.prompt: Why does each observer credit personal teaching for Edna’s success, while Edna thinks she has discovered the ability herself?
facilitatorNotes: The competing claims make the achievement a struggle over explanatory ownership. Lessons may have contributed, but her felt transition to unaided action cannot be reduced to any one instructor’s congratulation.
evidence: Each one congratulated himself

questions.prompt: How does the narrator qualify the distance Edna swims? Does Léonce’s assurance disprove her terror?
facilitatorNotes: The distance is small for an experienced swimmer but alarming to her untrained perception and strength. His outside measurement cannot erase the subjective encounter with danger; her triumph includes overconfidence.
evidence: what would have been a great distance for an experienced swimmer

questions.prompt: What does the final silence between Edna and Robert communicate that his invented Gulf-spirit story fails to communicate to her?
facilitatorNotes: She hears the story as banter although he has understood something of her mood. Shared silence allows desire to emerge without an adequate verbal explanation; the narrator names what the speakers leave unstated.
evidence: No multitude of words could have been more significant

days.title: The Awakening: the hammock and the departing boat
days.challenge: Test a declaration of freedom against the narration of habit, exhaustion, and impulse.
days.focus: Resistance and the uncertain meaning of choosing a direction.
days.context: After the swim, Edna remains outside in a hammock. The next morning she asks Robert to accompany her by boat to Chênière Caminada.
days.contentNote: The novel examines marital control, desire outside marriage, and women’s restricted choices. Its historical racial labels and assumptions about servants are preserved for critical reading.

excerpt.locator: Chapters XI–XII; begins “"What are you doing out here, Edna? I thought I should find you in bed," said her husband, when”; ends “hrimps, casting a look of childish ill-humor and reproach at Robert from the corner of her eye.”.

questions.prompt: What changes when Léonce moves from warning about cold and mosquitoes to saying he cannot permit her to remain?
facilitatorNotes: Practical concern gives way to explicit authority. Edna recognizes a history of unthinking compliance and refuses his manner of command, making an ordinary bedtime request reveal a marital power relation.
evidence: I can't permit you to stay out there all night

questions.prompt: Who appears to control the end of the hammock dispute, and why is a simple victory-or-defeat answer inadequate?
facilitatorNotes: Edna chooses to refuse but eventually yields to bodily exhaustion; Léonce stays until his own cigar is finished. Her new resistance is significant without giving her unlimited power over the circumstances.
evidence: The physical need for sleep

questions.prompt: How does the boat’s image of broken anchorage complicate the earlier statement that Edna follows impulse as though in alien hands?
facilitatorNotes: The sailing image feels like release and self-direction, yet the opening describes surrender of responsibility. Readers can see freedom and drift together rather than assuming every spontaneous action is fully considered agency.
evidence: freed her soul of responsibility

days.title: The Awakening: photographs, letters, and the essential self
days.challenge: Examine evidence that a longing character collects and the distinctions others cannot understand.
days.focus: The limits of substitutes for an absent person.
days.context: Robert has abruptly left for Mexico. As the Grand Isle season ends, Edna seeks traces of him in his family’s possessions and conversations.
days.contentNote: The novel examines marital control, desire outside marriage, and women’s restricted choices. Its historical racial labels and assumptions about servants are preserved for critical reading.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVI; begins “"Do you miss your friend greatly?" asked Mademoiselle Reisz one morning as she came creeping up”; ends “z, with a shrug, "rather pleasant, if it hadn't been for the mosquitoes and the Farival twins."”.

questions.prompt: Why do the album and letter attract Edna so intensely yet fail to supply the Robert she misses?
facilitatorNotes: The images preserve earlier selves, and the brief family letter supplies ordinary travel information rather than intimacy. Her minute attention to the envelope shows the emotional value she supplies to material that does not answer her central desire.
evidence: there was no recent picture

questions.prompt: Explain the difference Edna tries to draw between giving her life and giving herself. Why does Adèle find the distinction unintelligible?
facilitatorNotes: Edna is trying to protect an inward identity not exhausted by sacrifice of resources or even physical life. Adèle measures sacrifice by life as the greatest possible gift; the women are working with different definitions, and Edna admits hers is still emerging.
evidence: but I wouldn't give myself

questions.prompt: Why should Mademoiselle Reisz’s account of the Lebrun family be read cautiously even if it corrects Edna’s belief about the favorite son?
facilitatorNotes: She supplies counterevidence about money and favoritism but does so through contempt, gossip, and an uncertain memory of the quarrel. Her authority as an artist does not guarantee impartial knowledge about every person.
evidence: I don't remember what

days.title: The Awakening: visiting cards and the wedding ring
days.challenge: Connect social rituals and household objects to economic and marital authority.
days.focus: A rebellion whose material traces are quickly restored.
days.context: The Pontelliers have returned to New Orleans. Edna has stopped observing her regular Tuesday reception afternoon.
days.contentNote: The novel examines marital control, desire outside marriage, and women’s restricted choices. Its historical racial labels and assumptions about servants are preserved for critical reading.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVII; begins “The Pontelliers possessed a very charming home on Esplanade Street in New Orleans. It was a lar”; ends “Edna held out her hand, and taking the ring, slipped it upon her finger.”.

questions.prompt: What do Léonce’s comments on the visiting cards reveal about why Edna’s reception matters to him?
facilitatorNotes: The callers connect social respectability to his business interests and hierarchy of wealth. A duty presented as ordinary manners also performs unpaid work for his professional position.
evidence: His business is worth a good, round sum to me

questions.prompt: How does the cook become implicated in a conflict about Edna’s behavior? Compare the meal with Léonce’s office analogy.
facilitatorNotes: Complaints intensify during the disagreement, and he treats supervision of cooking as analogous to managing clerks. He makes Edna responsible for household performance even though she enjoys parts of the meal he rejects.
evidence: Suppose I didn't look after the clerks in my office

questions.prompt: Why end with Edna replacing the ring after failing to crush it and breaking a vase instead?
facilitatorNotes: The ring survives the symbolic attack; the vase absorbs displaced anger, and the maid restores the ordinary arrangement. The ending reveals the gap between inward refusal and changed material conditions, without proving her resistance has vanished.
evidence: slipped it upon her finger

days.title: The Awakening: the courageous soul and the withheld letter
days.challenge: Read aesthetic judgments alongside the small negotiations through which intimacy develops.
days.focus: Art, persistence, and communication through music.
days.context: In New Orleans Edna visits the pianist Mademoiselle Reisz, who has received a letter from Robert. Edna is also beginning to take painting seriously.
days.contentNote: The novel examines marital control, desire outside marriage, and women’s restricted choices. Its historical racial labels and assumptions about servants are preserved for critical reading.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXI; begins “Some people contended that the reason Mademoiselle Reisz always chose apartments up under the r”; ends “elle smoothed the letter out, restored it to the envelope, and replaced it in the table drawer.”.

questions.prompt: How does the room’s magnificent piano amid battered and dingy furnishings revise conventional measures of a successful household?
facilitatorNotes: The instrument occupies the central place usually given to display and comfort. The setting values artistic work while retaining its inconvenience and material limitations; the narrator does not turn the room into effortless glamour.
evidence: A magnificent piano crowded the apartment

questions.prompt: Why is “written about you, not to you” more than a technical distinction for Edna?
facilitatorNotes: The letter makes her central in Robert’s thoughts while maintaining a barrier against direct contact. Mademoiselle’s refusal and eventual surrender stage the difference between being a subject of conversation and an acknowledged recipient.
evidence: It was written about you, not to you

questions.prompt: What does Edna’s persistence demonstrate about the courageous soul, and what does it leave unproved?
facilitatorNotes: She risks frankness and persists with an abrasive companion, but winning a letter is not evidence of artistic talent or sustained creative courage. Music releases feeling while the question of her artistic achievement remains open.
evidence: The soul that dares and defies

days.title: Rain
days.challenge: Follow a shift from solitary sensation to imagined suffering and then to a qualified abstract claim.
days.focus: The unstable relation between cleansing, compassion and the desire for an end to disappointment.
days.context: The speaker listens to rain in a hut at night. Treat statements about death as the voice of this poem, whose final qualifications should be examined rather than converted into advice.
days.contentNote: Contains sustained thoughts about death and a speaker’s wish for release. Keep interpretation distinct from endorsement.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem RAIN; begins “RAIN, midnight rain, nothing but the wild rain”; ends “Cannot, the tempest tells me, disappoint.”.

questions.prompt: How can rain be both isolating and cleansing in the opening lines?
facilitatorNotes: Its repetition fills the hut’s world and reminds the speaker of mortality, but washing also suggests renewal or release. Those meanings remain in tension.
evidence: For washing me cleaner than I have been

questions.prompt: What does the prayer for former loved ones do to the speaker’s solitude?
facilitatorNotes: Imagining others awake, dying or listening creates sympathy across separation. The speaker’s claim of isolation does not prevent concern for other people.
evidence: But here I pray that none whom once I loved

questions.prompt: How does “If love it be” complicate the final claim about loving death?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker questions the word love even while proposing death as free from disappointment. The tempest’s apparent message is a projection of this moment; readings should retain the uncertainty.
evidence: If love it be towards what is perfect and

days.title: The Patriot
days.challenge: Compare parallel public scenes while evaluating a speaker whose account cannot be independently checked.
days.focus: Volatile acclaim and the search for judgment beyond the crowd.
days.context: A condemned public figure recalls a triumphant procession a year earlier. The poem supplies this speaker’s version, not a neutral explanation of the alleged misdeeds.
days.contentNote: Includes a procession toward execution, restraints and stone-throwing.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem THE PATRIOT; begins “AN OLD STORY”; ends “'Tis God shall repay: I am safer so.”.

questions.prompt: How do the opening bells and roses contrast with the present procession?
facilitatorNotes: Public celebration becomes stones, restraints and the scaffold. The repeated anniversary makes the change sharp while leaving its causes uncertain.
evidence: Stones at me for my year's misdeeds.

questions.prompt: What does the claim to have leaped at the sun reveal and fail to reveal?
facilitatorNotes: It conveys ambition or self-sacrifice, but its grand metaphor does not tell us what the speaker actually did. It may support sympathy without proving innocence.
evidence: Alack, it was I who leaped at the sun

questions.prompt: How does the final appeal to God answer public rejection?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker imagines earthly suffering creating grounds for divine repayment. Discuss whether this offers faith, self-justification, or both, without treating the imagined judgment as independently established.
evidence: I am safer so.

days.title: Sonnet VI
days.challenge: Resolve apparent contradictions between an opening dismissal and descriptions of inseparable attachment.
days.focus: The limits of physical distance as a way to end a relationship’s inward influence.
days.context: Sonnet VI begins with a command to leave, then imagines how deeply the beloved remains present. Follow the movement from doorway and hand to pulse, taste and prayer.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem VI; begins “Go from me.  Yet I feel that I shall stand”; ends “And sees within my eyes the tears of two.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the first sentence fail to establish a clean separation?
facilitatorNotes: The immediate Yet introduces an enduring shadow. Physical departure cannot restore the earlier sense of an entirely individual life.
evidence: Yet I feel that I shall stand

questions.prompt: How does the wine-and-grapes comparison differ from the image of a shadow?
facilitatorNotes: A shadow accompanies a person from outside; grape taste is constitutive of the wine. The metaphor makes the beloved’s influence intrinsic rather than detachable.
evidence: Must taste of its own grapes.

questions.prompt: What does the final prayer reveal about the boundaries of the speaker’s self?
facilitatorNotes: Even prayer for the self contains the beloved’s name and double tears. Readers can interpret this as intimacy, loss of independence, or a tension between both.
evidence: And sees within my eyes the tears of two.

days.title: Music
days.challenge: Compare observation with fantasy and evaluate the speaker’s selective attention.
days.focus: Artistic pleasure that depends on an imagined version of its maker.
days.context: The speaker hears a neighbor’s flute from bed but also sees the musician by daylight. Reread the contrasting portraits before deciding how much trust to place in the speaker’s preferences.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem Music; Macmillan 1914 printed pages 240–241; begins “The neighbour sits in his window and plays the flute.”; ends “And I go to sleep, dreaming.”.

questions.prompt: How do the notes acquire a physical presence in the room?
facilitatorNotes: They flutter, tap, collide and later press against ears and lips. Sound becomes intimate movement and touch; these effects describe the listening experience rather than the instrument’s literal actions.
evidence: And the round notes flutter and tap about the room,

questions.prompt: What do the speaker’s daytime evasions reveal about the limits of their appreciation?
facilitatorNotes: They enjoy the music while rejecting the musician’s ordinary appearance and labor. The sky and well become excuses for avoiding a person whose sound they value.
evidence: So I do not look at him,

questions.prompt: Does the beautiful nighttime portrait reveal the neighbor or reveal the speaker? Explain.
facilitatorNotes: The phrase “I think of him” marks an imaginative transformation rather than new factual knowledge. Its elegant clothing may reveal aesthetic or social preferences in the listener; beauty and unfairness can coexist in that response.
evidence: I think of him as a young man,

days.title: Elegy Before Death
days.challenge: Follow repeated exceptions and determine how the ending revises an apparent claim of insignificance.
days.focus: Nature’s continuation beside the loss of one person’s way of seeing.
days.context: An elegy mourns a death, but this title places the act of mourning before the death it imagines. Syringas are flowering shrubs and tamaracks are trees.
days.contentNote: The poem directly imagines a loved person’s death and burial.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem ELEGY BEFORE DEATH; begins “THERE will be rose and rhododendron”; ends “  Only the grace from simple stone!”.

questions.prompt: How does the repeated “still” make the natural world seem independent of the addressed person?
facilitatorNotes: Birds, plants and weather continue without interruption. The repetition presses the claim that one death will not stop seasonal life.
evidence: Spring will not ail nor autumn falter;

questions.prompt: Why are neglected land, weeds and a useless wagon exceptions to the claim that nothing will know?
facilitatorNotes: These marginal things may have been specially attended to by this person. Their small importance to others makes the relationship distinctive rather than objectively grand.
evidence: None but yourself sets foot upon;

questions.prompt: How does the final stanza alter the meaning of beauty being lost?
facilitatorNotes: Much external beauty remains, but the person’s perception supplied light and grace to ordinary things. The repeated “Only” can sound deliberately inadequate to the magnitude of that loss.
evidence: Only the grace from simple stone!

days.title: Silas Marner excerpt: A life that cannot be hoarded
days.challenge: Test an extended contrast against the messy practical scenes that follow it.
days.focus: Eppie changes the direction of Silas’s attention, work, and relations with the village.
days.context: Dolly has helped Silas name and care for Eppie. The narrator now follows her early childhood and the changes it brings to his daily life.
days.contentNote: Contains a child’s dangerous wandering, discussion of corporal punishment, and brief confinement in a coal closet.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIV, christening through the chapter’s closing image; from “Baby _was_ christened, the rector deciding that a double baptism was the lesser risk ” through “ds a calm and bright land, so that they look no more backward; and the hand may be a little child's.”.

questions.prompt: How do the repeated contrasts between gold and Eppie redefine what it means to possess a treasure?
facilitatorNotes: Gold needs no response and repeats the same cycle; a child has changing claims that demand learning and contact with others. The contrast is about relationships and time, not simply the market value of two objects.
evidence: Unlike the gold which needed nothing
an object compacted of changes and hopes

questions.prompt: Why is the failed coal-hole punishment more than a comic interruption?
facilitatorNotes: Eppie interprets the closet as play, defeating the intended lesson. Silas must reconsider his method and bear practical costs himself; love does not supply automatic knowledge of another mind.
evidence: This total failure of the coal-hole discipline

questions.prompt: What has changed when villagers begin asking Silas questions about child-rearing?
facilitatorNotes: He becomes a person with recognizable concerns rather than an uncanny useful worker. The closing child’s-hand image enlarges these ordinary exchanges into a story of rescue through relation.
evidence: a person whose satisfactions and difficulties could be understood
the hand may be a little child's.

days.title: Silas Marner excerpt: Trust without a complete explanation
days.challenge: Distinguish admitting uncertainty from abandoning ethical judgment or refusing another person’s pain.
days.focus: Patient conversation lets Silas connect a traumatic past to a present built on care.
days.context: Sixteen years have passed since Eppie arrived. This passage looks back at the conversations through which Silas told Dolly about his false accusation, then describes Eppie’s knowledge of her origins.
days.contentNote: Contains bereavement, false accusation, religious doubt, and an obsolete recommendation of tobacco as treatment.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVI, recollected conversations with Dolly through Eppie’s knowledge of her past; from “Silas had taken to smoking a pipe daily during the last two years, having been strong” through “ came out with Silas into the sunshine, it was the first object that arrested her eyes and thoughts.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Silas’s story need several conversations instead of one decisive disclosure?
facilitatorNotes: His difficulty explaining meets Dolly’s limited experience of unfamiliar practices. Time allows her to reconsider what she has heard, making listening a process rather than instant insight.
evidence: only by fragments, and at intervals

questions.prompt: What does Dolly concede after Silas says it would have been hard to trust?
facilitatorNotes: She recognizes the gap between advising trust and living through betrayal. Her humility qualifies her confident belief in goodness and makes the exchange less like a lecture.
evidence: them things are easier said nor done

questions.prompt: How does Silas’s openness about Eppie’s mother differ from an attempt to secure her affection by hiding the past?
facilitatorNotes: He recognizes that concealment would create a barrier between them. The preserved ring and repeated story allow Eppie to wonder about her mother without undermining the fatherhood she has experienced.
evidence: a painful barrier between their minds
a little lackered box shaped like a shoe

days.title: Silas Marner excerpt: What a late confession cannot restore
days.challenge: Separate the disclosure of facts from the different judgments husband and wife draw from them.
days.focus: Nancy redirects Godfrey’s confession from fear for his marriage toward the child he failed.
days.context: Draining the stone-pit has exposed Dunstan’s remains and Silas’s stolen gold after sixteen years. Godfrey returns to Nancy, now his wife, with this discovery and another secret to disclose.
days.contentNote: Contains discovery of human remains, a reference to possible suicide, parental abandonment, and grief over a baby’s death.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVIII, complete chapter; from “Some one opened the door at the other end of the room, and Nancy felt that it was her” through “'ll go together to Silas Marner's this very night, as soon as everything's quiet at the Stone-pits."”.

questions.prompt: Why does finding Dunstan make Godfrey speak about a different secret?
facilitatorNotes: The recovered body makes concealment seem temporary and prompts him to act before another person reveals his history. His motive includes fear, but he does take a step he has repeatedly postponed.
evidence: Everything comes to light, Nancy, sooner or later.

questions.prompt: How does Nancy’s first response overturn Godfrey’s expectation of her judgment?
facilitatorNotes: He expects rejection of himself; she regrets their failure to help the child. Her response exposes his mistaken estimate of her while leaving the lost years beyond repair.
evidence: we could have done some of our duty by the child

questions.prompt: Why does Nancy resist treating acknowledgment now as a complete solution?
facilitatorNotes: Eppie has grown up in another home, and past harm has shaped present relations. Duty remains, but the opportunity to form a particular childhood bond has passed.
evidence: It'll be different coming to us, now she's grown up

days.title: Silas Marner excerpt: An offer measured in the wrong currency
days.challenge: Compare the values speakers assume are shared with the values their listeners actually express.
days.focus: Godfrey’s generous offer misreads the household’s understanding of security and belonging.
days.context: Silas’s stolen money has been recovered. Godfrey has confessed to Nancy that Eppie is his daughter, and the couple now visits Silas and Eppie intending to take her into their wealthy home.
days.contentNote: Contains class prejudice and the threat of separation within an adoptive family.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIX, recovered gold through Eppie’s first refusal; from “Between eight and nine o'clock that evening, Eppie and Silas were seated alone in the” through “ing his virtuous resolves. The agitation with which he spoke again was not quite unmixed with anger.”.

questions.prompt: Why is the recovered gold arranged as before but no longer holding Silas in the same way?
facilitatorNotes: Its physical form is unchanged, but his relationships have altered its significance. He now imagines its use for Eppie and fears losing her more than losing money.
evidence: It takes no hold of me now

questions.prompt: What do the two meanings of work reveal when Godfrey responds to Silas’s account of the loom?
facilitatorNotes: Silas remembers work as a means of surviving emotional desolation; Godfrey hears an account of earning a living. The misunderstanding anticipates his reduction of Eppie’s welfare to provision and status.
evidence: applying Marner's words simply to his bodily wants

questions.prompt: How do Eppie’s gesture and refusal answer an offer Godfrey assumes must be attractive?
facilitatorNotes: Her hand supports Silas before she speaks, making attachment visible. She refuses the role of lady and names the people she would lose, identifying goods the offer cannot supply.
evidence: I don't want to be a lady
I couldn't give up the folks I've been used to.

days.title: Silas Marner excerpt: Eppie chooses her home
days.challenge: Weigh competing claims of duty against the daughter’s own account of a good life.
days.focus: The scene tests whether repentance creates a right to rearrange other people’s attachments.
days.context: After Eppie declines the offer of a wealthy home, Godfrey reveals that he is her biological father. Silas has raised her for sixteen years without knowing this.
days.contentNote: Contains parental abandonment, class contempt, and distress at the prospect of family separation.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIX, Godfrey’s claim of fatherhood through the visitors’ departure; from “"But I have a claim on you, Eppie--the strongest of all claims. It is my duty, Marner” through “vered her husband's abrupt departure, for Godfrey had gone straight to the door, unable to say more.”.

questions.prompt: What does Silas mean when he says repentance does not alter sixteen years?
facilitatorNotes: He does not deny the value of remorse; he denies that it cancels lived relationships. Shared meals and daily thoughts supply evidence of fatherhood that a new declaration cannot reproduce.
evidence: repentance doesn't alter what's been going on for sixteen year.

questions.prompt: Why is Silas’s willingness to let Eppie answer important even though he desperately wants her to stay?
facilitatorNotes: He worries that his own wish might obstruct her welfare and relinquishes control of the answer. Contrast this self-questioning with Godfrey’s certainty that his plan is for her good.
evidence: Speak to the child. I'll hinder nothing.

questions.prompt: How does Eppie make her final answer more than a repayment of a debt to Silas?
facilitatorNotes: She describes her own desired home, familiar community, and intended marriage. Loyalty is joined to an affirmative account of what she values, challenging the assumption that higher status is an unquestionable benefit.
evidence: I can't think o' no other home.
I'm promised to marry a working man

days.title: The Awakening: a house of her own, and Arobin’s kiss
days.challenge: Trace a stated motive as dialogue and narration successively revise it.
days.focus: Edna’s new independence, the desire Arobin awakens, and how the narrator separates desire from love.
days.context: While Léonce is away and the children are with family, Edna paints and sees Alcée Arobin. She tells Mademoiselle Reisz that she plans to move to a smaller house.
days.contentNote: The novel examines marital control, desire outside marriage, and women’s restricted choices. Its historical racial labels and assumptions about servants are preserved for critical reading. Chapters XXVII–XXVIII depict Edna’s first kiss with Alcée Arobin, the desire it awakens, and her response afterward.

excerpt.locator: Chapters XXVI–XXVIII; begins “Alcée Arobin wrote Edna an elaborate note of apology, palpitant with sincerity. It embarrassed ”; ends “ve which had inflamed her, because it was not love which had held this cup of life to her lips.”.

questions.prompt: How do Edna’s successive explanations for moving change from convenience to allegiance?
facilitatorNotes: She begins with servants and upkeep, then distinguishes her husband’s resources from her own, and finally recognizes the wish to belong to herself. The narrator reveals a motive that becomes clearer during the discussion rather than a fully planned argument she brought with her.
evidence: put away her husband's bounty in casting off her allegiance

questions.prompt: What supports Edna’s claim of independence, and what practical uncertainties remain in the account?
facilitatorNotes: Inheritance, gambling winnings, and sales make resources concrete; reliance on a servant and indefinite confidence about future arrangements qualify the claim. Readers can ask about stability without denying that the shift in ownership matters.
evidence: Conditions would some way adjust themselves

questions.prompt: Why does Edna answer the question of love with Robert’s hair, eyes, and crooked finger rather than distinguished achievements?
facilitatorNotes: She rejects a calculated ranking of eligible men and locates attachment in an irreducibly particular person. The playful list cannot logically prove why she loves him, and Mademoiselle recognizes that limit.
evidence: a little finger which he can't straighten

questions.prompt: Chapter XXVIII says that among Edna’s feelings after the kiss “there was neither shame nor remorse,” only regret. What does she regret, and how does Mademoiselle Reisz’s warning about “strong wings” in Chapter XXVII frame this awakening?
facilitatorNotes: The kiss is “the first kiss of her life to which her nature had really responded,” yet she regrets that it was not “the kiss of love”; the narrator separates awakened desire from her love for Robert and adds a new “understanding” of life as “beauty and brutality.” Reisz’s image of the bird that would soar “above the level plain of tradition and prejudice” needing strong wings can be read as encouragement or as a warning about the cost of flight; readers will meet a disabled bird again in the final chapter.
evidence: it was not the kiss of love which had inflamed her

days.title: The Awakening: the imagined reunion and the actual one
days.challenge: Compare a character’s interpretation of delays and gestures with what the scene actually establishes.
days.focus: Expectation, jealous scrutiny, and indirect admissions.
days.context: Edna has moved into the small “pigeon-house.” She goes to Mademoiselle Reisz’s rooms and unexpectedly encounters Robert, who has returned from Mexico.
days.contentNote: The novel examines marital control, desire outside marriage, and women’s restricted choices. Its historical racial labels and assumptions about servants are preserved for critical reading.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXXIII; begins “It happened sometimes when Edna went to see Mademoiselle Reisz that the little musician was abs”; ends “sting his head back in his chair. They remained in silence till old Celestine announced dinner.”.

questions.prompt: What does the repeated “day before yesterday” measure for Edna beyond elapsed time?
facilitatorNotes: It marks the gap between her imagined immediate reunion and his actual delay. She treats that gap as evidence against love, but his embarrassment and later admissions permit another explanation: conflicted restraint.
evidence: day before yesterday

questions.prompt: How does Robert’s response to Arobin’s photograph complicate the freedom Edna finds in her new house?
facilitatorNotes: He questions the man’s worth and suggests returning the picture, assuming authority over her associations. Her insistence that Arobin is her friend exposes a possessive expectation even within a desired romance.
evidence: he's a friend of mine

questions.prompt: Why does Edna repeat Robert’s account of waves, beaches, and work while changing the comparison to a machine?
facilitatorNotes: The echo discloses shared longing through apparent repetition, with her small change preserving a claim to conscious activity. His accusation of cruelty suggests that mutual feeling does not make direct acknowledgment easy.
evidence: with a little more comprehension than a machine

days.title: The Awakening: freedom to choose and the promise to a friend
days.challenge: Sustain incompatible meanings of freedom even during an apparent romantic resolution.
days.focus: Love, possession, and obligations that interrupt desire.
days.context: After avoiding Edna, Robert meets her by chance in a quiet garden café. Their conversation eventually reaches the attachment each has struggled to express.
days.contentNote: The novel examines marital control, desire outside marriage, and women’s restricted choices. Its historical racial labels and assumptions about servants are preserved for critical reading.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXXVI; begins “There was a garden out in the suburbs; a small, leafy corner, with a few green tables under the”; ends “hralled his senses, had deprived him of every impulse but the longing to hold her and keep her.”.

questions.prompt: What do Robert’s openly offered excuses reveal that a successful excuse would have concealed?
facilitatorNotes: Calling them subterfuges admits deliberate avoidance while refusing its explanation. His wound image makes disclosure painful and suggests that withdrawal need not mean indifference, although Edna experiences its cost.
evidence: idiotic subterfuges

questions.prompt: Why does Edna laugh at the imagined transfer from Léonce to Robert, and why does Robert grow pale?
facilitatorNotes: Robert imagines release through a husband and another marriage; Edna denies being transferable property and claims choice in herself. His surprise shows their declarations of love have not produced agreement about the relationship’s terms.
evidence: I give myself where I choose

questions.prompt: How does Edna’s decision to keep her promise to Adèle qualify “Nothing else in the world is of any consequence”?
facilitatorNotes: She says romantic union is everything but acts on a friendship obligation when summoned for childbirth. The contradiction may reveal surviving care and duty rather than mere insincerity; Robert’s plea to stay intensifies the competing claims.
evidence: I must go to my friend

days.title: The Awakening: the return to Grand Isle (final chapter)
days.challenge: Interpret an ending that withholds direct statement by connecting its images and memories to earlier chapters.
days.focus: Whether Edna’s final swim reads as freedom, defeat, or both, and how the narration shapes that judgment.
days.context: Since the last reading, Edna left Robert to attend Adèle Ratignolle during a difficult childbirth; Adèle urged her to think of the children. When Edna returned home, Robert had gone, leaving the note “Good-by—because, I love you.” Some time later she travels alone, out of season, back to Grand Isle.
days.contentNote: The novel examines marital control, desire outside marriage, and women’s restricted choices. This final chapter describes Edna standing naked on the empty beach and swimming out beyond her strength; her death is widely read as a suicide.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXXIX (the complete final chapter); begins “Victor, with hammer and nails and scraps of scantling, was patching a corner of one of the gall”; ends “walked across the porch. There was the hum of bees, and the musky odor of pinks filled the air.”.

questions.prompt: Victor’s account of the dinner opens the chapter before Edna appears. How does his storytelling frame her, and how does her actual arrival contrast with it?
facilitatorNotes: Victor turns the dinner into legend—golden goblets, Venus, diamonds—and Mariequita imagines rendezvous and admirers. Edna arrives “tired and a little travel-stained,” wanting rest and a meal. Readers may stress the gap between public story and private condition, or the comedy of the young pair misreading her.
evidence: looking tired and a little travel-stained

questions.prompt: The narrator says Edna “was not thinking of these things when she walked down to the beach.” Where, according to the chapter, was the thinking done, and what earlier statement to Adèle does she now understand?
facilitatorNotes: The thinking happened during the sleepless night after Robert left; the walk itself is “rather mechanical.” She now understands her claim that she would give up the unessential but never sacrifice herself for her children. Students may read the swim as a settled decision or as a drift the chapter refuses to narrate as a choice; the phrase “a way to elude them” supports discussion of both.
evidence: she would give up the unessential, but she would never sacrifice herself for her children

questions.prompt: The bird with a broken wing appears just before Edna stands naked “like some new-born creature.” How do these two images pull against each other?
facilitatorNotes: Birth language suggests liberation and a new self; the disabled bird circling “down, down to the water” suggests failure or a fall. Some readers take the ending as triumph over possession, others as defeat by the forces she resisted; the chapter places both images side by side and lets neither cancel the other. Readers may connect the disabled bird to Mademoiselle Reisz’s remark in Chapter XXVII that the bird that would soar above tradition “must have strong wings.”
evidence: A bird with a broken wing was beating the air above

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter end with sense memories—her father’s and sister’s voices, a chained dog, the cavalry officer’s spurs, bees, the smell of pinks—rather than with a direct statement of what happens?
facilitatorNotes: The final paragraph withholds an explicit statement and returns to the Kentucky childhood and the cavalry officer recalled in the beach conversation of Chapter VII, read earlier this year, as well as the blue-grass meadow. Readers infer the outcome; they can debate whether the return to childhood feels like release, regression, or the beginning of an awakening that ends where it started.
evidence: the musky odor of pinks filled the air

days.title: Ethan Frome: gathering a story from gaps
days.challenge: Distinguish information supplied by witnesses from the frame narrator’s organizing assumptions.
days.focus: How a community’s silences shape a story.
days.context: An unnamed visiting engineer recalls his first encounters with Ethan Frome in Starkfield, Massachusetts. A disabling accident lies twenty-four years in the past.
days.contentNote: These novel excerpts depict poverty, disability, caregiving burdens, marital dissatisfaction, and desire outside marriage. The narrator’s descriptions and historical assumptions invite scrutiny.

excerpt.locator: Prologue, opening through Harmon’s account of Ethan’s family burdens; begins “I HAD the story, bit by bit, from various people, and, as generally happens in such cases, each”; ends “nd trouble: that's what Ethan's had his plate full up with, ever since the very first helping."”.

questions.prompt: Why begin by saying each informant told a different story? What does that admission ask us to do with the narrator’s later reconstruction?
facilitatorNotes: It establishes mediation and incomplete agreement before offering vivid detail. The account may reveal emotional truth, but it cannot simply be treated as an unfiltered record of witnessed events.
evidence: each time it was a different story

questions.prompt: How does “too many winters” develop from Harmon’s comment into the narrator’s explanation? Identify where observation becomes inference.
facilitatorNotes: The narrator experiences harsh weather and imagines its cumulative effects on Ethan’s youth. The siege imagery makes isolation persuasive, yet the leap from climate to a particular life remains an interpretation.
evidence: the nucleus about which I grouped my subsequent inferences

questions.prompt: Why does Mrs. Hale’s refusal to tell the story attract the narrator more than plentiful local anecdotes? What ethical tension accompanies his curiosity?
facilitatorNotes: Her distress seems to promise knowledge unavailable in ordinary gossip. He recognizes doubts about delicacy but continues pursuing information, so the reader can question whether his desire to understand entitles him to another person’s pain.
evidence: some doubts as to my delicacy

days.title: The Sign-Post
days.challenge: Track multiple voices and separate literal directions from questions about an entire life.
days.focus: Uncertainty, mortality and renewed attachment to the possibility of choosing.
days.context: A traveler pauses at a finger-post, a sign giving road directions. The ensuing conversation may be read as dialogue, internal debate, or both; the poem does not conclusively identify its voices.
days.contentNote: Includes remembered despair and discussion of death; the final return to lived experience is open to interpretation.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem THE SIGN-POST; begins “THE dim sea glints chill. The white sun is shy.”; ends “Wondering where he shall journey, O where?"”.

questions.prompt: How does the second voice challenge the first voice’s confident account of being twenty?
facilitatorNotes: It recalls despair at the age the first voice idealizes as decisive. The disagreement exposes selective memory rather than establishing one simple life story.
evidence: At twenty you wished you had never been born.

questions.prompt: Why describe death as a remedy that is freely given?
facilitatorNotes: The phrase grimly treats burial as an end to regret, but its apparent consolation carries a cost: the ending also removes the ability to desire. Tone may mix humor, unease and resistance.
evidence: A mouthful of earth to remedy all

questions.prompt: How does the closing return to wondering about a journey change the opening indecision?
facilitatorNotes: What first looked like a problem becomes part of being upright, outdoors and alive. The poem can value the freedom to wonder without providing a chosen destination.
evidence: Wondering where he shall journey, O where?

days.title: Fears and Scruples
days.challenge: Distinguish reported evidence, emotional gratitude and hypothetical objections in an extended analogy.
days.focus: The tension between faith in a relationship and demands for verifiable grounds.
days.context: The poem begins as an account of an absent friend and ends by proposing a religious analogy. Read the argument once without anticipating the last word, then reconsider each earlier claim.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem FEARS AND SCRUPLES; begins “Here's my case. Of old I used to love him.”; ends “  What if this friend happen to be--God?”.

questions.prompt: Why do beautiful letters and famous actions stop functioning as secure proof?
facilitatorNotes: The letters’ authorship is disputed and the actions are known by hearsay or claimed by others. The speaker’s attachment exceeds what can be conclusively verified.
evidence: Only knew of actions by hearsay:

questions.prompt: What remains valuable to the speaker even if the friend’s existence or conduct is uncertain?
facilitatorNotes: The experience of trust has shaped how the speaker lives and feels gratitude. The poem distinguishes a belief’s emotional effect from the truth of its grounds.
evidence: Thanks for truth--tho' falsehood, gained--tho' lost.

questions.prompt: How does the final word alter the force of the accusation that the friend is a monster?
facilitatorNotes: It applies standards of reciprocal human friendship to a possible divine relationship. Readers may see critique, troubled faith or unresolved inquiry; the hypothetical wording prevents a single compulsory verdict.
evidence: What if this friend happen to be--God?

days.title: Sonnet XIII
days.challenge: Read a highly articulate poem that argues for the difficulty of putting love into words.
days.focus: Silence, self-protection and the paradox of offering a poem as a refusal of proof.
days.context: Sonnet XIII uses a torch held between two faces as its first image of expression. Discuss the speaker’s own account of womanhood as a historically situated voice rather than a rule for all women.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem XIII; begins “And wilt thou have me fashion into speech”; ends “Lest one touch of this heart convey its grief.”.

questions.prompt: What dangers are built into the image of speaking as holding a torch in rough wind?
facilitatorNotes: Speech would expose both faces but might be difficult to sustain or control. The dropped torch makes the promised illumination unreliable.
evidence: And hold the torch out, while the winds are rough,

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker resist holding inner feeling at a distance as proof?
facilitatorNotes: The feeling cannot be separated from the self and displayed as an object without loss. The doubled myself and me intensify that entanglement.
evidence: From myself—me—that I should bring thee proof

questions.prompt: How does the existence of this sonnet complicate its appeal to silence?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker successfully makes a verbal form out of the limits of verbal evidence. An interpretation should account for both the eloquence and the final protection of grief.
evidence: Lest one touch of this heart convey its grief.

days.title: A Lady
days.challenge: Analyze comparisons across senses and follow a reversal in the apparent value of age and youth.
days.focus: An older person’s subtle beauty beside a younger speaker’s conspicuous energy.
days.context: A boudoir is a private sitting or dressing room, and a harpsichord is a keyboard instrument whose strings are plucked. The poem’s comparisons draw on faded interiors, sound, color and scent.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem A Lady; Macmillan 1914 printed pages 242–243; begins “You are beautiful and faded”; ends “That its sparkle may amuse you.”.

questions.prompt: How does the first line resist treating faded beauty as lost beauty?
facilitatorNotes: The conjunction holds beauty and fading together. The old tune and sunlit silk develop appeal through age and softness rather than despite an explicitly stated defect.
evidence: You are beautiful and faded

questions.prompt: What is the effect of moving from eyes to a perfume of the soul?
