facilitatorNotes: Sight gives way to scent and an inward presence. The layered sensory comparisons suggest qualities that cannot be captured by a single sharp description.
evidence: And the perfume of your soul

questions.prompt: Why compare the speaker’s vigor with a penny offered for amusement?
facilitatorNotes: A newly minted coin is bright but of small denomination, making youthful energy less rich than the other person’s subtle qualities. Discuss whether the offering is humble, theatrical, or both.
evidence: My vigour is a new-minted penny,

days.title: Spring
days.challenge: Separate acknowledgment of sensory pleasure from an argument about its insufficiency.
days.focus: A speaker who refuses to let seasonal renewal answer mortality and suffering.
days.context: April is directly addressed as if it could offer an explanation. Read the short assertions against the longer descriptive lines, and distinguish the speaker’s position from a claim the reader must accept.
days.contentNote: Contains imagery of death and decay and a historically disparaging term in the final personification.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem SPRING; begins “To what purpose, April, do you return again?”; ends “Comes like an idiot, babbling and strewing flowers.”.

questions.prompt: What evidence prevents us from calling the speaker simply blind to spring’s beauty?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker notices new leaves, sunlight, crocuses and the good smell of earth. The objection is that these pleasures do not settle the larger question.
evidence: The smell of the earth is good.

questions.prompt: How does the question after the apparent absence of death change that optimistic appearance?
facilitatorNotes: It demands significance rather than accepting a seasonal illusion of immortality. The following image of brains decaying broadens the challenge beyond a pretty surface.
evidence: But what does that signify?

questions.prompt: How do the empty cup and uncarpeted stairs prepare for the final personification of April?
facilitatorNotes: They make life feel lacking in nourishment, comfort or purpose. April’s flowers then appear like an inadequate response to that emptiness; a dissenting reader should still explain the argument being rejected.
evidence: An empty cup, a flight of uncarpeted stairs.

days.title: My Ántonia excerpt: Who gets to tell her story?
days.challenge: Distinguish the unnamed framing narrator from Jim, whose manuscript follows.
days.focus: The title’s possessive word makes personal memory both the method and the limit of the narrative.
days.context: Two childhood friends meet on a train and discuss Ántonia, a girl they knew in Nebraska. This is the novel’s original 1918 introduction.
days.contentNote: Contains dismissive judgments about a woman’s political and artistic activity; those judgments belong to the fictional narrator.

excerpt.locator: Original 1918 Introduction, complete section; from “LAST summer I happened to be crossing the plains of Iowa in a season of intense heat,” through “ever written, but the following narrative is Jim’s manuscript, substantially as he brought it to me.”.

questions.prompt: How does the train’s landscape help the two friends claim a special kind of shared knowledge?
facilitatorNotes: Heat, dust, and weather revive bodily memories, and the friends describe their childhood knowledge as exclusive. Ask what their intimacy enables and what their claim that outsiders cannot understand might exclude.
evidence: It was a kind of freemasonry, we said.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator’s account of Genevieve complicate our trust in the frame?
facilitatorNotes: Specific public actions are followed by assertions about motives the narrator cannot directly know. Readers can recognize a candidly stated dislike without treating every judgment as established fact.
evidence: Another is that I do not like his wife.
I am never able to believe that she has much feeling for the causes

questions.prompt: What does adding “My” change after Jim first writes “Ántonia” on the portfolio?
facilitatorNotes: It identifies a version shaped by his experience rather than an exhaustive life of another person. His claim of unarranged recollection also becomes something readers can test against the narrative’s apparent design.
evidence: It’s through myself that I knew and felt her
making it “My Ántonia.”

days.title: My Ántonia excerpt: Beyond the familiar sky
days.challenge: Separate a bereaved child’s perceptions from the adult narrator’s shaping images.
days.focus: The journey west changes the meaning of scale, belonging, and the stories Jim carries with him.
days.context: Ten-year-old Jim has lost both parents and travels from Virginia to live with his grandparents in Nebraska. Jake, a young farm worker, accompanies him.
days.contentNote: Contains parental bereavement, xenophobic speech, and stereotyped comparisons involving Indigenous people. An illustration caption and its separate footnote marker are omitted.

excerpt.locator: Book I, chapter I, complete chapter; from “I FIRST heard of Ántonia on what seemed to me an interminable journey across the grea” through “felt erased, blotted out. I did not say my prayers that night: here, I felt, what would be would be.”.
excerpt.inlineReason: The night omits the footnote marker after the first narrative “Ántonia”, as its edition declares; the library text keeps Cather’s pronunciation footnote and its anchor (“Ántonia[1]”), so this passage is no longer an exact range of the work.

blocks.text: I FIRST heard of Ántonia on what seemed to me an interminable journey across the great midland plain of North America. I was ten years old then; I had lost both my father and mother within a year, and my Virginia relatives were sending me out to my grandparents, who lived in Nebraska. I traveled in the care of a mountain boy, Jake Marpole, one of the “hands” on my father’s old farm under the Blue Ridge, who was now going West to work for my grandfather. Jake’s experience of the world was not much wider than mine. He had never been in a railway train until the morning when we set out together to try our fortunes in a new world.

We went all the way in day-coaches, becoming more sticky and grimy with each stage of the journey. Jake bought everything the newsboys offered him: candy, oranges, brass collar buttons, a watch-charm, and for me a “Life of Jesse James,” which I remember as one of the most satisfactory books I have ever read. Beyond Chicago we were under the protection of a friendly passenger conductor, who knew all about the country to which we were going and gave us a great deal of advice in exchange for our confidence. He seemed to us an experienced and worldly man who had been almost everywhere; in his conversation he threw out lightly the names of distant States and cities. He wore the rings and pins and badges of different fraternal orders to which he belonged. Even his cuff-buttons were engraved with hieroglyphics, and he was more inscribed than an Egyptian obelisk. Once when he sat down to chat, he told us that in the immigrant car ahead there was a family from “across the water” whose destination was the same as ours.

“They can’t any of them speak English, except one little girl, and all she can say is ‘We go Black Hawk, Nebraska.’ She’s not much older than you, twelve or thirteen, maybe, and she’s as bright as a new dollar. Don’t you want to go ahead and see her, Jimmy? She’s got the pretty brown eyes, too!”
This last remark made me bashful, and I shook my head and settled down to “Jesse James.” Jake nodded at me approvingly and said you were likely to get diseases from foreigners.

I do not remember crossing the Missouri River, or anything about the long day’s journey through Nebraska. Probably by that time I had crossed so many rivers that I was dull to them. The only thing very noticeable about Nebraska was that it was still, all day long, Nebraska.

I had been sleeping, curled up in a red plush seat, for a long while when we reached Black Hawk. Jake roused me and took me by the hand. We stumbled down from the train to a wooden siding, where men were running about with lanterns. I could n’t see any town, or even distant lights; we were surrounded by utter darkness. The engine was panting heavily after its long run. In the red glow from the fire-box, a group of people stood huddled together on the platform, encumbered by bundles and boxes. I knew this must be the immigrant family the conductor had told us about. The woman wore a fringed shawl tied over her head, and she carried a little tin trunk in her arms, hugging it as if it were a baby. There was an old man, tall and stooped. Two half-grown boys and a girl stood holding oil-cloth bundles, and a little girl clung to her mother’s skirts. Presently a man with a lantern approached them and began to talk, shouting and exclaiming. I pricked up my ears, for it was positively the first time I had ever heard a foreign tongue.

Another lantern came along. A bantering voice called out: “Hello, are you Mr. Burden’s folks? If you are, it’s me you’re looking for. I’m Otto Fuchs. I’m Mr. Burden’s hired man, and I’m to drive you out. Hello, Jimmy, ain’t you scared to come so far west?”

I looked up with interest at the new face in the lantern light. He might have stepped out of the pages of “Jesse James.” He wore a sombrero hat, with a wide leather band and a bright buckle, and the ends of his mustache were twisted up stiffly, like little horns. He looked lively and ferocious, I thought, and as if he had a history. A long scar ran across one cheek and drew the corner of his mouth up in a sinister curl. The top of his left ear was gone, and his skin was brown as an Indian’s. Surely this was the face of a desperado. As he walked about the platform in his high-heeled boots, looking for our trunks, I saw that he was a rather slight man, quick and wiry, and light on his feet. He told us we had a long night drive ahead of us, and had better be on the hike. He led us to a hitching-bar where two farm wagons were tied, and I saw the foreign family crowding into one of them. The other was for us. Jake got on the front seat with Otto Fuchs, and I rode on the straw in the bottom of the wagon-box, covered up with a buffalo hide. The immigrants rumbled off into the empty darkness, and we followed them.

I tried to go to sleep, but the jolting made me bite my tongue, and I soon began to ache all over. When the straw settled down I had a hard bed. Cautiously I slipped from under the buffalo hide, got up on my knees and peered over the side of the wagon. There seemed to be nothing to see; no fences, no creeks or trees, no hills or fields. If there was a road, I could not make it out in the faint starlight. There was nothing but land: not a country at all, but the material out of which countries are made. No, there was nothing but land—slightly undulating, I knew, because often our wheels ground against the brake as we went down into a hollow and lurched up again on the other side. I had the feeling that the world was left behind, that we had got over the edge of it, and were outside man’s jurisdiction. I had never before looked up at the sky when there was not a familiar mountain ridge against it. But this was the complete dome of heaven, all there was of it. I did not believe that my dead father and mother were watching me from up there; they would still be looking for me at the sheep-fold down by the creek, or along the white road that led to the mountain pastures. I had left even their spirits behind me. The wagon jolted on, carrying me I knew not whither. I don’t think I was homesick. If we never arrived anywhere, it did not matter. Between that earth and that sky I felt erased, blotted out. I did not say my prayers that night: here, I felt, what would be would be.

questions.prompt: How does the Life of Jesse James influence Jim’s first reading of Otto’s face?
facilitatorNotes: A familiar adventure story supplies a ready interpretation of an unfamiliar man. The imagined desperado contrasts with Otto’s practical role of collecting trunks and driving the newcomers home.
evidence: He might have stepped out of the pages of “Jesse James.”

questions.prompt: What do the family’s bundles, shawl, and tin trunk communicate before Jim understands their language?
facilitatorNotes: Material details show migration as an experience of carrying and protecting possessions. The trunk held like a baby invites recognition across a language gap that Jake’s remark has framed as danger.
evidence: hugging it as if it were a baby

questions.prompt: Why does the open sky fail to reassure Jim that his parents are watching over him?
facilitatorNotes: His imagined connection with them belongs to familiar places. The immense unbounded setting erases those reference points; the passage represents dislocation rather than merely scenic wonder.
evidence: I had left even their spirits behind me.
I felt erased, blotted out.

days.title: My Ántonia excerpt: Learning the shape of shelter
days.challenge: Trace how domestic detail prepares for an expansive claim about happiness.
days.focus: Care in the farmhouse allows Jim to experience the surrounding world as something he can join.
days.context: Jim wakes after his first night at his grandparents’ Nebraska farm. His grandmother begins introducing him to the household and its surroundings.
days.contentNote: Contains bereavement, a snakebite reference, and historical ethnic comparisons and plant terminology.

excerpt.locator: Book I, chapter II, complete chapter; from “I DO not remember our arrival at my grandfather’s farm sometime before daybreak, afte” through “e dissolved into something complete and great. When it comes to one, it comes as naturally as sleep.”.

questions.prompt: How does the grandmother’s change of tone join her care for Jim to her own loss?
facilitatorNotes: The brisk question becomes a recognition of her dead son in his child. Bathing, clothes, and food convey affection through action where direct discussion of grief remains difficult.
evidence: My, how you do look like your father!

questions.prompt: Why does Jim describe both the grass and the earth beneath it as moving?
facilitatorNotes: Sea and buffalo imagery turn a seemingly still landscape into active life. He also admits that railway motion may shape perception, making memory imaginative without disguising its bodily origins.
evidence: the grass was the country, as the water is the sea
Perhaps the glide of long railway travel was still with me

questions.prompt: How does the warm pumpkin support the final definition of happiness?
facilitatorNotes: A concrete resting place leads to the wish simply to exist among other living things. The reflective ending grows from touch, stillness, and attention, rather than from success or possession.
evidence: leaned my back against a warm yellow pumpkin
to be dissolved into something complete and great

days.title: My Ántonia excerpt: Words that open a world
days.challenge: Notice where the child narrator misunderstands intention despite having the more powerful language.
days.focus: The first meeting connects linguistic dependence, exploitation, generosity, and the urgency of education.
days.context: Jim’s grandparents visit the newly arrived Shimerda family with food. The family bought an inadequate homestead through Krajiek, their only local interpreter.
days.contentNote: Contains exploitative treatment of immigrants, degrading descriptions of disability, and a historical creek name using a derogatory term for Indigenous women.

excerpt.locator: Book I, chapter III, complete chapter; from “ON Sunday morning Otto Fuchs was to drive us over to make the acquaintance of our new” through “eatingly, and said with an earnestness which I shall never forget, “Te-e-ach, te-e-ach my Án-tonia!””.

questions.prompt: Why does Krajiek’s role as interpreter increase the harm of his unfair bargains?
facilitatorNotes: He controls both transactions and access to outside advice. The inability to communicate urgent needs makes language a material form of power, not merely a social inconvenience.
evidence: could tell them anything he chose

questions.prompt: What does the effort to teach Jim which word she wants reveal about Ántonia?
facilitatorNotes: She already understands the comparison between eyes and sky and must make him perceive it. The difficulty is not a lack of ideas; the gestures show that meaning precedes her English vocabulary.
evidence: her eyes fairly blazing with things she could not say

questions.prompt: How do the ring and the alphabet book create different tests of Jim’s response to generosity?
facilitatorNotes: He reads the offered ring as recklessness but confronts the father’s urgent request for teaching. Invite readers to question the boy’s assumption that his refusal fully understands the family’s values.
evidence: something reckless and extravagant
Te-e-ach, te-e-ach my Án-tonia!

days.title: My Ántonia excerpt: Routes to friendship
days.challenge: Compare received stories about unfamiliar people with encounters that complicate them.
days.focus: Mobility and hospitality widen Jim’s world while exposing the limits of his inherited judgments.
days.context: Jim now rides his pony on errands and teaches Ántonia English. Her father has found two Russian neighbors with whom he can partly communicate.
days.contentNote: Contains stereotypes about immigrants, religious persecution, and comparisons that portray exploitation through animal predation.

excerpt.locator: Book I, chapters IV and V, complete consecutive chapters; from “ON the afternoon of that same Sunday I took my first long ride on my pony, under Otto” through “red me they were very good. We had to walk the pony all the way home to keep from spilling the milk.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Jim retain the sunflower legend after admitting that botanists do not confirm it?
facilitatorNotes: The legend gives roads an emotional association with freedom. Readers can distinguish that imaginative significance from a claim of botanical evidence; memory can preserve a story while qualifying its truth.
evidence: Nevertheless, that legend has stuck in my mind

questions.prompt: How does the account of the Russians expose a weak basis for calling Pavel an anarchist?
facilitatorNotes: Observers infer political beliefs from gestures when they cannot understand his speech. The passage makes visible the transformation of unfamiliar manner into a confident label.
evidence: since he had no means of imparting his opinions

questions.prompt: What changes when Ántonia offers to interpret at Peter’s house?
facilitatorNotes: The English learner becomes Jim’s guide, and direct hospitality replaces distant impressions. Food, music, and talk of a possible daughter reveal abundance and loss within the same welcome.
evidence: she could talk to them for me
perhaps by this time he would have had a pretty daughter of his own

days.title: Ethan Frome: the book, the lost house wing, and the storm
days.challenge: Connect material clues to interpretations while keeping the narrator’s uncertainty visible.
days.focus: The difference between access to a home and access to a life.
days.context: Ethan has agreed to drive the visiting engineer to the railway. Their limited conversations and a snowstorm eventually bring the visitor inside Ethan’s house.
days.contentNote: These novel excerpts depict poverty, disability, caregiving burdens, marital dissatisfaction, and desire outside marriage. The narrator’s descriptions and historical assumptions invite scrutiny.

excerpt.locator: Prologue, Ethan begins driving the narrator through the closing claim of a vision; begins “The next morning, when I looked out, I saw the hollow-backed bay between the Varnum spruces, an”; ends “. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .”.

questions.prompt: What does Ethan’s reaction to the science book reveal that his silent daily routine does not?
facilitatorNotes: His interest and resentment at unfamiliar discoveries suggest interrupted intellectual ambitions. Borrowing the book provides evidence of curiosity but does not give the narrator the complete story he hopes it will unlock.
evidence: surprised and slightly aggrieved at his own ignorance

questions.prompt: How does the narrator make the missing L of the farmhouse stand for Ethan’s condition? What language marks this as his interpretation?
facilitatorNotes: The lost connecting wing means reduced shelter and domestic continuity; he associates it with Ethan’s damaged body. “Perhaps” and his acknowledged connection of ideas signal a symbolic reading rather than Ethan’s explicit explanation.
evidence: the image of his own shrunken body

questions.prompt: What is the effect of calling the account a “vision” after the visitor hears the woman’s voice?
facilitatorNotes: The physical visit promises a clue, but “vision” retains the imaginative character of reconstruction. Suspense increases at the doorway without establishing that the narrator can know every later private thought.
evidence: this vision of his story

days.title: Ethan Frome: watching the dance from outside
days.challenge: Identify where close narration adopts Ethan’s jealous interpretations rather than independently confirming them.
days.focus: Intellectual companionship, possession, and anxious observation.
days.context: The narrative moves back to Ethan’s youth. He waits outside a church dance to walk home with Mattie Silver, his wife Zeena’s cousin and unpaid household helper.
days.contentNote: These novel excerpts depict poverty, disability, caregiving burdens, marital dissatisfaction, and desire outside marriage. The narrator’s descriptions and historical assumptions invite scrutiny.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I; begins “THE village lay under two feet of snow, with drifts at the windy corners. In a sky of iron the ”; ends “ith Denis Eady, a throng of disregarded hints and menaces wove their cloud about his brain. . .”.

questions.prompt: How does Ethan’s image of an exhausted receiver connect the winter scene to a life beyond farm work?
facilitatorNotes: The physics comparison recalls interrupted technological study and shows that scientific learning still shapes perception. His education may not have produced a career, but its imaginative force persists.
evidence: an exhausted receiver

questions.prompt: Why is Mattie’s pleasure in dancing weak evidence for Ethan’s conclusion that she is indifferent to him?
facilitatorNotes: Her enjoyment with others need not negate affection or shared pleasure with him. The narration exposes his assumption that only he should elicit her gestures and gaiety.
evidence: her gaiety seemed plain proof of indifference

questions.prompt: How does Zeena’s remark about shaving change the significance of her previous silence?
facilitatorNotes: Ethan has mistaken lack of comment for lack of observation. The specific change she notices suggests that she has drawn inferences, though it does not reveal all she knows or plans.
evidence: now you shave every morning

days.title: Ethan Frome: a misunderstood question and the locked door
days.challenge: Separate emotional meanings from the practical stakes of a character’s reply.
days.focus: Desire, economic dependence, and the return of an excluded reality.
days.context: After the church dance, Mattie refused Denis Eady’s offer of a ride and walked home with Ethan; they planned to go coasting on School House Hill, where Ned Hale and Ruth Varnum nearly ran into the big elm. He fears losing her to marriage, while she fears losing her place in the household.
days.contentNote: These novel excerpts depict poverty, disability, caregiving burdens, marital dissatisfaction, and desire outside marriage. The narrator’s descriptions and historical assumptions invite scrutiny.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, Ethan’s shifting interpretations through entering the bedroom; begins “These alterations of mood were the despair and joy of Ethan Frome. The motions of her mind were”; ends “owered head he went up in his wife's wake, and followed her across the threshold of their room.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Ethan’s hint that Mattie will leave produce a different fear in her from the one troubling him?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks of a rival and marriage; she hears possible dismissal by Zeena. Her weak employment position changes what the same words mean, making reassurance emotionally unequal.
evidence: You mean that Zeena—ain't suited with me any more?

questions.prompt: What should prevent us from reading “Where’d I go” simply as a declaration of love?
facilitatorNotes: It names a lack of alternatives and a fear of displacement. Ethan hears warmth and feels joy, but her dependence is not evidence that staying is an unconstrained romantic choice.
evidence: Where'd I go, if I did?

questions.prompt: How do the graves and the final bedroom threshold expose a gap in Ethan’s imagined future?
facilitatorNotes: He reinterprets family graves as permanence with Mattie and briefly wishes away Zeena. The locked door and his return to the marital room restore the living relationship his fantasy omitted.
evidence: followed her across the threshold of their room

days.title: Ethan Frome: Mattie’s dependence and Zeena’s journey
days.challenge: Use background information to reassess earlier claims about character and obligation.
days.focus: Family charity, limited work, and convenient explanations.
days.context: On the morning after the dance, Ethan works outdoors and reviews Mattie’s past. At home Zeena announces a journey to consult a new doctor.
days.contentNote: These novel excerpts depict poverty, disability, caregiving burdens, marital dissatisfaction, and desire outside marriage. The narrator’s descriptions and historical assumptions invite scrutiny.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III; begins “THERE was some hauling to be done at the lower end of the wood-lot, and Ethan was out early the”; ends “she pushed the empty bottle toward Mattie: "If you can get the taste out it'll do for pickles."”.

questions.prompt: What is ironic about the relatives’ Christian duty of returning good for evil?
facilitatorNotes: They offer abundant advice but little material help, then treat Mattie’s unpaid labor as compensation for her father’s wrongdoing. The religious language exposes a mismatch between professed generosity and practical burden.
evidence: all the advice at their disposal

questions.prompt: How do Mattie’s accomplishments differ from the skills and stamina required for the available jobs?
facilitatorNotes: Music, recitation, and decorative skills give her social polish without stable earning capacity. Bookkeeping study and prolonged standing damage her health, complicating any judgment that dependence results merely from unwillingness.
evidence: her equipment, though varied, was inadequate

questions.prompt: Why does Ethan’s relief at Zeena’s trip not establish that his earlier fears were groundless?
facilitatorNotes: He interprets travel for treatment as proof of her exclusive concern with illness because her absence suits his desire. His invented cash payment then creates a new practical consequence that the convenient explanation does not solve.
evidence: there being no prospect of his receiving cash payment

days.title: Ethan Frome: how companionship became silence
days.challenge: Compare explanations of a marriage while noticing Ethan’s participation in its habits.
days.focus: Isolation, pride, and socially permitted affection.
days.context: With Zeena away, Ethan anticipates an evening with Mattie. During a delivery to town, his thoughts return to the circumstances of his marriage.
days.contentNote: These novel excerpts depict poverty, disability, caregiving burdens, marital dissatisfaction, and desire outside marriage. The narrator’s descriptions and historical assumptions invite scrutiny.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, opening through seeing Ned and Ruth together; begins “AS soon as his wife had driven off Ethan took his coat and cap from the peg. Mattie was washing”; ends “n their hearts; but he felt a pang at the thought that these two need not hide their happiness.”.

questions.prompt: How does the account of Zeena’s arrival complicate her present role as an obstacle in Ethan’s thoughts?
facilitatorNotes: Her speech, competence, and care once released him from terrifying isolation. His later dissatisfaction does not erase what he received, while his winter-versus-spring speculation exposes the contingency of his decision.
evidence: Zeena's volubility was music in his ears

questions.prompt: What does “the charge was not wholly unfounded” add to Zeena’s complaint that Ethan never listens?
facilitatorNotes: The narration acknowledges his habit of withholding replies and then attention. Her silence can have several causes, including his behavior; a purely villainous explanation of her withdrawal is insufficient.
evidence: The charge was not wholly unfounded

questions.prompt: Why can Ethan neither explain his need for an advance nor admit difficulty when Hale asks?
facilitatorNotes: The request arises from a lie to Zeena, but pride and fear of appearing insolvent block disclosure. Hale’s own costs for an engaged couple underscore the difference between publicly supported marriage and Ethan’s concealed desire.
evidence: Ethan's pride retorted before his reason had time to intervene

days.title: The Glory
days.challenge: Keep track of accumulating questions and resist treating imagined natural happiness as established fact.
days.focus: Beauty that invites participation while making the speaker feel inadequate.
days.context: The speaker confronts a vivid morning but cannot decide how to respond. On rereading, distinguish confident sensory details from tentative claims about happiness.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem THE GLORY; begins “THE glory of the beauty of the morning,--”; ends “Is Time? I cannot bite the day to the core.”.

questions.prompt: How does the same glory both invite the speaker and produce self-scorn?
facilitatorNotes: The morning offers abundant beauty, yet comparison with it makes the speaker’s own capacities seem small. The poem does not assume beauty automatically consoles.
evidence: The glory invites me, yet it leaves me scorning

questions.prompt: Why are the natural creatures called happy-seeming rather than simply happy?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker recognizes limits to human knowledge of other lives. That caution also weakens the assumption that nature possesses an uncomplicated happiness the speaker lacks.
evidence: Hearkening to short-lived happy-seeming things

questions.prompt: What does the image of biting the day to the core suggest about the kind of experience the speaker wants?
facilitatorNotes: It imagines fully consuming or penetrating the present, something questioning and time frustrate. Accept readings of appetite, urgency or impossible completeness when linked to the preceding questions.
evidence: I cannot bite the day to the core.

days.title: Prospice
days.challenge: Follow several successive metaphors without flattening a declaration of courage into literal events.
days.focus: Facing mortality through combat, ascent and anticipated reunion.
days.context: The Latin title means look forward. The speaker addresses death directly and imagines meeting a beloved beyond it; the poem voices a conviction rather than supplying evidence about an afterlife.
days.contentNote: Contemplates death, pain and a hoped-for reunion with a loved one.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem PROSPICE; begins “Fear death? to feel the fog in my throat,”; ends “  And with God be the rest!”.

questions.prompt: How do fog, storm and mountain imagery make an abstract fear bodily?
facilitatorNotes: They place difficulty in throat, face and movement toward a summit, so death becomes an encounter the reader can imagine physically.
evidence: The mist in my face,

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker reject having the eyes bandaged?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker wants to confront rather than be shielded from the final struggle. That choice links courage to awareness, not an absence of pain.
evidence: I would hate that death bandaged my eyes,

questions.prompt: How does the last sequence of peace, light and the beloved’s breast alter the battle imagery?
facilitatorNotes: The destination changes from defeating an enemy to restored intimacy. Readers can trace whether the hoped-for reunion motivates the speaker’s courage throughout.
evidence: Then a light, then thy breast,

days.title: Sonnet XXII
days.challenge: Follow a surprising preference for imperfect earthly conditions over imagined heavenly perfection.
days.focus: Intimacy protected by limitation, silence and a bounded life.
days.context: Sonnet XXII imagines two souls approaching each other. Read the move toward heaven carefully: the poem considers that ascent and then asks to remain on earth.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem XXII; begins “When our two souls stand up erect and strong,”; ends “With darkness and the death-hour rounding it.”.

questions.prompt: What does the fire at the meeting wings suggest about the strength of the encounter?
facilitatorNotes: The souls are active, erect and close enough to generate an intense shared boundary. The image can suggest transformation or dangerous intensity; use its movement rather than treating fire as one fixed symbol.
evidence: Until the lengthening wings break into fire

questions.prompt: Why might the angels’ perfect song be unwelcome?
facilitatorNotes: The lovers value their own deep silence, so even an offered perfection could intrude. The sonnet makes harmony between two people distinct from additional heavenly music.
evidence: Into our deep, dear silence.

questions.prompt: How does the final death-hour affect the claim that earthly isolation is enough?
facilitatorNotes: The space for love is limited, which can make it precious or precarious. The poem accepts that boundary while choosing the present earthly place.
evidence: With darkness and the death-hour rounding it.

days.title: The Captured Goddess
days.challenge: Track a symbolic figure across changing settings and assess the witness’s final choice.
days.focus: The transformation of freely moving beauty into something traded and confined.
days.context: The goddess is presented through fragments of color before the speaker finds her in a market. Interpret the figure from these actions and images rather than assigning one fixed meaning in advance.
days.contentNote: A symbolic woman is shown bound, exposed, cold and offered for sale.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem The Captured Goddess; Macmillan 1914 printed pages 31–33; begins “Over the housetops,”; ends “Along the narrow streets.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the poem show colors before naming the goddess?
facilitatorNotes: The reader experiences elusive impressions before a personified explanation. The delayed naming recreates a pursuit driven by sensory fascination.
evidence: I have seen a shiver of amethyst,

questions.prompt: How do the cords and commercial bids reverse the earlier flight?
facilitatorNotes: Wings that crossed open air are fastened to her body, while beauty enters an exchange of commodities. The market changes freedom into possession and valuation.
evidence: Her fluted wings were fastened to her sides with cords,

questions.prompt: How should we judge the speaker’s flight from the market?
facilitatorNotes: The response registers shame or horror but does not free the goddess. Discuss the gap between devotion as a spectator and intervention, while recognizing that the poem gives no practical rescue plan.
evidence: Hiding my face I fled,

days.title: Rosemary
days.challenge: Assess the difference between recovering the past and staging signs of it.
days.focus: Objects, household practices and old-fashioned speech used to approach vanished experience.
days.context: Rushes were used as floor covering; a crane here is a support for a cooking pot over a fire. These meanings help identify what the speaker proposes to recreate.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem ROSEMARY; begins “FOR the sake of some things”; ends “  "Alack!" and "Well-a-day!"”.

questions.prompt: How do the planned actions make memory tangible?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker changes the floor, doorway, rain collection and cooking equipment. Memory is approached through repeated domestic sensations and practices, not through description alone.
evidence: I will strew rushes

questions.prompt: What changes when the poem moves from furnishing a room to learning old expressions?
facilitatorNotes: The reconstruction becomes verbal and performative as well as material. The speaker might recover an atmosphere, but adopting phrases cannot literally restore the people or occasions.
evidence: I will learn to say,

questions.prompt: Does the poem express confident recovery or awareness of irrecoverable loss? Use its tense choices.
facilitatorNotes: Future actions coexist with statements that things are dead and gone. The ritual can honor or evoke the past without claiming to reverse that fact; different tones are possible when read aloud.
evidence: Many things be dead and gone

days.title: My Ántonia excerpt: A song carried in her hair
days.challenge: Follow one fragile sound as it links an insect, a remembered singer, and a homesick father.
days.focus: Sensory resemblance briefly restores a shared past within an unfamiliar landscape.
days.context: As the first Nebraska winter approaches, Jim and Ántonia sit outdoors for a reading lesson. Her father has struggled to feel at home since emigrating from Bohemia.
days.contentNote: Contains animal hunting, a gun, homesickness, and a historical derogatory creek name. The illustration caption is excluded.

excerpt.locator: Book I, chapter VI, complete chapter; from “ONE afternoon we were having our reading lesson on the warm, grassy bank where the ba” through “ Ántonia and her father went off hand in hand, and I buttoned up my jacket and raced my shadow home.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the insect’s thin song make Ántonia both laugh and cry?
facilitatorNotes: Its frailty recalls Old Hata, whose songs depended on children’s hospitality. The present act of warming a small creature becomes a remembered pattern of welcoming a vulnerable person.
evidence: a thin, rusty little chirp
Old Hata

questions.prompt: How does the magnificent sunset sharpen rather than cancel the father’s sadness?
facilitatorNotes: The landscape is described as triumphant while he walks without purpose. Shared beauty does not make every inhabitant experience the scene alike; his later listening creates a more particular connection.
evidence: a lifting-up of day
as if he had no purpose

questions.prompt: What does the exchange over the gun reveal that Jim’s judgment about giving things away cannot fully explain?
facilitatorNotes: The gun carries a story of the father’s musical skill and social ties. Offering it expresses a past identity and a hoped-for bond; Jim notices extravagance but may miss those meanings.
evidence: My papa play for his wedding
so full of sadness, of pity for things

days.title: My Ántonia excerpt: Making a dragon-slayer
days.challenge: Compare the encounter, its immediate retelling, and the adult narrator’s correction.
days.focus: A story of courage also reveals chance, gender expectations, and the need for an admiring witness.
days.context: Jim and Ántonia borrow a spade from Peter, then stop to investigate prairie-dog burrows. Jim resents being treated as the younger child.
days.contentNote: Contains a graphic snake killing, an ethnic slur, sexist assumptions, and inaccurate claims about rattlesnake age voiced by a child.

excerpt.locator: Book I, chapter VII, complete chapter; from “MUCH as I liked Ántonia, I hated a superior tone that she sometimes took with me. She” through “nd she never took a supercilious air with me again. I had killed a big snake—I was now a big fellow.”.

questions.prompt: How does Jim’s opening complaint shape his anger when Ántonia warns him in Bohemian?
facilitatorNotes: He wants a status reversal and resents dependence on her. His rebuke overlooks that she saw the danger first and responded under stress; language becomes a vehicle for his wounded pride.
evidence: I was a boy and she was a girl

questions.prompt: How does Ántonia’s retelling begin changing Jim’s memory before they reach home?
facilitatorNotes: Her admiration turns an involuntary cornered response into apparent chosen heroism. The adult narrator acknowledges the transformation rather than presenting the boy’s pride as a transparent record.
evidence: I began to think that I had longed for this opportunity

questions.prompt: What remains of Jim’s achievement after the adult calls it a mock adventure?
facilitatorNotes: He did act, but an available tool, an old snake, and an enthusiastic witness shaped the outcome and its reputation. Readers can credit action while questioning a self-sufficient heroic story.
evidence: the game was fixed for me by chance
to appreciate and admire

days.title: My Ántonia excerpt: A story the wolves left behind
days.challenge: Follow a story told at third hand (Pavel to Mr. Shimerda, Ántonia to Jim, Jim to the reader) and notice what each layer adds or withholds.
days.focus: How a European catastrophe enters a Nebraska childhood, and why the listeners treasure it.
days.context: In Chapter V Jim and Ántonia rode on Jim’s pony to the log house of the Russian bachelors Peter and Pavel, where Peter welcomed them; Pavel, the tall one with the hoarse cough, was not at home. Since then Jim has killed a rattlesnake and become, in Ántonia’s telling, a hero; the season is turning toward winter.
days.contentNote: Includes a dying man coughing blood and a story in which a wedding party is killed by wolves and a man throws a bride and groom from a sledge to save himself.

excerpt.locator: Book I, chapter VIII, complete chapter; from “WHILE the autumn color was growing pale on the grass and cornfields, things went badl” through “e horses, dashing through a country that looked something like Nebraska and something like Virginia.”.

questions.prompt: Before the story itself, Jim describes Pavel’s sickroom: the wind, the coyotes, the blood on the cloth. How does this setting prepare the listener, and why does Ántonia whisper “It’s wolves, Jimmy”?
facilitatorNotes: The coyotes’ howl stirs Pavel’s terror; Jim hears the wind as “defeated armies” and ghosts. The prairie night carries the old-world story into the new world, and Ántonia is the translator who first gives it shape.
evidence: It’s wolves, Jimmy

questions.prompt: The wedding story is precise about sledges, horses and words spoken, yet Pavel “never remembered exactly how he did it.” Why might the decisive act be the one blank in the account?
facilitatorNotes: Readers may see trauma, self-protection or guilt; Peter also “saw nothing.” The gap leaves listeners to judge an act the teller cannot face directly, and students may disagree about whether it excuses or condemns him.
evidence: He said he never remembered exactly how he did it

questions.prompt: What do the words “fed the bride to the wolves” do to Pavel and Peter for the rest of their lives?
facilitatorNotes: The phrase becomes a label that follows them from village to town to America, driving them into exile and bad luck. Mr. Shimerda listens and grieves for them, while the village judged them once and permanently; readers can weigh survival, cowardice and sacrifice.
evidence: the two men who had fed the bride to the wolves

questions.prompt: Jim admits the story gave him and Ántonia “a painful and peculiar pleasure.” What does this admission reveal about listening to stories of horror, and how does the last image join Russia, Nebraska and Virginia?
facilitatorNotes: The children guard the secret and relive it, taking possession of another people’s catastrophe; Jim’s imagined sledge crosses a landscape partly Nebraska and partly Virginia, so memory of immigrants’ pasts becomes part of an American childhood. Some readers find the pleasure troubling, others honest.
evidence: a painful and peculiar pleasure

days.title: My Ántonia excerpt: The work of keeping warm
days.challenge: Read descriptions of adventure beside the labor that makes a household’s security possible.
days.focus: Winter exposes dependence on practical knowledge, repeated chores, and uncelebrated generosity.
days.context: The first snow has arrived on the Nebraska prairie. Jim takes Ántonia and her sister Yulka for a sleigh ride before returning to the warmth of his grandparents’ home.
days.contentNote: Contains an unsubstantiated story of Indigenous torture, illness, and historical judgments about class and intelligence.

excerpt.locator: Book I, chapter IX, complete chapter; from “THE first snowfall came early in December. I remember how the world looked from our s” through “d helped him out of many a scrape when he did n’t realize that he was being protected by Providence.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the paragraph about the circle in the grass give two competing explanations?
facilitatorNotes: The visible mark does not establish the violent story Jake and Otto attach to it. Grandfather offers a less sensational possibility; readers can notice that Jim’s sense of an omen is yet another interpretation.
evidence: grandfather thought they merely ran races or trained horses there.

questions.prompt: How does the sleigh ride change the force of the kitchen’s comparison to a boat?
facilitatorNotes: Pleasure in open space turns to dangerous exposure as wind rises and light fades. The image makes ordinary walls and warmth a form of collective protection within a threatening environment.
evidence: like a tight little boat in a winter sea

questions.prompt: What does Otto’s account of helping with the triplets add to the claim that he has nothing to show for his labor?
facilitatorNotes: The comic embarrassment contains sustained, inconvenient care. The passage invites a measure of a life based on fidelity to people rather than money or social advancement.
evidence: though, as grandmother said, he had nothing to show for it
to carry some of them

days.title: My Ántonia excerpt: A tree full of other places
days.challenge: Trace how repurposed objects gather stories from several homes and traditions.
days.focus: A snowbound Christmas becomes a test of hospitality across religious difference.
days.context: A snowstorm prevents the Burdens from buying Christmas gifts in town. The household makes gifts and decorations, and Mr. Shimerda later visits to thank them.
days.contentNote: Contains religious difference, a historical depiction of Black people as enslaved attendants in paper decorations, and poverty. The illustration caption is excluded.

excerpt.locator: Book I, chapters XI and XII, complete consecutive chapters; from “DURING the week before Christmas, Jake was the most important person of our household” through “m, grandfather looked at me searchingly. “The prayers of all good people are good,” he said quietly.”.

questions.prompt: What do the homemade picture-book and Otto’s paper figures reveal about what the household has carried west?
facilitatorNotes: Objects preserve pieces of earlier places and relationships. The improvised holiday combines Virginia memories, Austrian gifts, and shared work rather than simply substituting poorer goods for shop purchases.
evidence: legends and stories nestled like birds in its branches

questions.prompt: Why does Jim call Jake’s and Otto’s rough faces unprotected?
facilitatorNotes: Their lack of polished social manner leaves their feelings exposed. The adult recollection reverses the assumption that roughness necessarily means emotional hardness.
evidence: what unprotected faces they were

questions.prompt: How does grandfather’s final statement clarify his restrained response when Mr. Shimerda kneels?
facilitatorNotes: He does not need to adopt the visitor’s practice to respect its sincerity. The gesture of bowing and the later sentence replace a possible doctrinal confrontation with an act of welcome.
evidence: The prayers of all good people are good

days.title: Ethan Frome: a borrowed domestic scene and the broken dish
days.challenge: Read repeated arrangements and symbolic objects without losing their practical consequences.
days.focus: The fragility of an imagined replacement household.
days.context: Ethan returns to the farm for an evening alone with Mattie. She has prepared a special supper using one of Zeena’s treasured possessions.
days.contentNote: These novel excerpts depict poverty, disability, caregiving burdens, marital dissatisfaction, and desire outside marriage. The narrator’s descriptions and historical assumptions invite scrutiny.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, the journey home through hiding the pickle-dish; begins “He fetched the grays from Hale's stable and started on his long climb back to the farm. The col”; ends “g a big log down the mountain to his mill he had never known such a thrilling sense of mastery.”.

questions.prompt: Why repeat the previous night’s doorway scene with Mattie holding the lamp in Zeena’s place?
facilitatorNotes: The identical staging makes replacement imaginable while differences in Ethan’s descriptions expose the force of desire. The household structure remains the same even as he imagines another woman within it.
evidence: She stood just as Zeena had stood

questions.prompt: Why is the broken pickle-dish more serious than an ordinary accident with a replaceable plate?
facilitatorNotes: It is a preserved wedding gift deliberately taken from a high shelf. Its use already crosses Zeena’s boundary, and its breakage threatens discovery of the evening’s attempted domestic substitution.
evidence: It was a wedding present

questions.prompt: What is troubling about Ethan’s sense of mastery after he arranges the fragments on the shelf?
facilitatorNotes: He has concealed damage rather than repaired its cause, and Mattie’s unexamining obedience gives him pride. The apparent success depends on delayed discovery, making the emotional triumph materially insecure.
evidence: the impossibility of detecting from below that the dish was broken

days.title: Ethan Frome: the last coast
days.challenge: Track how a scene of play turns into a joint decision, and weigh who is responsible for it.
days.focus: Desire, despair, and agency in the novel’s central event.
days.context: Zeena has returned from her visit to the doctor, announced that Mattie must leave to make way for a hired girl, and found the broken pickle-dish. Ethan, unable to raise money to go west with Mattie, is driving her to the train; on the way they stopped at the pond where they once met at a church picnic. Text note: the 1911 first printing used here left blanks where type failed to print; this night supplies ‘s’ in “so yourself” and ‘e’ in “under his palm” from Scribner’s Modern Student’s Library printing (copyright 1911, 1922).
days.contentNote: These novel excerpts depict poverty, disability, caregiving burdens, marital dissatisfaction, and desire outside marriage. This chapter depicts two lovers deliberately sledding into a tree to die together, and the injuries that follow.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, from “They had reached the top of School House Hill” to the end of the chapter (closing row of points omitted); begins “They had reached the top of School House Hill and Starkfield lay below them in the twilight. A ”; ends “up the hill, he heard the sorrel whinny, and thought: "I ought to be getting him his feed. . ."”.

questions.prompt: Ethan proposes the first coast. What does he want from that ride, and how does Wharton make the big elm matter before the second run?
facilitatorNotes: He wants to postpone the parting and recover the plan they missed; his boast that he can “measure distances to a hair’s-breadth” and the elm’s “deadly elbow” plant the danger. Readers can trace how a moment of play becomes the setting for what follows.
evidence: where the big elm thrust out a deadly elbow

questions.prompt: Mattie asks to be taken “Right into the big elm.” What reasons does she give, and how does Ethan’s resistance give way?
facilitatorNotes: She fears being alone and pictures a stranger sleeping in her bed; Ethan sees the stairs and “the woman who would wait for him there.” He comes to feel her as “the embodied instrument of fate”; students may debate whether that phrase shares responsibility or shifts it onto her.
evidence: So 't we'd never have to leave each other any more.

questions.prompt: Why does Ethan insist on sitting in front, and what interrupts his aim at the last instant?
facilitatorNotes: He says he wants to feel her holding him; he may also be placing himself to take the blow. Zeena’s face “thrust itself between him and his goal” and makes him swerve; readers can argue whether that image is guilt, obligation, or the marriage itself, and whether the swerve changes the outcome.
evidence: his wife's face, with twisted monstrous lineaments

questions.prompt: After the crash, Ethan mistakes Mattie’s voice for a small hurt animal. What does the sequence show, and what is the effect of ending with the sorrel’s whinny?
facilitatorNotes: Recognition comes slowly through touch and sound; the pity he feels for the “little animal” becomes horror when he finds her face. His last thought returns to the farm’s daily duty, suggesting that ordinary obligation resumes even now; some readers find this pitiful, others ironic.
evidence: I ought to be getting him his feed

days.title: Ethan Frome: the Epilogue
days.challenge: Reread the Prologue’s mysteries in light of what the reader now knows, and judge a narrator’s final verdict.
days.focus: Dramatic irony and the frame narrator’s limited knowledge.
days.context: The Epilogue returns to the night of the blizzard more than twenty years after the accident, when Ethan took the narrator into the farmhouse; the next morning the narrator talks with Mrs. Hale, who was Ruth Varnum. Text note: the 1911 first printing used here left blanks where type failed to print; this night supplies ‘r’ in “for her” and ‘s’ in “considering” from Scribner’s Modern Student’s Library printing (copyright 1911, 1922).
days.contentNote: These novel excerpts depict poverty, disability, caregiving burdens, marital dissatisfaction, and desire outside marriage. The Epilogue describes lasting disability and poverty, and a character’s view that it would have been better if Mattie had died.

excerpt.locator: Epilogue, complete (section ornament omitted); begins “THE querulous drone ceased as I entered Frome's kitchen, and of the two women sitting there I c”; ends “veyard; 'cept that down there they're all quiet, and the women have got to hold their tongues."”.

questions.prompt: At first the narrator cannot tell which woman in the kitchen has been speaking. What does the reader learn when Ethan introduces them, and why might Wharton hold back the second name until the end of the scene?
facilitatorNotes: The querulous invalid is Mattie and the tall caregiver is Zeena; delaying the name forces readers to see Mattie before recognizing her, reversing the roles the earlier chapters established.
evidence: And this is Miss Mattie Silver

questions.prompt: Mrs. Hale says the village “could never rightly tell” what Ethan and Mattie were doing coasting that night. What does the village know, and what does only the reader know?
facilitatorNotes: Gossip knew only that Zeena had sent Mattie away; readers know the decision on the hill. The gap creates dramatic irony and recalls that the Prologue’s narrator built his story from fragments; even Mrs. Hale admits “Nobody knows Zeena’s thoughts.”
evidence: could never rightly tell what she and Ethan were doing that night coasting

questions.prompt: How has Zeena changed, according to Mrs. Hale, and how does she explain it?
facilitatorNotes: The invalid has become the caregiver for twenty years; Mrs. Hale describes it as being “raised right up just when the call came to her.” Readers may see duty, endurance, a kind of power, or irony in the reversal; the text supports more than one reading.
evidence: she seemed to be raised right up just when the call came to her

questions.prompt: Mrs. Hale ends by saying she sees little difference between “the Fromes up at the farm and the Fromes down in the graveyard.” What makes this verdict so bleak, and should it be taken as the novel’s last word?
facilitatorNotes: It equates the household with the dead, except that the women still talk; the final clause turns silence into the only peace. Students may accept the verdict or push back with Ethan’s endurance, Zeena’s care, or Mrs. Hale’s own grief and partiality.
evidence: the women have got to hold their tongues

days.title: The Red Badge of Courage: rumor and the untested self
days.challenge: Compare public accounts of war, imagined heroism, and a private question that cannot yet be answered.
days.focus: The sources and limits of confidence before experience.
days.context: Henry Fleming is a young Union volunteer awaiting his first battle during the American Civil War. The opening follows camp rumor and his memories of enlistment.
days.contentNote: These war-fiction excerpts contain battlefield violence, death, injury, profanity, and historical racial language. The narrative critically examines heroic expectations and a frightened soldier’s self-justifications.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I; begins “The cold passed reluctantly from the earth, and the retiring fogs revealed an army stretched ou”; ends “of the untried men possessed a great and correct confidence. He now was in a measure reassured.”.

questions.prompt: How does the chain of supposedly reliable informants make the marching rumor sound persuasive while exposing its weakness?
facilitatorNotes: Each link borrows credibility from another person, without direct evidence reaching the listeners. Jim’s refusal to supply proof can itself appear authoritative, separating confidence from verification.
evidence: disdaining to produce proofs

questions.prompt: Why does Henry find his mother’s farewell disappointing? How do the socks, potatoes, and tears challenge his prepared scene?
facilitatorNotes: He expects ceremonial heroism and a speech about glory. Her practical care and painful moral advice refuse that performance; the mundane actions make war’s cost personal and continuous with home.
evidence: He had privately primed himself for a beautiful scene

questions.prompt: Why does Jim’s admission that he might run reassure Henry more than an absolute promise of bravery would?
facilitatorNotes: It makes uncertainty shareable and links action to the group rather than an untested essential identity. Henry discovers he may not be uniquely deficient simply because he cannot predict himself.
evidence: He had feared that all of the untried men possessed a great and correct confidence

days.title: The Red Badge of Courage: measuring courage by faces
days.challenge: Question inferences drawn from outward confidence when private experience remains hidden.
days.focus: Fear, spectacle, and the desire for another person’s confession.
days.context: The first marching rumor proves false, but Henry’s fear of his own conduct persists. Eventually the regiment moves out.
days.contentNote: These war-fiction excerpts contain battlefield violence, death, injury, profanity, and historical racial language. The narrative critically examines heroic expectations and a frightened soldier’s self-justifications.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II; begins “The next morning the youth discovered that his tall comrade had been the fast-flying messenger ”; ends “e wall of his tent until, exhausted and ill from the monotony of his suffering, he fell asleep.”.

questions.prompt: What does the comparison to a chemist clarify about Henry’s failed calculations?
facilitatorNotes: He lacks the conditions under which the relevant behavior can occur, so thought alone cannot establish his response. The analogy also shows his wish to observe himself as an experiment, a detachment battle may not permit.
evidence: with a mental slate and pencil derive an answer

questions.prompt: How does the horse-stealing incident interrupt the regiment’s grand sense of its mission?
facilitatorNotes: The soldiers become spectators in a small conflict and support the girl against one of their own. Comedy displaces heroic scale while showing a local moral judgment that does not depend on battlefield glory.
evidence: entirely ceased to remember their own large war

questions.prompt: Why does Wilson’s confidence leave Henry feeling like a mental outcast? Does their conversation establish that Wilson has no fear?
facilitatorNotes: Henry wants a confession resembling his own and hears refusal as proof of difference. Wilson’s public assurance is evidence of what he says, not complete access to his inner state; Henry’s insulting challenge also discourages candor.
evidence: He was a mental outcast

days.title: As the Team's Head-Brass
days.challenge: Follow interrupted dialogue and reconstruct a chain of counterfactual consequences.
days.focus: How distant war alters local work, chance encounters and imagined alternatives.
days.context: A seated observer speaks with a ploughman during the team’s turns. Fallow is unplanted farmland, charlock a yellow-flowered weed, and the share the cutting blade of the plough.
days.contentNote: Discusses wartime death and possible bodily injury without graphic description.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem AS THE TEAM'S HEAD-BRASS; begins “As the team's head-brass flashed out on the turn”; ends “After the ploughshare and the stumbling team.”.

questions.prompt: How does the plough’s movement determine the form of the conversation?
facilitatorNotes: The speakers can exchange words only when the team returns. The repeated long intervals make ordinary agricultural work the timing mechanism for discussion of war.
evidence: One minute and an interval of ten,

questions.prompt: How does the fallen elm connect the dead worker to the observer’s present position?
facilitatorNotes: Had the worker remained alive, the tree could have been removed, so the observer could not have sat in it. One death changes even a seemingly accidental meeting.
evidence: He had stayed here we should have moved the tree.

questions.prompt: Why does the poem place the lovers’ return beside the crumbling clods rather than ending with a clear judgment on the war?
facilitatorNotes: Ordinary desire and labor continue after the unresolved claim that seeing all might make all seem good. The ending provides movement and matter instead of proving that consolation.
evidence: The lovers came out of the wood again:

days.title: My Last Duchess
days.challenge: Infer a silent listener’s situation and weigh what a controlling speaker reveals unintentionally.
days.focus: Possession, status and the gap between a speaker’s self-image and a reader’s judgment.
days.context: A duke displays his late wife’s portrait to an envoy connected with a proposed new marriage. Ferrara is the dramatic setting. Do not assume every accusation against the duchess is true merely because the duke states it.
days.contentNote: A controlling husband implies responsibility for his wife’s death. The discussion distinguishes his claims from the poem’s presentation.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem MY LAST DUCHESS; begins “FERRARA”; ends “Which Claus of Innsbruck cast in bronze for me!”.

questions.prompt: How does the curtain anticipate the duke’s account of his marriage?
facilitatorNotes: He controls who sees the portrait, giving him a power over the image that he resented lacking over the duchess’s responses in life. The portrait can be displayed only on his terms.
evidence: The curtain I have drawn for you, but I)

questions.prompt: Why does he resent the duchess responding warmly to cherries, daylight and other ordinary gifts?
facilitatorNotes: He believes his inherited title deserves a uniquely superior response. The list may show her generosity of pleasure while he interprets it as insufficient rank-consciousness.
evidence: My gift of a nine-hundred-years-old name

questions.prompt: What can and cannot be concluded from the commands and stopped smiles?
facilitatorNotes: The juxtaposition strongly implies that his intervention ended her life or freedom, but it omits the method and details. The ending’s new marriage negotiation and tamed sea-horse extend the pattern of control.
evidence: This grew; I gave commands;

days.title: Sonnet XXIV
days.challenge: Track a sequence of protective images and ask how each changes the source of safety.
days.focus: Love imagined as shelter from social hostility, with a final limit on human power.
days.context: Sonnet XXIV first imagines the world’s sharpness as a folding knife, then turns to growing lilies. Neither image needs to be treated as a literal report of danger.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem XXIV; begins “Let the world’s sharpness like a clasping knife”; ends “God only, who made us rich, can make us poor.”.

questions.prompt: How is the threatening knife made harmless without being destroyed?
facilitatorNotes: It closes upon itself inside Love’s hand. The image redirects sharpness rather than pretending it never existed.
evidence: Let the world’s sharpness like a clasping knife

questions.prompt: What changes when the lovers become lilies rooted beyond human reach?
facilitatorNotes: Protection becomes growth and nourishment rather than a hand gripping a weapon. The flowers can draw heavenly dew while remaining vulnerable to something beyond ordinary human interference.
evidence: Alone to heavenly dews that drop not fewer;

questions.prompt: How does the last line qualify the claim of perfect safety?
facilitatorNotes: Human antagonists are diminished, but divine power remains able to alter the lovers’ condition. The ending combines confidence in shelter with recognition of a higher limit.
evidence: God only, who made us rich, can make us poor.

days.title: The Tree of Scarlet Berries
days.challenge: Distinguish visible facts, imagined effects, desire and an unsupported conclusion.
days.focus: How frustrated desire can produce a convenient explanation.
days.context: The speaker reaches for red berries in a rain-soaked garden. Track the verbs that establish what is seen, wished or merely guessed.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem The Tree of Scarlet Berries; Macmillan 1914 printed pages 94; begins “The rain gullies the garden paths”; ends “Probably, too, they are bitter.”.

questions.prompt: What changes when the speaker thinks the rain should be colored by the berries?
facilitatorNotes: The observation becomes a visual wish or expectation that redness might spread beyond the fruit. The poem does not report that the rain actually turns red.
evidence: Should be tinged with colour.

questions.prompt: How does the phrase “at the end of my arm” prepare for the failed attempt to take the fruit?
facilitatorNotes: The tree seems within reach, making desire immediately actionable. Mist and thorns then complicate this apparent accessibility.
evidence: A tree, at the end of my arm, is hazy with mist.

questions.prompt: What evidence supports the final claim that the berries are bitter, and what alternative motive might explain it?
facilitatorNotes: No tasting is reported, and “Probably” marks uncertainty. The claim may rationalize frustrated desire; a cautious prediction is also possible, but neither should be mistaken for observed flavor.
evidence: Probably, too, they are bitter.

days.title: Lament
days.challenge: Trace repeated practical instructions and hear how a final qualification unsettles them.
days.focus: Parental care continuing through grief that cannot yet explain itself.
days.context: A surviving parent speaks to children after their father’s death. Read the short lines aloud without adding a settled emotion to every repetition of the central phrase.
days.contentNote: A parent tells children that their father has died.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem LAMENT; begins “LISTEN, children:”; ends “I forget just why.”.

questions.prompt: How do clothing, pennies and keys make the father present after the opening announcement?
facilitatorNotes: His possessions enter the children’s ordinary lives through reuse and play. Their specific traces complicate the later instruction to forget the dead.
evidence: Things he used to put there,

questions.prompt: What do the breakfast and medicine instructions demonstrate that the general statements alone do not?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker continues to care for particular children and their needs. Practical responsibility operates even when a satisfactory explanation for continuing is unavailable.
evidence: Dan, take your medicine;

questions.prompt: How does the final line change the repeated insistence that life must go on?
facilitatorNotes: It exposes uncertainty beneath the phrase’s apparent authority. The speaker still acts, so a reading of total surrender should account for ongoing care.
evidence: I forget just why.

days.title: My Ántonia excerpt: The morning after a death
days.challenge: Distinguish a child’s excitement from the adults’ grief, and compare how each speaker reads the same evidence.
days.focus: How a death is reported, interpreted and imagined in one household.
days.context: After a hard winter in their sod dugout, the Shimerdas have struggled; Mr. Shimerda, a musician who never settled into prairie life, has grown more withdrawn. At Christmas he visited the Burdens and seemed, for an afternoon, content.
days.contentNote: Describes a father’s suicide by gunshot, the condition of his body, adults speculating about murder, and religious beliefs about suicide and Purgatory.

excerpt.locator: Book I, chapter XIV, complete chapter; from “XIV” through “imerda had not been rich and selfish; he had only been so unhappy that he could not live any longer.”.

questions.prompt: Jim says he “looked forward to any new crisis with delight.” How does the chapter show the gap between a child’s excitement and the adults’ grief, and does Jim’s attitude change by the end?
facilitatorNotes: He is eager, then proud of his “extension of power and authority” when left alone; by night the idea of Purgatory comes back “crushingly.” The adult narrator’s irony toward his younger self frames the change.
evidence: I looked forward to any new crisis with delight.

questions.prompt: Fuchs, Jake and grandfather read the scene in the barn differently. What does each notice, and how does grandfather propose to settle the question?
facilitatorNotes: Fuchs reads the careful preparations as deliberate; Jake suspects Krajiek because of the axe and his panic; grandfather proposes a physical test of the wound. Grandmother’s “don’t you go trying to add murder to suicide” shows how fear and evidence mix.
evidence: If he shot himself in the way they think, the gash will be torn from the inside outward.

questions.prompt: Why does Fuchs dwell on how “fixy” Mr. Shimerda was to the last—the shave, the clean shirt, the folded neckcloth?
facilitatorNotes: The details show deliberation and dignity rather than madness, and they preserve a character trait Fuchs respected. Readers may find them more painful than the violent details because they show care.
evidence: fixy he was to the last

questions.prompt: Alone in the house, Jim imagines Mr. Shimerda’s spirit resting there. How does that imagined visit differ from Ambrosch’s belief about his father’s soul, and which consolation does the chapter leave standing?
facilitatorNotes: Jim believes “homesickness” killed him and that his tired spirit rests in their house on its way home; Ambrosch and Jake speak of torment in Purgatory. Jim protests, then shudders at the idea; the final sentence, that he “had only been so unhappy that he could not live any longer,” offers his own judgment without settling the religious question.
evidence: I knew it was homesickness that had killed Mr. Shimerda

days.title: My Ántonia excerpt: Where a stranger may be buried
days.challenge: Track a community’s competing judgments about religion, custom and belonging through a series of small scenes.
days.focus: Mercy and exclusion in the burial of a man who took his own life.
days.context: Mr. Shimerda’s body lies frozen in the barn while the family waits for the coroner and a priest. Otto Fuchs has ridden to Black Hawk through deep snow to fetch them.
days.contentNote: Continues the aftermath of a suicide: a coffin is built, neighbors debate whether a suicide may be buried in their cemeteries, and the body is seen at the burial. Includes a remark about Swedes and an Italian miner in a story of mine deaths.

excerpt.locator: Book I, chapters XV and XVI, complete consecutive chapters; from “XV” through “unset. Never a tired driver passed the wooden cross, I am sure, without wishing well to the sleeper.”.

questions.prompt: Anton Jelinek and grandfather disagree about prayer for the dead. What experience grounds Jelinek’s belief, and how does grandfather answer him?
facilitatorNotes: Jelinek carried the Sacrament through a cholera camp and was untouched; grandfather states his own belief that Christ is the only intercessor yet says he “would never be the one” to deny that Jelinek was in God’s care. The scene shows respectful disagreement without resolving it.
evidence: I believe in prayer for the dead. I have seen too much.

questions.prompt: Why do the sounds of Fuchs building the coffin seem cheerful to Jim? What does the chapter suggest about work and grief?
facilitatorNotes: Skilled work seems to “promise new things for living people,” and Fuchs handles the boards as if blessing them; the incongruity with their purpose is the point. Readers can connect this to the unusual talk that fills the house during these days.
evidence: seeming to promise new things for living people

questions.prompt: The Norwegian church refuses burial and the family chooses the corner of their own land where roads may one day cross. How do grandmother, Jelinek and grandfather each respond, and what does grandfather predict?
facilitatorNotes: Grandmother is indignant and vows a more “liberal-minded” graveyard; Jelinek remembers an old custom and has promised to help; grandfather defers to the widow’s wish while predicting that the roads will not be built over the grave.
evidence: if she thinks she will live to see the people of this country ride over that old man’s head, she is mistaken

questions.prompt: Read grandfather’s graveside prayer and the final paragraph about the roads. How does the ending turn a sentence of exclusion into an image of mercy?
facilitatorNotes: The prayer refuses to judge and asks forgiveness for anyone who neglected the stranger; years later the roads swerve around the grave, “the error from the surveyed lines,” which Jim loves as “the spirit that could not carry out the sentence.” Readers may see community conscience, the land itself, or the adult narrator’s nostalgia.
evidence: the clemency of the soft earth roads

days.title: My Ántonia excerpt: The strength that costs her school
days.challenge: Hear the difference between Ántonia’s public pride in work and her private longing to learn.
days.focus: Jim’s judgments about manners obscure the unequal demands placed on his friend.
days.context: Mr. Shimerda has died by suicide during the winter. Neighbors have helped his family build a house, and fifteen-year-old Ántonia now works long days in the fields with her brother.
days.contentNote: Contains a reference to a parent’s suicide, exploitative expectations of a girl’s labor, and sexist and class-based judgments. The illustration caption is excluded.

excerpt.locator: Book I, chapter XVII, complete chapter; from “WHEN spring came, after that hard winter, one could not get enough of the nimble air.” through “ Mr. Shimerda, who could say so little, yet managed to say so much when he exclaimed, “My Án-tonia!””.

questions.prompt: How does the opening celebration of spring complicate the account of Ántonia’s new responsibilities?
facilitatorNotes: The season promises vitality and growth, but that growth includes exhausting work and a loss of educational time. Renewal is experienced differently by the observing boy and the working girl.
evidence: There was only—spring itself
Ántonia was busy with other things.

questions.prompt: What do Ántonia’s tears and later request reveal about her claim that school is for little boys?
facilitatorNotes: The boast defends an imposed role but does not eliminate her desire for knowledge. Her father’s learning remains important; she asks Jim to share what she cannot currently obtain herself.
evidence: School is all right for little boys.
you will tell me all those nice things you learn at the school

questions.prompt: What does Jim notice physically at supper that could support an interpretation other than lost refinement?
facilitatorNotes: Yawning, aching arms, and stretching are signs of fatigue after field work. Readers can assess his disappointment against evidence of exertion rather than accepting manners as the best measure of her character.
evidence: as if they ached
She was out in the fields from sun-up until sun-down.

days.title: My Ántonia excerpt: Who may dance with whom?
days.challenge: Connect a public leisure space with the economic history behind the town’s social divisions.
days.focus: The dance tent briefly brings together people whose work and origins otherwise separate them.
days.context: A traveling dancing pavilion arrives in Black Hawk. Jim enjoys its Saturday gatherings with Ántonia, Lena, Tiny, and other young women working in town.
days.contentNote: Contains ethnic and class prejudice, objectifying descriptions of women, and indirect references to pregnancies outside marriage.

excerpt.locator: Book II, chapters VIII and IX, complete consecutive chapters; from “THE Harling children and I were never happier, never felt more contented and secure, ” through “glare at young Lovett from a distance and only wished I had some way of showing my contempt for him.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the tent’s sound matter in a town whose silence seems to reprove laughter?
facilitatorNotes: Music creates a public permission for energy and sociability. Yet orderly rules and timed closing complicate any simple picture of the dances as disorder.
evidence: one could laugh aloud without being reproved by the ensuing silence

questions.prompt: How does the account of wages sent home challenge the label of unrefined hired girls?
facilitatorNotes: Their work finances machinery, debt repayment, and siblings’ schooling. The narrator contrasts the social stigma of service with its role in creating the community’s prosperity.
evidence: sent home those hard-earned dollars

questions.prompt: What does Sylvester’s marriage reveal about the limits of the tent’s neutral ground?
facilitatorNotes: He dances with Lena but hides from respectable observers and ultimately marries a property-owning widow. Attraction crosses a boundary that his choices about status preserve; Jim’s hope for a transforming marriage proves naive.
evidence: The respect for respectability was stronger than any desire
who owned a half-section

days.title: My Ántonia excerpt: A plough against the setting sun
days.challenge: Hold several speakers’ accounts of migration beside Jim’s final, highly composed image.
days.focus: A picnic connects homesickness, family labor, historical imagination, and the transformation of an ordinary tool into a symbol.
